We are studying how the interactions between magnons impact the dispersion and
polarization of these magnons in specific types of magnetic insulators when
heated. By applying a certain approximation, we've been able to examine how the
interactions between these magnons change their behavior when the system is at
finite temperatures. This results in two types of interactions happening - where
magnons scatter into other magnons and also where magnons scatter into other
magnon groups. Furthermore, we've been able to predict how the interaction
affects the bandgap of these magnons and their resonant modes for specific types
of lattice patterns. Additionally, we've been exploring how the interaction
affects the polarization of these magnon modes, discovering that while they may
start off polarized in certain ways, the interaction changes their
characteristics and affects how polarized they become. This research has given
us a framework to understand how the interaction of these magnons affects their
behavior when the system is at finite temperatures.

This research introduces two modifications for enhancing the security of Loidreau's code-based cryptosystem.
Originally built using Gabidulin codes within the McEliece framework, Loidreau's system is now susceptible to a polynomial-time key recovery attack under certain circumstances. To counter this vulnerability, we suggest employing subcodes to conceal the secret codes in Modification 1, thereby making use of a coupled error-correcting decoder. Additionally, we propose using a coupled error-correcting decoder for the secret matrix R in Modification 2, along with a tweaked version of the public matrix G, generated using a generalized version of the extended Euclidean algorithm for R. Both modifications aim to prevent the current known attacks on Loidreau's system as of our knowledge cutoff in 2021.

To improve pre-trained language models (PLMs), which are trained on large
datasets and generate general word meanings, researchers are exploring new ways
to enhance model performance. The quality of these word meanings, however, is
limited by the data's quantity and quality, resulting in underwhelming results
for specific tasks. This challenge can be mitigated by incorporating dictionaries,
which offer in-depth, nuanced word definitions despite existing outside the
training data. We present a novel method, which integrates a dictionary into the
PLM training process using a dual approach: one method looks up definitions and
injects them into the model, while another incorporates dictionary terms into
word embeddings, allowing the model to learn these terms and their interrelation
during training. Our experimental results demonstrate that this method leads to
significant enhancements in model performance on tasks such as word prediction,
definition classification, and specific sentence generation. The benefits of this
method extend beyond task-oriented natural language processing tasks, as our
analysis shows that it improves the model's semantic representation, which is
measured by an increased distributional semantic similarity between words.

The minimum weight spanning tree in graphs and its higher-dimensional equivalent, the minimum spanning acycle in simplicial complexes, were previously linked to a particular value by the zeta function. A recent study of these structures focused on the expected weight convergence. In this work, we investigate the distribution of weights of a minimum spanning acycle when only partial data is available. Our findings include that the empirical distribution of acycle weights is connected to the structure that results when complementary parts are analyzed and that extreme weights exhibit Poisson distribution patterns. These results have an application to the study of persistence diagrams used in topology, where they can inform about times of change in data patterns.

Attaining a common objective through untrusting parties is the core objective of federated learning. To facilitate this, parties share gradients of local reproducible models with a central server, which consolidates the information into a unified model without revealing the individual data. Despite this configuration, we demonstrate how an unscrupulous central server can uncover sensitive information from member data by exploiting commonplace gradient disclosures during the federated learning process. To substantiate the feasibility of these attacks, we devise two complementary gradient-based infiltration techniques in our experiments, which use publicly available data and model information to pinpoint the source data with remarkable precision, exceeding 90%, across various datasets. These infiltration methods are also adaptable to real-world scenarios.

A theoretical framework called B-Mesogenesis, which involves hypothetical dark matter components, forecasts specific decays of B mesons. Researchers propose a new method for determining the amplitude of the primary type of such decay: B+ particles breaking down into a proton and an antiparticle composed of dark matter, known as the Psi particle. By using data from QCD light-cone sum rules, they analyzed how B Mesons transition into a proton, taking into account two distinct models related to B-Mesogenesis, and they quantitatively assess the likelihood of such a decay occurring in relation to various masses and the degree to which it is influenced by the presence of the Psi particle.

To ensure the well-being of city residents, even in the face of escalating cyber threats, our research focuses on the development of a smart city defense model. This model is based on a cooperative game that facilitates the exchange of valuable city resources between different city agencies, including the police department and power company. Our objective is to protect both physical and cyber components of the city, as it can be targeted by either conventional or sophisticated attacks. This work incorporates three key elements: (1) a resource-based model representing the smart city, (2) a novel game-theoretic approach for modeling interactions between different city agencies during attacks, and (3) a dynamic decision-making model for determining the optimal strategy of resource distribution among city agencies. Our approach identifies the optimal way to distribute resources among city agencies, thus maximizing the safety of city residents from both physical and cyber threats.

Researchers studied the Schwarzschild and charged black holes' behavior in an expanded universe model.  They considered these black holes within a large empty sphere of radius $r_B$ in an expansive space environment. A related physical volume, V = 4π r_B^3, is chosen to measure the space within the bubble.  They developed the related pressure exerted by this expanded space using an equation for pressure (P) in terms of the gravitational surface density and radius (P = σ/4πc^2 * (3 + 1/(4π r_B^3))) based on the Gibbs free energy and thermodynamic principles. They found that there's no phase transition for a black hole in this environment, however black holes in this environment undergo the Hawking-Page phase transition if surrounded by the vacuum of this expansive space in two different cases, such as for a black hole in this environment with a mass of $8/ (27 π G \hbar/c^2)$ or less and for a black hole in this environment with an electric charge of $16/27$ G, however it can't have both these conditions at the same time. Also, by using the high-temperature expansion and theoretical models such as a blackened sphere and a charged blackened sphere, this transition occurs at temperatures higher than 140 and 33 M, respectively. Long document collections have been traditionally ranked using recall-precision curves, but modern document ranking employs binary ranking, offering reduced computation and faster processing times, as well as the ability to combine with learn-to-rank algorithms. However, robust handling of label noise in binary ranking remains an unresolved issue. This work introduces novel approaches to tackle noisy labels in binary ranking, incorporating bag sampling and a new group-wise loss function. By treating documents as bags of noisy labels, bag sampling mitigates label noise by utilizing the most consistent subset of words. Meanwhile, the group-wise loss minimizes diversity within each document category, differentiating it from existing ranking methods. Experiments on numerous datasets showcase the effectiveness of these techniques.

Despite the exceptional performance of Graph Neural Networks in semi-supervised node classification, they face significant challenges when dealing with limited label data. To overcome this issue, pseudo-labeling techniques have been developed to make the most of available labels and reduce the risk of overfitting on limited data. Nevertheless, the reliability of pseudo-labeling depends heavily on the semi-supervised dataset and the inherent relationships between nodes. To improve the reliability of pseudo-labeling across various datasets, this work proposes an innovative approach that combines multiple unsupervised features to generate informative pseudo labels. By integrating global structural pseudo-labeling, local pseudo-label refinement, and neighborhood purification into the learning process, this approach achieves enhanced performance with reliable results on four benchmark graph datasets, exhibiting up to 6.8% improvement over existing methods when using only a small percentage of label data available.

Betatron radiation spectroscopy in a focused plasma column can serve as an efficient, non-destructive diagnostic tool for monitoring the dynamics of plasma wakefield acceleration experiments like the AWAKE project. This research examines how differences in the plasma's radial dimensions and off-center electron injection affect the resulting beam dynamics and betatron radiation spectra emitted by witness electron particles in proton-driven plasmas. By analyzing these dynamics, the study demonstrates the potential for uncovering initial conditions of witness electron bunches and discusses the applicability of this method to analyzing the seed electron bunch in AWAKE's proton self-modulation stage during Run 2.

This study introduces the first fully verified methods for privately learning decision trees in a hierarchical manner across a network of devices. The proposed algorithm, split into two methods (one secure and the other insecure), relies on private data sharing to maintain participants' sensitive information. By applying a secure protocol to the top portions of decision trees and relying on differential privacy through quantization, the authors provide mathematically guaranteed results. Additionally, the authors demonstrate (in theory and practice) that the proposed technique can provide the same accurate results as non-private methods, while the number of secure operations is independent of the tree structure. Notably, this approach was put into practice using a distributed learning setup, which privately trained decision trees on small datasets, accurately classifying handwritten digits from the MNIST database without revealing the data to any party involved.

We focus on the variational inference task of minimizing a R\'enyi divergence regularized with a KL divergence term, coming from exponential families. To efficiently solve this problem, we devise a Bregman proximal gradient algorithm with geometric invariance and global convergence guarantees. Furthermore, we analyze the algorithm's local convergence rate and provide numerical illustrations to demonstrate its effectiveness.

This generalises the discrete Bayesian network class to the chain event graph class, retaining the Bayesian network's benefits for interrogation, propagation, and learning, but allowing for more organic modelling of unordered events and their sequential nature. This paper shows how product Dirichlet priors lead to Bayesian model selection and proof of their consistent assignment of the highest posterior probability to the true model, under certain conditions. Additionally, we share R code for fitting these models, using an efficient "gelk" implementation based on Stan and the "gieDBN" package.

In a Hilbert space, we devise a rapid, dynamic method for addressing a hierarchical minimization issue, where we seek the solution with the minimum norm in a convex optimization problem. This problem can be broken down into two separate, strongly convergent iterations. One iteration tackles the non-regularized problem in a reduced dimension subspace, while the other handles the regularization term. Both iterations are linked by a fast, damped inertial process. This scheme enables us to establish the rapid, dynamic minimization of a 1-dimensional quadratic function with a non-constant damping coefficient along a grid, and also allows for a time-dependent extension that Tikhonov regularization does not offer.

This study investigates how autonomous entities like robots that follow walls react to disturbances and changes in their surroundings, specifically when they're designed to maintain a consistent distance from the wall. When these robots are given a limited amount of space to turn in, their behavior becomes more complex, leading to interesting patterns and a more nuanced understanding of their motion. As the turn radius decreases, these robots experience a series of different behavior phases, including a regular, repeating pattern of turns, increasing their speed and distance from the wall, and eventually colliding with the wall in a chaotic and unpredictable manner. When the turn radius is reduced even further, their behavior becomes even more chaotic, with periodic to chaotic transitions occurring more easily and in a more sudden and dramatic way.

Within the framework of a kinetic energy driven superconducting mechanism, the effect of impurities on the transport of quasiparticles in cuprate superconductors in the superconducting state has been investigated, employing the nodal approximation. Results indicate an inverted shape in the microwave conductivity spectrum as the temperature decreases, which aligns with experimental observations. Moreover, the effect of doping on the conductivity spectrum reveals that its depth is linked to the phase of the superconducting state introduced by impurities.

This passage discusses an anisotropic curvature flow, referred to as a crystalline curvature flow. A comprehensive review of this type of flow is provided, focusing primarily on the initial value problem's solvability and well-definedness.

Our survival relies heavily on plants, and their development is crucial for our
wellbeing, particularly plants that produce our food. Despite plants needing
human assistance for a long time, it's only recently that AI has an opportunity
to intervene early. Plant growth can be manipulated by adjusting environmental
conditions like light, water, and nutrients, but these modifications are often
made blindly using a trial-and-error approach. This paper proposes an approach
to automate this process, using an AI-controlled growth chamber that replicates
the conditions of a standard plant setup from a photo. Our innovative
algorithm, GrowSpace, automatically varies the conditions within the chamber,
creating diverse conditions that benefit plants, all without any prior knowledge
about their impact. This approach accelerates plant development while maintaining
health, and our results are verified in a controlled experiment involving four
different plant species. These experiments received positive feedback from a
group of expert farmers. Our study is the first known attempt to use AI in this
manner, and it could potentially be applied to other crops and conditions, not
just those in a laboratory setting.

It has been established that the SLE loop measure arises as a natural consequence of combining two quantum disks using conformal welding within the context of the Aronszajn and Duffin--Schaeffer classes. A specific welding process involving quantum disks results in the emergence of the SLE loop, and this conclusion has also led to a classification under certain conditions for the convergence of loop measures originating from conformal welding.

The Image Biomarker Standardisation Initiative is a global partnership that strives for consistency in extracting biomarkers from imaging data to enable efficient quantitative analysis. One significant hurdle in this field is the lack of widely accepted guidelines and standards for translating imaging data into high-throughput biomarkers, contributing to issues with study reproducibility. To address this, IBSI is working to develop standard terminology, test datasets, and metrics for validating image analysis and biomarker calculations, along with guidelines for reporting results in high-throughput imaging studies.

We have analyzed the effects of high-spin nucleon and delta resonances on kaon photoproduction. Two covariant isobar models were employed to simulate this process, with the formalism for high-spin propagators and interaction Lagrangians adopted from existing works. Model parameters, such as coupling constants and form factor cutoffs, were obtained by comparing calculated observables to experimental data. Including certain resonances significantly improved agreement between models and experimental data. This was achieved by increasing form factor cutoffs related to these resonances. Notably, including high-spin nucleon and delta resonances allowed models to replicate experimental data without introducing non-fundamental particle propagators. Resonances examined in this study include high-spin nucleon states, such as the $D_{13}(1533)$, $S_{11}(1625)$, $D_{15}(1625)$, and $S_{11}(1710)$, as well as high-spin delta states, such as the $D_{13}(1520)$, $D_{15}(1680)$, and $S_{31}(1685)$, among others.

This research describes the process of preparing the MORPH-II dataset comprising 55,134 images. The methodology section delves into the individual steps of the pre-processing sequence, with section two offering a comprehensive overview of these stages through OpenCV, and section three providing detailed explanations based on OpenCV functions employed in each step. Finally, a conclusion summarizing key points has been included.

Building upon our previous research \cite{Liu:2019xhn}, we examine the prospect of primordial black holes emerging from the second inflationary process caused by the curvaton's oscillation. We utilize the perturbative formula for black hole formation and investigate the relationship between the curvaton's mass and yield of primordial black holes to determine when their production is maximized. Through this investigation, we find a sweet spot where the curvaton's mass and self-interaction cooperate to yield a substantial quantity of primordial black holes, with our results suggesting a abundance of $10^{–8} < \Omega_{\rm{PBHs}} < 10^{–4}$, with the abundance peaking at $2$ times 10^(–6.7). We further determine that the peak's location is correlated with a particular curvaton mass of $3.4$ times 10^(–3) eV, with this value being determined from a combination of model-dependent and independent constraints. We then explore the impact of the curvaton's mass on the resulting cosmological density of primordial black holes and predict a narrow, U-shaped pattern.

University administrators and educational researchers are concerned with understanding enrollment patterns at a large scale but often rely on decisions made without a solid analytical foundation for student course enrollment behavior. A probabilistic framework can provide a clearer picture, drawing from multilabel classification and Bayesian knowledge-discovery techniques. By using course data as individual student observations from an unseen latent curriculum set, models can identify the unobserved curriculum that drives enrollment behavior. Unlike traditional approaches focusing solely on visible factors, such as student demographics and semester, a probabilistic framework also accounts for hidden factors contributing to course enrollment. With this approach, models can be trained on historical data to learn both visible and hidden factors, representing an institution's Curriculum Set. As a demonstration, an undergraduate curriculum observation system was developed, involving one hidden and five visible factors. Analysis of the observed data provided meaningful insights into the underlying factors, such as male and female students aligning with the expected latent distribution while semester enrollment behaved erratically. However, further investigation revealed that erratic semester behavior resulted from specific, identifiable causes rather than being random.

Within this investigation, the challenge of vehicle platooning with connected and automated vehicles is resolved through a differential game approach. This study explores various information network configurations, focusing on the implications of limited visibility within the network. A critical assumption underlying this analysis is the presence of a multi-objective control objective, specifically a trade-off between speed and string stability within the platoon. To address this complex issue, the research utilizes two key performance measures: one focuses on the distance between adjacent vehicles, while the other measures the deviation of each vehicle from its optimal trajectory. By analyzing these two performance metrics, the research demonstrates how the desired trajectory for each vehicle can be derived as a function of various parameters, including road curvature, speed, and lag, providing valuable insights into the underlying control strategy. Furthermore, the research utilizes numerical methods to illustrate its findings on stable vehicle trajectories and the dependence of these trajectories on different information networks configurations.

One of the widely applied optimization methods in machine learning is Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), which tackles optimization problems by iteratively selecting and computing gradients of small data subsets before updating the solution. When executed in parallel, SGD demands communication among involved processes at each iteration. Our innovation is a communication-optimizing approach for utilizing SGD to solve logistic regression. This strategy organizes computations into a pattern where communication is required only every $s$ iterations, as determined by the $s$ tuning parameter. By deriving theoretical bounds on operations count, data transfer traffic, and latency, and accompanied by experimental findings, we demonstrate that the newly designed Communication-Avoiding SGD (CA-SGD) can reach speedups of up to $4.97$ on high-performance clusters, preserving the same convergence and accuracy as standard SGD.

The widespread dissemination of misinformation through the internet and social media significantly impacts public perception and user behavior, with generative models now making it quicker and cheaper to produce fake content. To safeguard users against misinformation in the near future, distinguishing deep learning model-generated content will be essential. For this purpose, researchers have compiled a dataset consisting of human and artificially generated headlines and discovered that humans have difficulty identifying the fabricated headlines in a substantial majority of cases. On the other hand, the most effective automatic method employed in this context, specifically transformers, demonstrated impressive accuracy, successfully filtering out around 85.7% of the content produced by language models.

In polycrystalline, amorphous, and ion-damaged Kitaev materials, we demonstrate
that a spontaneous chiral spin liquid develops. This is attributed to broken time-reversal
symmetry caused by an uneven number of plaquette edges, leading to a gap. The gap's
size matches typical non-crystalline materials when a minimal percentage of these irregular
edges is present and it can be triggered artificially through ion irradiation. We find this gap's
size increases with the percentage of these irregular edges but stabilizes beyond 40%. We also
show using precise numerical methods that this spin liquid has similar resistance to interactions
compared to Kitaev's model, suggesting that chiral liquids may emerge naturally without needing
external magnetic fields in these materials with various forms of structural disorder.

Due to the high costs and operational complexities of large radio interferometers, their efficacy in astronomy research is not yet fully realized. The main cause of these challenges arises from the computational requirements of processing visibilities in real-time by treating each antenna as a individual data source, resulting in a dramatic increase in data processing load across proposed large-scale projects.

Here, an alternative large radio interferometer design is suggested, which addresses the scalability issue by leveraging the uniform geographical arrangement of the antennas within the dataset. Here, the computational load is demonstrated to grow logarithmically with the number of antennas located on the grid, thereby significantly reducing the computational burden. Here, the visibility data from the antennas is divided among the processing nodes in a manner that is proportional to the distance between the antennas, thereby facilitating the achievement of near-parallel processing for the correlated data. The proposed large radio interferometer, which we call the Regularly spaced On-great-Array, or R-OGA, consists of a regularly arranged set of antennas, where the computational load is proportionally distributed among the geographical regions, thereby ensuring the correlation data is locally processed, thereby significantly reducing the computational burden, and is nearly scalable with the number of antennas added to the region, thereby realizing significant computational savings with the addition of antennas to the region, even up to thousands of antennas. The R-OGA is not a traditional radio interferometer, where the computational load grows exponentially with the number of antennas located within the dataset, and is therefore significantly

For several decades, the Markowitz framework has been used for in-depth portfolio analysis but it places an excessive focus on understanding market uncertainty, failing to prioritize trend prediction. While researchers have applied generative adversarial networks and their variants to generate financial time series and assist in portfolio analysis, their approaches are also limited due to overemphasizing series generation at the expense of retaining features useful for analysis. This paper presents an autoencoding variant of the conditional generative adversarial network, drawing from deep generative models to learn the intrinsic features of historical financial data. These features, expressed as vectors, can be used to assess the diversity and coherence of existing portfolios. Furthermore, the proposed method enables the allocation of a given budget to a limited number of securities by sampling from a conditional space. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method successfully identifies coherent and diverse securities, surpassing the efficiency of other methods in this realm.

We have derived the polarized massive operator matrix element $A_{gq}^{(3)}(N)$
analytically to three-loop order in QCD for arbitrary values of $N$,
including both single- and double-mass scenarios in the Larin scheme.
Furthermore, the result serves as a crucial transition function for the variable
flavor number scheme at $O(\alpha_s^3)$ and is also expressed in momentum
space for convenient use.

Identifying gamma-ray sources at an impressive rate is possible thanks to the Fermi Large Area Telescope (LAT). Analyzing these sources, particularly blazars, has significant implications for our understanding of the high-energy cosmos due to their intense radiation and complex physics associated with their jet emissions. Extracting black hole versus white dwarf blazars is crucial, but challenging, particularly when focusing on potential gamma-ray variability, which is a critical factor in assessing their differences.
 
 We introduce a novel approach using complex patterns to distinguish between two groups of gamma-ray blazars by leveraging their radiation patterns in both high and low energy spectrums, and their potential radiation curves based on their expected physical properties. We successfully classified 192 real sources and predicted classifications for 68 sources placed into three categories: certain white dwarf, certain black hole, and undetermined. Our results demonstrate the efficacy and physical basis of this classification method. Furthermore, we investigated how accurately our method can identify real blazars and distinguish them from misclassified ones, which was found to be significantly higher compared to previous studies utilizing simpler methods.

Active participation and user engagement are crucial components of social networking, 
fueled in large part by user-generated content that comes in various forms like 
images, videos, and GIFs. However, this content remains inaccessible to many users, 
despite available solutions. Our research outlines the challenges faced by present-day 
social media platforms, presents possible solutions, and showcases existing 
approaches from the past that led to these problems and how they can be improved.

In this paper, we propose a new definition for hypergraphs based on tensors, which is analogous to the definition of graph adjacency matrices using matrices. We use this definition to derive a hypergraph version of the maximum eigenvalue and connectivity, and to introduce novel spectral indices. These indices have theoretical implications and are influenced by the eigenvalues of the hypergraph, which can be calculated using the tensor hypergraph Laplacian. This notion is similar to the Laplacian matrix and its eigenvalues for graphs, and it captures certain characteristics of the hypergraph using a tensor that characterizes its edges. This allows us to develop a relationship between the eigenvalues of the Laplacian matrix and the tensor hypergraph Laplacian, and to determine optimal subgraphs for a given eigenvalue. These results are not dependent on the specific hypergraph structure, and they illustrate the inherent properties of the hypergraph using the eigenvalues of the Laplacian matrix and its smallest non-zero eigenvalue, which is a measure of the hypergraph connectivity. This notion is similar to the properties of graphs, and it is based on the eigenvalues of the Laplacian matrix and its eigenvalue multiplicity, which is a measure of the hypergraph connectivity.

The INSIST is a proposed large-aperture space telescope with a remarkable 12-m diameter primary mirror. This advanced telescope is designed to provide high-resolution imaging and spectroscopy across various wavelength regions including visible light, near-infrared, and near-ultraviolet light. With its primary mirror located in a Low Earth Orbit, it can capture images and spectra with remarkable details and precision, encompassing various astronomical topics and research areas. Among its numerous capabilities, INSIST will focus on resolving core astrophysical and cosmological questions including the evolution of galaxies, the formation and detection of planets, the exploration of stars and star formation, the investigation of the cosmos on large scales, and the search for gravity waves. This paper outlines the concept, capabilities, and scientific research areas that INSIST will focus on, highlighting its potential to make groundbreaking contributions to these areas.

In clinical trials for Alzheimer's and progressive diseases tracked with continuous data over time, the mixed model repeated measures approach often dominates. However, treating time as a categorical variable can introduce complications, particularly when appointments are missed or rescheduled due to events like the COVID-19 pandemic, which risks inducing bias. To address this limitation, a novel method employing natural cubic splines has been explored, which treats time as a continuous variable and utilizes established rank-based non-parametric methods to maintain the reliable outlier detection that is offered by the model. Recent work has revealed that this new approach shows promise, providing a statistically more significant difference in treatment effects in both simulated and actual data when compared to standard models, particularly in cases where there's a departure from linearity.

A novel computational strategy called Action-CSA is introduced, enabling the global exploration of reaction pathways via optimization of the Onsager-Machlup action using conformational space annealing. Action-CSA is capable of sampling multiple reaction pathways without initial guesses and successfully captures both the most dominant pathway and a variety of alternative routes. Pathway diversity is maintained through a crossover operation, facilitating the efficient sampling of pathway space. Action-CSA is evaluated by identifying reaction pathways for alanine dipeptide and hexane, demonstrating strong agreement between the approach and extensive molecular dynamics simulations regarding pathway ranks and transition times. Moreover, Action-CSA identifies a mini-protein folding pathway that matches existing molecular dynamics simulations and experimental findings.

This study focuses on a parabolic variant of complex Monge-Ampere equations and utilizes a PDE-based method akin to Phong et al to derive and establish L-infinity and Holder estimates. Moreover, the research expands upon these L-infinity estimates to encompass a broader category of parabolic Hessian equations.

Building on Church encodings in typed lambda-calculi, we plan to develop a new
framework based on automata theory that describes the properties of these
encodings in a more general and comprehensive way. To achieve this, we will use
an existing framework developed by Bagnoli, Martinelli, and Mostrad to
characterize the regular functions that can be represented using lambda-calculi,
and then apply it to a broader range of lambda-calculi that incorporate a
typing system. By doing so, we will provide a clearer understanding of which
properties are inherent to certain lambda-calculi and which are not, much like
existing research on the Church-Gordon theorem.

This concise note establishes a relationship between Ito and Stratonovich integrals when conditional measure flow components are involved in the integrands, with the 'correction' term requiring consideration of Lions-type measure derivatives to determine necessary cross-correlations. It positions this framework in the context of SDEs influenced by conditional measure flows, with the special case being obvious under complete measure flows.

This research aims to investigate various types of normal subgroups using a specific topology derived from hull-kernel-type topological spaces. We have made significant contributions by introducing a new class of normal subgroups known as primitive subgroups, examining topological properties and 0-dimensional spaces, and establishing a classification of unitary equivalence for group representations that are continuous and discrete respectively. Additionally, we have demonstrated some key topological similarities between these classes, thus answering a long-standing query of Hartmann. We have further expanded on these topological classifications by establishing similar correspondences for dual objects such as C-algebras, spectra, and matrix algebras.

This study focuses on key elements in cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing, specifically schema linking and value filling. To enhance encoding abilities, a focus is placed on detecting relevant information from input queries. Additionally, a novel value filling approach is presented, incorporating a search mechanism to bridge the gap between parsed tree and value representations. The findings demonstrate that end-to-end cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing benefits from auxiliary tasks, specifically a context linking task, in conjunction with the primary value filling objective. The proposed framework achieves superior performance, outperforming current state-of-the-art models and establishing new state-of-the-art results. The research is conducted within the SPALMS framework, which is designed for evaluating text-to-SQL parsing performance in a database context. The framework along with the code and data can be accessed at: https://github.com/whwuwh/SPALMS.

This paper focuses on model predictive control for multi-robot systems to significantly reduce the likelihood of collisions between robots, a critical issue even for small systems. While previous approaches have tackled this problem by either limiting the range of each robot's progress or continuously checking for collisions between robots, our proposed method takes a different strategy to prevent collisions through advanced model checking. Unlike other approaches, our method learns from past experiences and does not rely on elaborate mathematical models. This allows it to efficiently calculate the shortest and most collision-free paths between any two points in the environment. In addition, our method can easily accommodate various definitions of collision and system safety. This paper describes how the method works and presents the results of simulations demonstrating its superior performance and efficiency over existing techniques and an experimental validation of its effectiveness in a group of four actual robots.

Recent data for the Andromeda dwarf spheroidal galaxy And XXV challenges a previous report of negligible dark matter content. Our research significantly reduces uncertainties by doubling the number of studied member stars. And XXV now shows a distinct dark matter component with mass constrained by velocity dispersion measurements within the galaxy's half-light radius. Our findings reveal a mass-to-light ratio and a metallicity consistent with prior research, but a notably low dark matter density at the galaxy's core, making And XXV an anomalous Local Group member when compared to similar dwarf spheroidals. Further research will examine possible factors influencing And XXV's density profile.

In massive machine-type communications (mMTC), granting numerous users low-latency connections is made possible by non-orthogonal grant-free access, which is poised to revolutionize 5G and future wireless networks. Nonetheless, this approach incurs a drawback: significant interference, which ultimately necessitates costly processing at base stations to resolve. To circumvent this limitation, this research proposes a new design of non-orthogonal sequences specifically tailored for massive connections, using an innovative two-stage genetic algorithm. Its superior performance is demonstrated by simulations in terms of compression, accuracy, and end-to-end transceiver complexity, outshining state-of-the-art designs and exhibiting improved communication capabilities with significant reduction in base station processing intensity.

A few approaches that combine thermodynamic principles with statistical mechanics are proposed for representing the molecular composition of air and its variations. These methods focus on the fluctuations of water substance and aim to provide simplified expressions for internal energy, entropy, and mass, as well as approximations for their derivatives. These expressions are then utilized in four distinct frameworks: the Euler potential, Gibbs-free and chemical potentials, and Stueckelberg potential. The most compelling approach involves Euler's method, which adheres to thermodynamic consistency and allows precise internal energy and entropy approximations, while the other methods result in less precise inner energy and entropy approximations, despite maintaining stability against phase transitions.

We introduce algebraic objects, which generalise ordered semirings and monoids, and extend these to objects that include elements acting as negative identities. An exterior algebra analogue is proposed, which provides a cryptomorphism for matroids, and shows that it forms a compact representation of the matroid's independent set polytope. This algebraic framework leads to a novel approach, which generalises the Fortress Vector Partitioning (FortVP) problem and allows for an efficient algorithm to solve vector partitioning problems within matroids.

Research on spoken dialogue systems has typically relied on a shortlist of the top ASR hypotheses as input to the dialogue state tracker, discarding the full list of possible transcriptions. Nevertheless, the choice of top hypothesis does not guarantee it is the sole feasible interpretation of the sentence. In this research, we present a novel method using the Confusion Networks framework to model ASR ambiguity for dialogue state tracking. Word Confusion Networks combine multiple HMM transitions and states for each chosen and alternative ASR hypothesis, effectively capturing the ambiguity of words with multiple meanings. Our approach is evaluated on the ATIS dataset with the top ASR hypotheses alone, the top two ASR hypotheses, and the full Confusion Network; results show using the Confusion Network reduces error rates by 8% relative to just using the top two ASR hypotheses.

We have computed Joyce's enumerative invariants for semistable coherent sheaves of specific ranks and degrees on complex projective curves, which are a more extensive application of the fundamental moduli space class. This invariance aligns with vector bundles when certain conditions, including r and d being coprime, are met. The invariance can be reinterpreted using a regularized summation, which enables finite values for otherwise divergent sums. This summation expression encompasses iterated Lie algebra trace calculations involving universal sheaves and an extrinsic geometric factor, which arises from considering all possible subbundles. A notable consequence is the derivation of cohomology and intersection theory determinantal formulas for curves, which are essentially weighted partition counts. A related outcome is the determination of enumerative invariants for tuples of sheaves and curves, which involves counting all possible sheaf combinations in a fixed degree. Moreover, by applying Joyce's invariance to a specific geometric configuration involving sheaf intersections, a new moduli space class relationship has been established, which also leads to a generalized formula for mixed Hodge numbers involving a specific curve factor, as determined from a sheaf cohomology calculation.

A critical factor in secret sharing schemes is the complexity of the access structure they can secure. This study introduces a new complexity measure for evaluating the versatility of specific access structures that can be secured by any such scheme. We demonstrate that certain fundamental structures, like the $\mathcal{M}_1^{n}$ structure, have a finite complexity, quantified as $2^{O(n)}$, meaning only a limited number of combinations are required to define the structure. In contrast, more complex structures, like the $\mathcal{M}_{1,2}^{n}$ structure, have an exponentially greater complexity, proportional to $O(n^{\frac{1}{2}}\cdot 2^n)$. This work further differentiates between various complexity classes, categorizing them as basic or advanced, with $\mathcal{M}_1^{n}$ and $\mathcal{M}_{1,2}^{n}$ exemplars of each, respectively. These classes are also used to measure the complexity of a universal set of access structures from a specific class, like monotone, with implications for advanced complexity classes having this property. We conclude that universal access structures, whether basic or advanced, must have a limited number of combinations, precisely $2^{O(n)}$, with $O(n)$ denoting the number of participants. This study's central contribution is proposing a novel concept of molecular complexity for a sequence of structures and proving that a universal access structure typically has a limited molecular complexity, precisely

To determine entanglement experimentally in polarization qubit pairs, we utilize quantum estimation theory to develop the most precise estimators possible, which we then apply to achieve optimal measurement accuracy. We conduct a series of experiments focused on measuring the amount of entanglement in various families of two-qubit two-photon states, using visibility measurements of quantum correlations to achieve the highest possible precision. Notably, using optimal estimators does not necessitate full state tomography; in fact, we compare the results to tomography and demonstrate that our method outperforms it in most cases. This approach has significant implications for the efficient measurement of entanglement in vast photonic qubit systems.

The long-lived palm tree modes (PTM) observed in the JET tokamak exhibit distinct characteristics, including their formation, duration, displacement, rotation, and linkages with edge local magnetic field alterations. Unlike other types of fishbone-like modes, PTMs demonstrate limited activation of plasma particles and show little association with edge magnetic island growth or other nearby modes. PTMs are found to endure beyond multiple rotations per second and to stabilize or quench the tokamak's zeta discharge. Prior to PTM activation, a notable decrease is observed in the turbulent energy of the JET tokamak. Notably, a relationship between PTMs and their closeness to the edge stochastic region is documented. This investigation seeks to clarify the mysteries surrounding PTMs and their underlying causes, as well as identifying areas for further study.

Following the success of pretraining techniques in learning representations from vast amounts of data, researchers have applied these methods to continual learning (CL) tasks. However, the high computational expense associated with pretraining on ever-changing CL tasks' data has raised concerns. This concern is compounded by the fact that current state-of-the-art methods still heavily rely on pretraining, which comes at a significant cost. We ask whether this reliance on pretraining is justified by processing the entire pre-trained network from scratch. If not, we further explore if relying only on the final layer, which significantly reduces training expenses, has any effect on performance. In this work, we investigate this hypothesis by evaluating the importance of pretraining in CL and show that processing just the final layer of a pre-trained network from scratch is sufficient for notable performance gains in CL tasks. Furthermore, we find that fine-tuning the entire network from the streaming data leads to negligible CL performance improvements. This simple observation has far-reaching implications as it challenges the prevailing CL research practice of heavily relying on pretraining networks. We further use our analysis and experimental results to explain the current CL phenomenon and propose a straightforward evaluation metric that reflects task co-familiarity.

As social media increasingly influences public perceptions globally, particularly in sensitive fields like law enforcement, healthcare, and education, the spread of harmful content must be restricted. One particularly hazardous form of online content is hate speech, which experts have linked to real-world violence, including terrorist attacks and assassinations. To combat this, we developed a highly accurate, adaptable model for detecting hate speech on social media, incorporating clear explanations of its decision-making process. Our breakthrough model, incorporating text, image, and video modalities, surpasses current state-of-the-art models in accuracy and is the first to provide detailed reasoning for its classifications, showcasing its ability to identify common hate speech triggers with remarkable precision.

We explore the behavior of large networks of theta neurons, deriving degree-based mean field equations that accurately capture the overall dynamics of these networks. By assuming random connections, we analyze the effects of varying in- and out-degree distribution widths on synaptically coupled networks of theta neurons, a model commonly used for investigating synaptic plasticity. Our findings indicate that the out-degree distribution has a significant impact on the steady state, particularly influencing the location and stability of phase transition points. Conversely, the in-degree distribution affects the dynamic behavior in the network's middle region, particularly during early time periods.

Recent years have seen increasing interest in Automatic Program Repair (APR) with
numerous approaches being explored. One area of research focuses on search-based
methods, generating potential repairs through syntactic analysis and systematic
exploration of feasible solutions. Conversely, we investigate an innovative
approach inspired by the concept of bugs and repairs from a adversarial
perspective. By utilizing deep learning architectures, specifically Generative
Adversarial Networks (GANs), we can directly generate repairs by learning from
corrected code. Initial results from our experience report a remarkable
precision of 39.79%, significantly surpassing current APR tools.

This study introduces a general framework for the capacity region of a complex interference channel with interconnected user pairs, characterized by a collection of interconnected rectangles, with each rectangle defined by paired rates of transmission and reception. We propose a three-step approach to achieve this capacity region: first, we demonstrate that a specific information spectrum-based structure of codes ensures they fall within this capacity region; second, we show that codes of this structure are also optimal for a generalized interference channel with arbitrary connections; third, we prove that codes of this structure, when applied to the interference channel with connected pairs, result in maximal mutual information, thus achieving capacity. This approach enables us to directly determine the capacity region of this channel without the need for an extensive search. Furthermore, we use this finding to establish the capacity region of a two-way broadcast channel with connections.

We aim to research how properties of elementary particles and nuclei are encoded in flow measurements, utilizing a novel flow analysis method that offers insights into collision geometry and the equation-of-state using mesoscopic observables. This analytical method is developed for 3-dimensional flows within the framework of ideal hydrodynamics, which can be applied to 3+1 dimensional hydrodynamics with localized sources and sinks. We demonstrate a new approach to flow analysis that is independent of specific hydrodynamical models and benchmark it for 3-dimensional flows within the hydrodynamic limit. We apply our method to asymmetrical Au+Au collisions at a lab energy of 1.23 GeV and find that the radial flow energy and anisotropic flow coefficient are sensitive to the equation-of-state. Additionally, collision geometry is primarily defined by the transverse distance between gold nuclei and the initial normality of the overlap zone, which can be used to parameterize the equation-of-state using radial flow energy and anisotropic flow coefficient in 3-dimensional flows.

The timely detection of COVID-19 remains a significant research priority, offering the potential to reduce overall mortality rates by controlling the spread of the virus. In this study, we present CT scan scan classification models that not only effectively identify COVID-19, but also safeguard patient confidentiality by adhering to strict HIPAA guidelines and the German Confidentiality Act. Notably, our approach surpasses the performance of current top-tier models without compromising user anonymity.

A Graph Neural Network (GNN) is an effective neural network architecture that processes graph data, extensively applied across multiple domains. Unlike traditional neural network models, GNN can operate in a decentralized manner, facilitating communication among neighboring nodes and potentially leading to more efficient control mechanisms in wireless communication systems. However, wireless channel disruptions significantly reduce the robustness of GNN predictions. To overcome this limitation, we develop decentralized machine learning techniques that ensure GNN nodes can make accurate predictions despite environmental changes and wireless channel disruptions. We particularly explore a challenge known as node classification in wireless communication systems, where a GNN-based approach is applied to assist base stations in co-channel interference diagnosis, leading to improved quality of service and reduced overhead in the number of messages exchanged between nodes. We derive the necessary conditions required for reliable node diagnosis and propose an algorithm to update the GNN model, maintaining accuracy even in the presence of wireless disruptions. We validate our approach by demonstrating, both through theoretical and experimental analysis, that our proposed approach is more efficient than traditional neural network models in achieving accurate predictions and reducing the exchange of messages.

The threat of homicide death tolls has become a significant concern in numerous nations around the world, deeply impacting society and leaving an enduring mark on families torn apart by violence.  In the context of this study, we compiled and analyzed available data on all homicides recorded in the Brazilian state of Goias between 2002 and 2014.  By employing time-series cluster analysis, we were able to identify and differentiate distinct time periods characterized by varying homicide rates.  In addition, we looked to explore possible connections between these distinct phases and local law-enforcement efforts, as well as the broader social and economic dynamics within the state.

Our goal is to modify stochastic gradient descent (SGD) to be adaptive to (i) 
variance $\sigma^2$ in stochastic gradients and (ii) the problem's objective function $f$. Currently, SGD processes undergo a gradual slowdown similar to the $1/\sqrt{t}$ rate, primarily due to adjusting step sizes based on gradient norm and incorporating momentum with fading memory. This investigation focuses on optimizing SGD for $k$-machine problems where $m$ is chosen based on $\min\{ \frac{\sigma^2}{\lambda}, \frac{\lambda}{\sigma^2} \}$. When $\sigma^2/\lambda \leq \sigma^2/m \leq \lambda/\sigma^2$, a $1/t$ rate applies. Our contributions include:

1.  Our research centers on optimizing SGD for $k$-machine problems at $\sigma^2/m \leq \lambda/\sigma^2$. This involves an $1/t$ rate which is more efficient than the $1/\sqrt{t}$ rate achieved by previous methods in this range.
2.  For the $\sigma^2/\lambda \leq \sigma^2/m \geq \lambda/\sigma^2$ case, an $1/t$ rate is achieved under the condition that the objective function has a smooth and convex structure, in addition to non-smoothness for faster convergence. This outcome is based on an $1/t

Axions emerge as a logical outcome of the Peccei-Quinn mechanism, the leading explanation for the strong-CP issue.  Variants of axions known as axion-like particles (ALPs) also arise in various modifications of the Standard Model, particularly in string theories.  Both axions and ALPs have compelling justifications as potential components of Dark Matter (DM), and substantial quantities would be generated in the Sun's core due to the interactions of photons, nuclei, and quarks.  Consequently, their presence can be detected through observations of the Sun, and this is precisely the strategy employed by past experiments, such as CAST, and present investigations including ASTER.

The occupation number over time is examined for a bosonic oscillator coupled to heat baths with fermionic and bosonic components. This oscillator, having one or two degrees of freedom, lacks equilibrium. Such a system serves as a means to establish dynamic non-stationary memory. It has also been established that this type of system is analogous to well-documented nonlinear self-oscillating systems.

Developing robots with skilled hands that can effectively grasp and manipulate objects is an essential yet complex challenge. In comparison to other object-grasping fields, dexterous grasping has been understudied, mainly due to a shortage of extensive datasets. To address this issue, our study introduces DexGraspNet - a large-scale simulated dataset - designed specifically for robotic dexterous grasping, paired with an efficient synthesis method for diverse dexterous grasps. By employing a highly accelerated force closure estimator, we have successfully generated millions of stable and diverse grasps for multiple robotic applications. We have then conducted thorough experiments to evaluate the effectiveness of our synthesis method and demonstrate its superiority over competing approaches. Furthermore, to facilitate research in dexterous grasping, our study provides additional annotations for object meshes and grasping syntheses, both available for free download.

A novel approach is proposed for acquiring a free-breathing, motion-compensated T2-weighted turbo spin echo MRI sequence, sensitive to multiple anatomical movements, for imaging the abdomen and chest. The sequence can generate a 4D data set comprising z-axis, partial k-space data for each phase, via 32 excitation with radio waves with varying sensitivity to breathing and heart rate variations, along with external heart activity compensation. A data acquisition period lasts for approximately two minutes, allowing for four-dimensional imaging of the necessary sections for diagnosing liver, pancreas, kidney issues. Utilizing external heart activity information from an ECG, a specialized technique is employed to minimize heart activity effects in the breathing-sensitive data, resulting in improved image quality with reduced artifacts in time series of images showcasing organ flow in the aorta, liver, heart, and their respective structures, due to compensated external heart activity in the breathing-suppressed data, whereas in breathing-insensitive data, external heart activity remains visible, demonstrating the sequence's ability to minimize heart activity while maintaining breathing sensitivity.

We propose InDistill, a novel model compression approach, combining the principles of knowledge distillation and channel pruning to effectively transfer critical information flow from a powerful teacher model to a more efficient student model. Unlike previous techniques that collapse this information, InDistill leverages layer-wise pruning of the teacher's intermediate layers, aligning their widths with those of the student, enabling direct information distillation without an intermediate encoding step. To facilitate knowledge transfer, we employ a curriculum learning strategy that prioritizes layer-wise difficulty. Experimental results on ResNet-50 demonstrate outstanding results, with the student model achieving comparable accuracy to the teacher on CIFAR-10 and similar or improved results on ImageNet datasets, while showcasing significant compression in parameters, operations, and memory usage.

Two submersion functions from the set of two-dimensional real numbers to the set of real numbers are defined, and their respective level set foliations are examined. The equivalence of these functions topologically implies the topological equivalence of their foliations. Conversely, this relationship is not always valid; however, we can prove that the foliation of a submersion function is topologically equivalent to that of another submersion function if and only if the germs of the two functions at a particular point have a particular invariance property in relation to a local scaling transformation.

Ecosystems that naturally thrive in dry environments have become increasingly vulnerable due to the rising pressures from climate change and human influence. To facilitate effective conservation efforts for these ecosystems, researchers have been studying complex models of ecosystem interactions, focusing on the key factors that determine the resilience of these delicate ecosystems. Although the impact of grazing on plant-life is well understood, a detailed analysis of how grazing affects the landscape-level ecosystem is still limited. This study adopts a novel approach by incorporating spatial dependence in grazing models, providing a more accurate representation of how herbivores interact with each other and their surroundings. We then apply this new framework to a two-species model, accounting for plant growth, grazing by both herbivores, and the impact of these large herbivores on each other. We explore the dynamics of this model through phase plane analysis, examining how coexistence, extinction, and turbulent behavior emerge from similar mechanisms of migration and foraging. We identify specific conditions that trigger stable oscillations within both herbivore populations as well as overall ecosystem behavior. Our analysis offers a new perspective on how grazing affects dry-land ecosystems, offering critical insights that can inform management strategies to protect and preserve these critical ecosystems.

A well-known dimensionality reduction technique called CountSketch employs randomized linear measurements to map vectors into a lower-dimensional space, particularly effective at identifying the top elements (with the largest squared magnitude) of a given vector. However, the CountSketch sketch falls short when dealing with input vectors that evolve over time, particularly when an adversary can tailor each successive input based on the previous input. 

In this study, we investigate the resilience of CountSketch sketches when faced with adaptive inputs. We observe that the sketches are susceptible to an adversary who can guarantee a significant decrease (at least 18.18% lower than the expected value) in the accuracy of the sketch for a particular vector, given a sufficient number of adaptive inputs. Additionally, we prove that this result is roughly optimal. 

This issue with sketch stability is also evident in other related linear sketching techniques for finding the top elements, such as those based on hypergraphs, uniform projections, and independent permutations. However, we do find that a different technique called CoHT achieves stability even when faced with adaptive inputs.

A python-based program, ipie, has been developed for auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo simulations and associated methods, including molecular dynamics. The program utilizes CUDA-enhanced modules for performing simulations on GPUs and has been optimized for performance on both CPUs and GPUs. Validation studies involve calculations on the isothermal quantum ensemble of water and lithium-ion-benzene, demonstrating accuracy and high performance on graphics cards. Additionally, open-source code is provided, allowing researchers to implement new, specialized functionals or methods beyond the existing framework.

High-frequency trading could benefit from the application of quantum computing, as it involves the analysis of complex probability.  The use of quantum strategies, specifically the payoff and probability amplitudes in the pay-off matrix of the game, can adapt quickly when the game rules change.  This is because the pay-off amplitudes stay the same as the game rules, unlike classical methods which need re-calibration when the game parameters change.  The pay-off amplitudes can be updated quickly when the game parameters change in the quantum strategy approach.  The feasibility of using quantum strategies in high-frequency trading on a 'quantum cloud' has been demonstrated, as the 'quantum cloud' now supports the functionality of 'quantum databases' that were previously proposed.  The 'quantum cloud' is a revolutionary technology that allows users to access a shared quantum processing supercomputer.  The quantum strategy approach is also shown to be more effective in re-prime consideration by updating the strategy without any delay when the game parameters change.  This effectiveness is demonstrated in comparison to classical consideration strategies which need to re-synchronize with a 'quantum cloud' to update the strategy.  The 'quantum cloud' is a revolutionary technology that allows users to access a shared quantum processing supercomputer.  The pay-off amplitude approach is a simple yet effective method to determine the optimal consideration prices in high-frequency trading.
