Recent research has shown significant progress in improving recommender system performance through leveraging reviews for predicting ratings, however the current methods have several limitations. The existing techniques often use complex neural networks, which make it challenging to easily understand reviewer sentiments, causing a significant drop in their effectiveness when applied to new datasets. To overcome these challenges, this study introduces a novel approach called SIFN, which accurately models reviewer attitudes at an individual level, then uses these to effectively predict ratings from reviews in a variety of scenarios, including when provided with limited data. The proposed approach uses a simple yet efficient model to capture reviewer sentiments, then combines these with review content and item attributes to generate recommendations. Experimental results demonstrate that SIFN surpasses current methods in accuracy and performance on review datasets, as well as showcasing its capabilities to provide high-quality recommendations when provided with minimal user-item interaction data, outshining state-of-the-art solutions in such settings. The approach also exhibits superior performance on two public datasets, showcasing its potential as a valuable tool for providing recommendations.

Developing CS datasets is crucial for training CS models, yet the challenging task demands extensive resources, particularly in languages with non-Latin script, like Arabic-English CS. We delve into alternatives to create CS-data augmentation tools for the AEMEA13 dataset, focusing on English-Arabic CS. We explore four data augmentation approaches, evaluating their effectiveness in each possible context: zero-padded, cloze-style filling, word-punning, and text-filling. Our findings show that simply replacing words from dictionaries, after removing special characters, is the most efficient method across all settings, achieving significant improvements in model performance. Notably, this straightforward approach outperforms more complex methods in several contexts, highlighting the value of exploring primitive data augmentation techniques beyond word-level for CS data augmentation.

We show that any subgroup of homeomorphisms of a compact surface that fix the boundary, whose action within the surface's interior is highly transitive, cannot be topologically compact when using the compact-open topology's inherited structure.

We're investigating integrable boundary conditions that can be geometrically interpreted as D-branes within specific theoretical models based on products of group- and coset-spaces, which are generalized versions of lambda deformations. Utilizing a sigma-model approach, we found that all the established conformal brane geometries in the context of products of WZW models satisfy the relevant boundary conditions, thereby maintaining their integrability. Additionally, we identified new, cohomology-based boundary conditions that correspond to discrete holo-graphic D-brane embeddings, whose properties in various examples are thoroughly examined.

As modeling and simulation needs have increased, research into improving mesh quality has continued, driving advancements in reliable and efficient mesh modifications. Though standard transformations like vertex moving and edge rotating are well-understood, their potential is limited by their inherent constraints. To overcome these restrictions, novel transformations called Tetrahedrons removal have been developed - an extension of edge splitting introducing new vertices without new edges, and subsequent vertex cuts leading to multiple tetrahedron deletions with multiple vertex cuts. These transformations have the added benefit of maintaining the windings of all oriented data and a small number of vertices and edges. We present an implementation of up to 58 tetrahedrons removal, untangling Hex meshes, providing a tight upper bound for this process. Additionally, the method is further optimized by proving the removal process can be stopped sooner than previously thought. We validate our findings through a detailed comparison with established local modifications like K-flow and Butterfly on a range of tests, revealing our approach performs better in untangling Hex meshes.

The tasks of relation extraction and knowledge graph link prediction share a
common link in their objectives, allowing them to complement each other in the
process of predicting a subject-object relationship in a sentence. Specifically,
when a model identifies an object and its related subject, this relationship can
be utilized by another model to anticipate a list of potential objects associated
with the subject, indicating the original object should also be included in the
list. In our study, we utilized this connection by implementing a multi-task
approach, training existing relation extraction models alongside knowledge graph
link prediction to ultimately boost the models' overall performance and
accuracy. Additionally, we discovered that our integrated strategy allowed the
models to gain a more in-depth understanding of the word's semantic representation
within the context of the sentence.

This study introduces an innovative analytical delay model specifically tailored for deep submicron CMOS inverters. Developed based on the critical recognition that inverter delay is a complex interplay of multiple process variables and load capacitance, the proposed model incorporates parameterized equations derived using Curve Fitting Toolbox in Matlab to accurately capture these dynamics. In comparison to simulation results generated by SPICE and the BSIM4 transistor model, analytical delay model errors typically fall within a 5% margin. Notably, the precision of the analytical delay model can be further enhanced with a precision margin of 2%, albeit at the cost of adjusting the threshold voltage in accordance with the gate width, a phenomenon attributed to channel length depletion. To illustrate its practical applications, the theoretical framework is employed to design a wide-band CMOS inverter with optimal rise and fall times, which in turn enables a 10% reduction in total gate area when compared to its non-optimised counterpart.

Making optimal decisions in complex, continuously changing environments requires
assuming certain conditions. Often, researchers assume a certain level of consistency
in the decision-making model known as the Q-function. However, in numerous real-world scenarios,
this condition does not hold true. Instead, we propose a more adaptable way of measuring the consistency of Q-functions
in various complex environments. This new approach enables us to establish tighter limits on our model's behavior, resulting
in better performance and faster learning in challenging scenarios. Additionally, we provide a theoretical understanding of our approach
and discuss its potential applications to different types of continuous decision-making systems.

The underlying mechanisms of animacy detection, a crucial component of higher order mental functions, are still poorly understood from a neural perspective. Recent breakthroughs in high-resolution imaging and 3D printing technology have made it possible to create highly realistic computer-generated images of animates and inanimate entities, allowing for the development of a new neuroimney-based approach. By employing this approach in a study, researchers found that the ventral temporal cortex, a key processing hub for visual stimuli, displays distinct activation patterns in response to images of animals, humans, and inanimate objects. Notably, the center for object processing versus the integration of biologically meaningful information with object information appears to be located approximately 8mm posterior to the fusiform face area, a region previously identified as the CVN. When exploring further the mechanisms of animacy detection, researchers observed that the CVN exhibits a greater response to images of adults than those of children, indicating an underlying gradient of animacy detection that is also influenced by age. These findings have significant implications for our understanding of how the brain processes visual information, particularly in relation to higher-order cognitive functions like face recognition.

In scientific simulation, achieving accurate reproduction of flow characteristics is of paramount importance. However, numerical schemes, which are based on approximate mathematical models, can introduce errors consisting of both formal and physical invariants violations. A previously developed poten-tial-based framework is used in this study for the development of novel, invariant-preserving schemes for multidimensional Finite Element-based computations. By integrating convex optimization techniques, the potential-based approach is generalized for a wide range of conservation laws written in weakly hyperbolic systems. A number of monolithic and multi-stage invariant-preserving schemes are generated using this potential-based framework. Specifically, the study presents the application of the framework to Finite Element-based simulations of shallow water, Euler equations, and Boussinesq models. Ultimately, the efficacy of these potential-based filters is validated through high-resolution simulations of test cases, which highlight the ability of these methods to accurately preserve physical invariants in the presence of approximation errors, thereby rendering them suitable for the post-processing of simulated data.

Quasi-periodic oscillations type C, typically observed in low-hard and hard-intermediate states of black hole X-ray transients, have been investigated using the MAXI J1535-571 data collected by Insight-HXMT. By applying a novel time-dependent Comptonization model and a relativistic reflection model, researchers have demonstrated its ability to accurately describe X-ray data up to 100 keV in the hard-intermediate state. Observations show the type C QPO frequency remains stable or slightly varies, ranging between 5.99 to 6.06 mHz. Notably, as the system transitions from the hard-intermediate to intermediate states, the amplitude of these QPOs decreases, while their width increases, suggesting a significant role in the corona dynamics.

In the context of multi-agent reinforcement learning, particularly for tasks requiring cooperation and communication, MARL agents are prone to being brittle due to their potential for overfitting on the policies of their training partners. As a result, they may adapt policies that work only when interacting with the specific training partners from which they originated. To address this issue, we have developed a method called transfer empowerment that aims to improve the robustness of such agents by incorporating novel elements into the structure of the value functions. These new elements represent the achievable influence an agent can have over its environment, accounting for both its own actions and those of its partners. By incorporating this into the structure of the value functions, agents can better utilize the policies of their partners and, as a result, achieve higher rewards when interacting with a range of partner policies. To achieve this, we have devised a method for determining the partner-conditional empowerment values through a cooperative optimization approach. As we have discovered, agents optimized using this method produce gradients that contain partner-conditioned empowerment values, allowing them to be transferred to a variety of partner policies, effectively motivating them to adopt more empowering policies. Moreover, we have demonstrated empirically that our approach, as specified, promotes transfer and, as a result, significantly improves the robustness of such agents by causing them to adapt policies that work for a wide range of partner policies. We have verified this through our analysis of the internal representations of the agents, as well as by evaluating their performance with a range of

We introduce MatSim, a comprehensive synthetic dataset, benchmark, and 
approach to streamline and automate material identification. MatSim includes 
physically authentic images and 3D models of over 7,000 distinct materials, 
cross-platform material comparisons, and detailed specifications for material 
appearance. A comparative material benchmark, implemented across various platforms 
material comparison, reveals existing shortcomings in current approaches. 
 Leveraging contrastive learning, our proposed Material Embedding Network (MEN) 
is capable of learning and embedding visual connections between materials 
regardless of their context and producing exceptional one-shot recognition results 
on multiple datasets. Furthermore, MN generates meaningful embeddings that can 
be utilized across various applications, including zero-shot learning and 
search. MEN's source code and material data are openly accessible on 
https://github.com/aidenaeaton/material_embedding_network.

Two equivalent formulations of Lie 2-algebras are recalled: one as a categorification of Lie algebras and another as 2-term L∞-algebras. The paper proceeds by introducing four different types of Lie 2-algebras derived from 2-plectic manifolds, Courant algebroids, homotopy Poisson manifolds and multivector fields on a Lie groupoid. The Lie 2-algebra cohomology is also reintroduced and its lower-degree instances analyzed. The integration of strict Lie 2-algebras to strict 2-groups is also a point of discussion in the paper.

We introduce a novel method for local image feature matching, where instead of a sequential process, we first identify pixel-wise dense matches at a basic level and refine the good matches at a detailed level. In contrast to other dense methods, we leverage self and cross attention mechanisms in the Transformer model to derive feature descriptors that are context-dependent for both images. This approach allows our method, known as LoFTR, to effectively find dense matches in low-texture regions where traditional detectors face difficulties. Experiment results on indoor and outdoor datasets demonstrate that LoFTR surpasses current state-of-the-art methods with significant margin and excels on visual localization tasks, with notable performance on occluded and low-texture cases.

The study of the Sun aims to understand and analyze complex magnetic phenomena responsible for space weather. To this end, the Solar Magnetic Field Working Group within the International Space Environment Service has initiated efforts to create a unified global data platform, integrating multiple spacecraft observations to recreate the Sun's magnetic field in three-dimensional space. However, current inverse modeling techniques are prone to significant uncertainties and biases, particularly when dealing with noisy data, resulting in substantial discrepancies between these proxy data and actual solar magnetic field measurements. To highlight the magnitude of these inaccuracies, our research focuses on removing apparent biases from mock solar magnetic field data, simulated using the PHANToM open-source code, which models the Sun's magnetic field using first-order diffusion and nonlinear feedback mechanisms. The results demonstrate that by accounting for existing biases, the mock data can be refined to within 50 Gauss in magnitude and 30 degrees in orientation, particularly when adjusting for localized fluctuations. The proposed bias correction technique may also contribute to future development of the unified global data platform, providing an essential approach for evaluating and improving the accuracy of inferred spacecraft data.

This research explores a real-world scenario in which consumers selfishly aim to minimize their energy bills by scheduling their energy usage in advance. To effectively persuade these consumers to alter their loading patterns, the utility company instantiates a time-dependent pricing strategy. In response, these consumers engage in a strategic interaction where they solve a game that utilizes the Lagrangian relaxation of an optimistic saddle-point minimization problem to achieve equilibrium outcomes. To validate the feasibility of this interactive game-based approach, the authors demonstrate its unique properties and prove its equilibrium outcomes to be achievable in real-world settings. To accommodate the diverse requirements of these consumers, the authors develop an efficient solution method for the aggregative game that yields nearly cost-circumventable outcomes while accounting for variations in user demand.

We investigate the thermal phenomenon of black string decay in the context of Rastall theory of gravity. By applying the generalized Einstein-Hilbert equation from this theory, we derive the modified black string metric, accompanied by its associated thermodynamic properties. In this framework, we find that the energy E and horizon area A are connected as predicted by the first law of thermodynamics. For specific conditions involving suitably chosen parameters and an angular charge Q, we detect the occurrence of the Hawking thermal radiation phenomenon, influenced by gravity. Furthermore, our model displays asymptotic behavior characterized by an inverse hyperbolic potential.

The results demonstrate that the power spectra of ergodic transformations, discrete or continuous, contain essential information about the rate of convergence in the averaged versions of the ergodic theorem. Specifically, a minimal lower bound on the decay rates within the spectral measure leads to optimal convergence rates in the ergodic theorem, while its upper decay rates define such optimal rates uniformly for all ergodic transformations. In cases of discrete spectra, type III von Neumann algebras are involved, revealing new characteristics. Additionally, M. Sh. Birganskii's recent work for nilflows is included in the list of studied transformations.

The research on extremely old and metal-poor stars within our Galaxy is instrumental in grasping its chemical evolution and the origin of star formation. These stars are rare, and only five have been detected so far with a metal content below -5.0. Recent data release from Gaia, which covers 219 million sources, presents an immense opportunity to identify metal-poor stars. An efficient method for identifying metal-pool stars using BP/RP spectra is presented, which incorporates a synthetic spectrum model combined with extreme vectorial line broadening. This method has a metal content detection limit of approximately -3.0 and demonstrates high efficiency in pinpointing metal-pool stars, which can then be further studied with high-resolution spectra.

This research splits the Earth into a grid of hexagonal cells to collect and analyze worldwide data on the severity of ongoing and historical wildfires from NASA's FIRECAMS network. It enables the assessment of fire severity within each region and globally, utilizing standardized indices such as the Fire Danger Index (FDI) and the Fire Season Severity Index (FSSI). Real-time data collection occurs every 24 hours and historical data is accessible via a web application, which can be utilized for both regional and global forecasting. This technology has been successfully applied in various contexts, including a case study in Greece where a 2021 wildfire warning was successfully issued 12 days in advance.

We've conducted a thorough examination of eight distinct methods for evaluating the morphological intricacy of languages. These measures have different prerequisites for data annotation, yet our study identifies both similarities and disparities among them. We compare the methods visually and statistically to ascertain how they correlate with typological characteristics. This investigation seeks to determine whether these measures assess the same underlying aspect of language or, alternatively, measure different facets of morphological complexity. The results from principal component analysis suggest that a substantial portion of variation across the eight measures is linearly associated.

Researchers at Meneghetti et al recently discovered that moderate self-interactions of dark matter can cause the halos of rich galaxy clusters to deviate from their expected shapes due to gravitational forces. Building upon their previous findings, we now examine how self-interactions might impact the bending of light by dark matter in these clusters, using a computational model to simulate strong and weak gravitational lensing patterns. Our analysis shows that self-interactions can cause variations in the mass distribution within galaxy cluster halos, leading to distinct patterns in gravitational lensing, which could be identified and distinguished from other astrophysical phenomena through a closer examination of flux ratios of multiple image pairs. Our study expands upon the computational model developed by Bode et al, incorporating a simplified representation of gas cooling that more accurately represents real-world galaxy cluster evolution. Our findings suggest that self-interacting dark matter can explain features such as line catalog substructure and outer richness plateau, which are commonly observed in rich galaxy clusters. When applied to four distinct galaxy clusters, our model demonstrates that self-interactions can cause minor discrepancies in mass distribution that are consistent across a range of parameters, ultimately affecting the shape of dark matter halos and their innermost mass profiles in a manner that is consistent with other gravitational forces at play.

This research focuses on reducing the complexity of parametric partial differential equations (PPDEs) by finding an accurate approximation space for the solutions of the equations. Given incomplete information, we use two primary sources: initial assumptions about the solutions and partial measurements from the equations. Based on these sources, we have developed methods to generate effective approximation subspaces and analyzed their performance. By tapping into the underlying structure of the equations, we update these subspaces with newly acquired information and achieve improved results. To facilitate our approach, we have developed efficient tools for evaluating the performance of the approximating spaces and updating them efficiently. We have thoroughly tested our methods and evaluated their performance through detailed numerical experiments, demonstrating their value and versatility.

This research introduces the m-arcsinh Kernel (m-ar-K) Fast Independent Component Analysis (FastICA) method, an efficient extension of ICA techniques that are widely used in neuroimaging. We combine kernel tricks with independent component analysis, incorporating m-arcsinh data transformation for enhanced robustness. This innovative method enables the application of ICA algorithms, which were previously restricted to traditional linear models, to nonlinear data through kernel trick. By leveraging this kernel approach, we can identify independent components in complex, curved data distributions. Furthermore, we establish that the employed kernel whitenening matrix is a generalization of the traditional ICA whitening matrix derived from Principal Component Analysis (PCA). We perform thorough evaluations of our method using real-world brain MRI scans from the ABCD National Child Health and Development Study and the public Hammersley gene mapping dataset. These experiments confirm the effectiveness of our approach in identifying important genetic factors associated with brain structure, including the discovery of novel links between the X-chromosome and total brain gray matter.

Identifying trending social media events in real-time across various geographical locations is crucial, particularly for anticipating incidents such as accidents, protests, or breaking news. The dynamic nature of social media data poses challenges to traditional approaches, including ambiguous event timelines and spaces. An innovative solution, this research introduces an adaptive spatio-temporal event detection framework, leveraging social media data linked to specific geographical locations over a specified period. An algorithm is developed to optimize detection accuracy, precision, and memory usage. Real-world testing using 1.5 million geo-tagged social media posts confirmed the effectiveness of this approach, accurately predicting events and performing better than established benchmarks in terms of accuracy, memory usage, and recall. The proposed framework is implemented and demonstrated using Azure Stream Analytics, enabling real-time execution and overcoming data retention limitations associated with conventional approaches.

We establish the optimal Lipschitz regularity of very weak solutions for the measure-valued elliptic PDE $-\mathrm{div}(A(x) \nabla u) = Q \; \mathcal{H}^{n-1} \llcorner \Gamma$ within a smooth domain. Our analysis focuses on the model equation $-\mathrm{div}(x \nabla u) = 1 \; \mathcal{H}^{n-1} \llcorner \Gamma$ and leverages a regularity result for boundary value problems along a smooth hypersurface $\Gamma$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$.

Advanced permanent magnets made from rare earth and transition metal alloys achieve high magnetization due to high transition metal content. By utilizing computational searches based on fundamental laws, researchers predicted 37 cobalt-rich compounds, specifically 17 YCo$_{16}$ and 20 YCo$_{20}$, which were identified as stable with a high likelihood. These cobalt-rich alloys were discovered to exhibit increased phase stability at elevated temperatures, attributed to increased vibrational entropy. Notably, YCo$_{16}$ and YCo$_{20}$ displayed enhanced magnetization and Curie temperatures compared to the extensively studied compound Y$_{2}$Co$_{17}$, specifically 0.22 T and 102 K for YCo$_{16}$, and 0.29 T and 104 K for YCo$_{20}$.

A crucial task in online display advertising is setting a bidding strategy. To obtain a target number of impressions with the lowest expenditure, an optimal bidding approach needs to balance achieving a high click-through rate and keeping costs under a set budget. However, since advertisers typically have limited information about future traffic, a dynamic environment requires constant adjustments to the approach based on changing conditions such as competition, cost per click thresholds, and the overall state of ad inventory. To address these challenges, a new bidding strategy called ARAB is developed, which adapts to varying display ad environments by utilizing real-time data about the ad slots, including prices, durations, and the bidder's own click history along with estimated click-through rates. By utilizing these elements, the ARAB approach calculates an optimal bidding decision by applying a modified version of the well-known Thompson Sampling technique. To reduce computational overhead associated with generating random samples, the ARAB algorithm combines this approach with an accelerated Monte Carlo method for efficient execution. Furthermore, ARAB can utilize a range of variety-specific bidding models. To evaluate its performance, ARAB is compared against multiple state-of-the-art approaches on a large dataset containing 1.6 million impressions and an extensive set of 97,103 floods, demonstrating superior results.

Nonclassical properties in continuous-variable quantum systems can be assessed through several nonlocal indicators. This work focuses on linking the capability of one system to influence another without sharing information, known as quantum steering, to the emergence of nonclassical properties in entangled states. We examine the connection between quantum steering and the formation of certain indicators in one part of an entangled system, determined by another's state. Specifically, we look into how positive Wigner negativity in one system is triggered by both classical and quantum measurements from another, as well as the relations between these nonlocal properties. We also show that specific previous results in this field are a consequence of a broader proposition, involving general conditions for the generation of particular nonclassical properties in one system, determined by another's state.

Accurate secure boundary analysis is crucial for practical quantum key distribution systems, but the current approach overlooks a critical aspect – the randomness consistency of seeds used in privacy amplification. We introduce and prove a quantum leftover hash lemma that applies to non-uniform random seeds, leveraging min-entropy, and subsequently establish a detailed, precise QKD secure boundary analysis leveraging this new framework. Additionally, we present an efficient algorithm to approximate the entropy of a non-uniform random seed. Through this analysis, we achieve more precise, refined boundaries for practical QKD systems, taking into consideration real-world limitations such as practical source strength, distance effects, and the random seed's uniformity, all of which are highly relevant in real-world QKD implementations.

This research, specifically in a k-dimensional Euclidean space, focuses on a new type of curve, namely a Bertrand curve, and an old type called a Frenet curve, both in a 4-dimensional Euclidean space. Our key finding is that a Bertrand curve is also a Frenet curve when the component tangent to a scalar field is absent, under certain conditions. Additionally, we have derived the general equation for a curve in a 4-dimensional Euclidean space that satisfies the Bertrand condition, as well as geometric interpretations of this association.

We'll examine the diffusion process described by the equation $u_t(t, x) =
\tfrac{1}{2}x^{-\alpha}(b(x)u(t, x)_t + \frac{1}{2}x \cdot u(t,
x)_t) = \lambda \delta(t) u(t, x)$, where $u(0, x)$ is given as $u_0$
and $u(t, x)$ is continuous with probability one for all $t, x > 0$. 
This system involves the Feller equation, used particularly for models with
population growth as well as models featuring accumulation mechanisms, notably
diffusion with accumulation and recent immigration, and diffusion with trapping,
which includes models featuring the standard Wiener process and Brownian motion
with a reflecting barrier. We will focus on the Feller equations involving
population growth models with drivers and accumulation mechanisms. We'll determine
the possible joint distributions of the surviving extant times, examine their
relationships, and prove convergence in distribution. We'll also explore how
these results relate to a random sample drawn from a population over time, 
particularly focusing on the cases of recent immigration and trapping.

In this work, we explore diagrammatic methods in waveguide QED systems that facilitate non-resonant many-photon interactions. A specific focus is placed on outlining the underlying principles and assumptions of this formalism, with a separate section devoted to explaining a powerful yet efficient effective theory for two-photon processing. To further demonstrate its utility, we develop and explain a new method for calculating scattering matrices in waveguide QED systems that consists of simple and effective diagrams. With this framework, we successfully calculate the scattering matrices for two prominent many-body interactions: two-photon scattering by a V-groove cavity and interactions involving multiple photons and Rydberg atoms. These calculations with the new framework yield results that are in close agreement with more complex diagrammatic approaches. With its utility proven, we believe this effective diagrammatic approach will provide a straightforward and efficient means for exploring complex interactions in waveguide QED systems that involve many photons.

A potential way to study low-mass dark matter using terrestrial laboratories may involve the scattering of boosted dark matter off nuclei. To investigate this, we examined the non-relativistic dark matter-nucleus scattering cross section, focusing on its dependence on the nucleon's spin. We found this cross section to be significant enough to be studied using advanced laboratory detectors like the ones employed by CMO-50 and future similar experiments. We established specific requirements for the sensitivity of these experiments in order to fully understand the parameter space of boosted dark matter. Specifically, we found that a particular model, which is based on a vector-like fermion, can be fully constrained by a mobile detector with a liter in volume and operation period of one year, with the ability to detect events of approximately 1 keV. Similarly, we found another model, which is based on a fermionic non-relativistic particle, can be fully constrained by a stationary detector with a ton in mass and an annual operation with the ability to detect events of approximately 1 keV.
This note employs Faulhaber's Formula to elucidate why odd Bernoulli numbers equate to zero.

Continuous phase modulation detection using conventional differential detection techniques is highly resistant to various channel disturbances and noise interference. Nevertheless, its widespread adoption has been limited by its relatively high power consumption and processing delays, which can cause issues in real-time applications. To address this challenge, an efficient detection method based on differential detection was developed, which employs a conventional receiver architecture while significantly reducing power consumption and processing delays through a new optimization approach. By using more efficient demodulation algorithms and simplifying the differential detection architecture, the new detection method aims to improve performance. To evaluate its effectiveness, simulations were conducted on various CPM formats, which demonstrated substantial delay and power savings. Specifically, the method resulted in delay reductions of up to 9x and power consumption reductions of up to 13x in different CPM formats, with only negligible performance loss, which was found to be less than 0.3 dB in most cases, with a maximum loss of 0.5 dB in the 8PAM case.

A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons. To overcome this limitation, we propose grouping multiple comparisons together and allowing human labelers to rate their collections at the same time. Through data manipulation techniques, we transform these evaluations into aggregate scores that can be used to train a reinforcement learning agent. Our approach incorporates advanced methods for organizing comparisons based on the agent's previous experiences and suggests simplifying the process by leveraging the agent's already acquired knowledge to create the comparisons from the beginning. Our results indicate the success of our Visually Assisted Cluster Ranking approach by showing a notable reduction in the required number of individual comparisons, an increase of at least two-fold, while still yielding comparable performance. Our time-efficient method successfully combines the strengths of efficient labeling and the rapid learning associated with incremental training.

We're exploring nucleon structure functions within noncommutative space-time, using the doubling trick within this theoretical framework. By applying noncommutativity to momentum operators, we translate physical observables from standard to noncommutative space-time at a suitable momentum scale. Our calculation involves the parton distribution functions (PDFs) and corresponding structure functions for the proton and neutron, expressing them in terms of commutative nucleon PDFs and nucleon mass. We provide explicit formulas for the first two moments, explaining how noncommutativity affects the parton distribution functions and highlighting scaling variations, especially in the case of a large scale parameter. Our analysis includes plots to illustrate these effects, showing parton distribution variations and structure function differences at various scales.

In typical topological systems, significant disruptions trigger a phase shift, but we have developed an adjustable version of the Toric code that remains stable under even extreme external influences, and surprisingly, still shows resilience against disorder once the parameters are readjusted, exhibiting a "hidden" topological characteristic. This model showcases the intricate relationship between frustration, disorder, and topology. Moreover, we have established a general method to identify the topological properties of this line defect, and our analysis shows that the correlation of spins decays at a different rate along and perpendicular to the line, revealing a model that efficiently preserves information through the process of cutting and pasting. This property makes it an appealing candidate for applications in topological quantum coding.

We investigate the eigenspectra of large, randomly constructed Hermitian block matrices, whose structure is perturbed by a finite rank complex modification. Given that the band's width expands faster than the square root of the matrix's size, our analysis demonstrates that the statistical distribution of the imaginary components of the eigenvectors aligns with the results from the Gaussian Unitary Ensemble. This finding was achieved using the methods and approaches developed in the arXiv paper, 1802.03813.

Recent advancements in dialogue tasks have been achieved through pre-trained language models. However, models reliant on surface-level dialogue text struggle to comprehend dialogue context, particularly in extracting the underlying semantic meaning. In an effort to bridge this knowledge gap, we introduce the use of Abstract Meaning Representation as a means of pre-training language models with explicit semantic information, which captures the essence of dialogue during the pre-training phase. Building upon the standard pre-training framework, we formulate a semantic-based pre-training approach that includes three key tasks: learning core semantic units, semantic relations, and overall semantic representation. Empirical results from the analysis of casual and task-based conversations confirm the superiority of our proposed model. Furthermore, we contribute a novel paradigm by integrating a deep semantic representation into the pre-training of dialogue models.

To establish trust and ensure fairness, as well as hold developers accountable, algorithmic interpretability must be measured. This study draws on insights from cognitive science to create a new metric, the Cognitive Complexity Score (CCS), which quantifies how easily humans can learn an algorithm's decision-making logic. By learning this logic, humans can effectively communicate and apply the algorithm's insights. Following a defusion of common misconceptions about learning, the researchers pinpoint three specific barriers to learning: being unclear, having inconsistent rules, and presenting complex information. They then create a protocol for evaluating algorithms based on these learning obstacles and propose the CCS as a universal measurement standard. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, the researchers test and assess its metrics across various algorithms in different fields, including social media moderation rules and medical diagnosis algorithms.

Anomaly detection without labeled data is a difficult anomaly detection task, making it even more challenging when working with limited computational resources. The detection of unlabeled data relies on the use of unsupervised and semi-supervised techniques to identify anomalies based on the assumption that the normal data pattern is repeated in the exceptions. In this research, we present an innovative approach by merging Isolation Forest algorithm, known for its simplicity and efficiency, with the principles of weak supervision to identify anomalies. Due to its properties, Isolation Forest is particularly suitable for this approach as it doesn't require any preconceived idea of what anomalies might look like and can handle small training sets effectively. To further simplify deployment, we designed a Python-based tool utilizing this method along with visualization capabilities to streamline the anomaly detection process. This solution is particularly useful in scenarios with limited computational resources and can be applied to diverse problems, showing its effectiveness through experiments conducted in anomaly detection, data balancing, and other anomaly-related tasks, resulting in notable performance gains.

A typical strategy for modelling extreme events involves considering occurrences beyond a high threshold as exceeding this threshold and modelling them as happening as part as a larger sequence. The traditional way of doing this involves working with a transformed variable, but this often requires additional steps to account for the data's non-uniform sampling intervals. The method we're proposing allows for a direct modelling of the extreme events without transformation, and thus automatically takes into account the varying time steps. The method is then applied in a Bayesian framework by estimating parameters from a sequence of the time-series blocks. The method is demonstrated in the context of a stability analysis of estimating a scale parameter and in an analysis of comparing two models for the occurrence of earthquakes in Sicily.

This analysis addresses the challenge of optimizing cross-sectional area through a specific point within a geometric form. To generalize this concept, the approach is expanded across multiple dimensions. Nonetheless, the optimal average cross-sectional volume cannot be achieved at stationary points of the mean value function. Instead, such stationary values are associated with minimal cross-sectional variances. We establish and investigate a nonlinear model that describes regions exhibiting stationary cross-section averages. Using this model, we demonstrate the possibility of multiple stable states and examine the structural characteristics of associated forms. Additionally, we provide a qualitative analysis of equilibrium conditions, as well as quantitative solutions for specific contexts.

There's been a growing trend in the study of natural language understanding with a renewed focus on developing models that capture common sense knowledge represented as a graph. This has led to the development of multiple graph datasets, with (Guo et al., 2020) being one example, that seeks to provide a standardized, widely-applicable, and common-sense based knowledge graph. This study examines the potential of symbolic and neural models on the revised COMET-ATOMIC 2020 knowledge graph. COMET-ATOMIC 2020 expands on (Guo et al., 2020) with an updated version of the ATOMIC dataset that includes new causal concepts and more data. This new dataset is used to test the potential of various machine learning models that draw from both symbolic and neural paradigms in a large-scale evaluation. The results of this study are made available at a new website.

We introduce the data processing pipeline developed for the Hi-GAL survey. This critical component is an integral part of the Herschel satellite project that's mapping the Galactic plane's inner regions. Leveraging a combination of Herschel Interactive Standard Environment capabilities and new, custom-designed tools, our pipeline effectively handles data reduction tasks. These include accurate data filtering, noise assessment, and efficient map generation, which utilizes a highly modified ROMA algorithm previously validated on large-scale cosmological surveys. This work extensively examines the properties of Hi-GAL Science Demonstration Phase dataset.

A recent photometric study of first population stars in the globular cluster NGC 2808 revealed heterogeneity in iron content, contradicting initial photometric assessments that were consistent within the cluster. Contrary to previous findings with lower precision, our high-precision spectroscopic analysis of iron and other elements also failed to support uniform iron abundance across these stars. Specifically, two brighter stars had higher iron content compared to two fainter stars, resulting in a spread of approximately 0.25 dex. This disparity is consistent with previous high-precision and temperature-based analyses within the same cluster. Notably, our analysis resolved the uncertainty surrounding a previously reported, brighter first population star, confirming it had higher iron content. Overall, our results align with previous studies, further establishing the diversity of iron content within NGC 2808.

To facilitate a deeper understanding of one-dimensional physical systems, we consider a simplified single file model. We derive an analytical solution for the complete first exit time statistics of an overdamped single file with absorbing boundary conditions, after which we apply these findings to investigate the speed-accuracy relationship, examining how this property is influenced by the mean exit time and the spread of exit times around this mean value. Additionally, by employing the principle of minimum entropy production, we develop a simplified expression for the optimal search speed in a directed search process.

Quantum Mechanics contradicts the universally assumed, classical cause-and-effect relationship established by Bayes' rule in physics. While believed to hold universally, Bayes' rule has consistently been applied despite its potential conflict with Quantum Mechanics. This paper examines the validity of this presumed conflict. We begin by addressing an ongoing misconception that Quantum Mechanics lacks a basis for applying Bayes' rule. We then present an argument based on an extended version of Bayes' rule, proposing it retains its truth despite its potential failure in Quantum Mechanics. The latter part of the paper addresses potential ambiguities in interpreting the input-output processes of an inquiring-inquired pair, a phenomenon prevalent in quantum experiments. We define input-output processes using quantum entropy, maintaining consistency with inferences made by Bayes' rule.

We initially report findings regarding corrections to system size for the state equation, trace anomaly, and speed of sound, using two specific theoretical frameworks: a model for massless scalar fields and another based on quenched QCD, both applying periodic boundary conditions. Additionally, we share ongoing results involving the application of Dirichlet boundary conditions to quenched QCD.

Consider the universal cohomology algebra $A$ generated by $x, s^1, \dots, s^{k-1}$, where $k\ge 2$, based on the Steenrod algebra and the cohomology algebra $\mathrm{H}^{\bullet}(A)$ with cohomology generators $x_0,\,\dots,x_{k-1}$ where $x_0\) has degree $k$. Since the rank of the subgroup consisting of non-trivial elements in $\mathrm{H}^{2i}_{A}$ is at least $i+1$ for $i$ equal to $2, \dots, 2k-1$, it follows that the rank of the said subgroup for $i=2,\,\dots, 2k-1$ is $i+1$. Furthermore, the dimension of the said subgroup for $i=k$ is $k$.

Space-based telescopes have taken nearly all of our UV light (a small fraction of the Sun's output) since 1972, but a significant portion of this market remains inaccessible due to interference from Lyman-alpha radiation. Developing Lyman-alpha filtered cameras would enable astronomers to take accurate measurements in a significant portion of the UV spectrum by reducing emissions from the Lyman-alpha band centered at 121 nanometers by a factor of approximately 40,000. We explored various technologies for a ground-based prototype filter and assessed its capabilities. Different design variations were modeled and refined through Monte Carlo simulations, and a optimized version was identified. This prototype could reduce Lyman-alpha emissions by a factor of approximately 33,000, and capture about 76% of the remaining UV radiation from the Sun. It could also be used in space-based telescopes to take accurate measurements of the polarimeter's spectral response.

Optimal distributed controller design under communication limitations can be
complicated unless certain system structure conditions, like sparsity or
temporal consistency, are established. Drawing from graph signal processing,
this study develops a class of Graph Symmetric Systems, which exhibit graph-based
symmetry in dynamic transitions. For systems belonging to this category, a
digitally controlled optimal distributed controller is designed, which can be
executed using a centralized estimate of the graph's eigenvalues and a localized
calculation of the graph filter. Furthermore, robust versions of this solution
are presented to address uncertainties in the graph, as well as performance
bounds for a basic adaptive algorithm derived to tackle optimization challenges.

Image search algorithms that retrieve and identify copied images from large databases comprise two main components: a neural network that converts an image into a transformation-resistant vector, and a high-performance but imperfect search algorithm. This paper introduces active indexing to optimize the interplay between these components, reducing a representation's loss through subtle, imperceptible modifications to images before their release. Our modifications have a negligible impact on image quality, are easily implemented in software or even hardware, and can be tuned to maximize the model's accuracy without needing the original image. Moreover, active indexing can be combined with existing quantization techniques, requiring only a shallow neural network to produce the index. In our experiments on a diverse set of images, a small amount of induced noise yields significant improvements - up to a 50% increase in the model's accuracy on a widely-used image database (ImageNet-VS). Additionally, this technique is highly efficient, taking minimal time and exceeding 1000 times more efficient than traditional fine-tuning the model, while also being virtually unnoticeable to humans.

This study confirms that physical layer-based authentication is achievable in
Gaussian noise environments, with the caveat that an all-knowing adversary cannot be
beated. An examination of a model comprising encoder, decoder, and adversary was
carried out, with the latter possessing unlimited transmission capabilities and
unlimited access to the transmitted message. It was demonstrated that an all-encompassing
attack cannot be thwarted unless an excessive amount of time or data is invested in
the transmission process. An optimal authentication code was defined and it was
proven that an all-encompassing attack can be repelled if a predetermined level of
time or data is exceeded. Furthermore, a detailed analysis of a specific code type
was undertaken with results showing that authenticating information can be seamlessly
integrated into the existing communication process without impacting standard
data-rate and spectral usage, provided that an all-encompassing attack is not
launched.

Reevaluating the "dispersionless transport regime" of Brownian particles in inclined periodic potentials, we found that after entering a running state under the influence of a constant force, these particles exhibit typical diffusive behavior without reaching an ultimate stationary state. Notably, our analysis applies to any soft potential, and the final drift velocity obtained dispersively depends on both the exponent of the potential and the symmetry of the potential shape. In the case of soft potentials with even coefficients, the particles' drift velocity will be lower than in the case of hard potentials (with odd coefficients), while for odd-coefficient potentials, the difference is negligible. This phenomenon has significant implications for real-world particle systems, as it might provide a way to control the final velocity by choosing an appropriate potential softness. Under certain conditions, the particles' behavior can even transition from diffusive to ballistic. This transition, facilitated by the particle's inertia, might be faster than the typical time scale of the system and could be the primary reason for the apparent "dispersionless transport regime" observed in some studies.

This paper presents an adaptable, localized predictive technique that builds upon Jord\'a's (2005) model, expanding it to a non-linear framework by combining a flexible base with a smoothness penalty. The novel estimation approach is validated through simulations and implemented in a real-world context to examine the short-term effects of monetary and oil price fluctuations on stock market instability, specifically during the COVID-19 pandemic and the Bertrand war.

We investigate the influence of the electromagnetic quantum vacuum on the angular momentum of a charge q moving in a uniform magnetic field. The orbital angular momentum generated is due to photons in the vacuum that emit an energy back to the charge in proportion to n^2, a greater increase than that of the -2n\hbar of a charge in a Landau level.

The primary goal of Fine-Grained Named Entity Typing (FG-NET) is to accurately classify various entity types, often exceeding hundreds, by considering the context of each mention. However, the common approach to acquire supervised training data through distant supervision introduces label noise by assigning type labels without considering the context. In order to mitigate this issue, FG-NET research adopts a Euclidean model which has its limitations when dealing with a vast number of entity types. This is because the quality of the refined entity type predictions degrades as the angular distance between the input mention's embedding and the nearest neighbor in the latent space increases. In an attempt to address this limitation, this work proposes an approach which leverages an alternative space with a different metric in its nature, namely hyperbolic space. The proposed FGNET-RH is comprised of two components: the distillation of label-free pre-trained hyperbolic models; and a refinement module that iteratively corrects the type annotations of the noisy data set using a nearest neighbor search within an adapted hyperbolic k-nearest neighbors framework. The efficacy of the proposed FGNET-RH is evaluated through experiments on six data sets, resulting in an overall percentage improvement of 3.32 and outperforming the state-of-the-art by a notable 2.06.

This paper establishes upper limits of the Hankel determinants for the $f(z)$ within the $\mathcal{U}$ class and a general special class $\mathcal{S}$, with alternating convexity properties, in relation to the natural logarithm. Specifically, we identify two types of these determinants, characterized by normal functions and extreme cases, which involve the distortion factor $|1-\zeta|^2$ and its reciprocal, respectively. By utilizing Distortion Theorem, Carath\'{e}odory's Extension Theorem, alternating convexity properties, and specialization techniques, we are able to transfer known results from the $\mathcal{U}$ class to the general $\mathcal{S}$ class. Furthermore, we examine the Hankel determinants' behavior as $z$ approaches infinity within the $\mathcal{U}$ class, revealing a relationship involving the Hankel transform of $2|1-\zeta|^2$.

Achieving efficient and sustainable operation in cloud data centers largely relies on load balancing, and virtualization enables this by using a proactive load balancing approach that prevents service disruption and ensures stability. Virtually separating VM groups based on anticipated workloads and processing times enables this proactive strategy, allowing predicted fluctuations to be mitigated before actual traffic arises. And, by forecasting future workload patterns based on historical data and applying the Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average model, the prepartition load balancing approach can effectively maintain desired performance.

In modeling systems of rival agents as games, assuming each party makes rational decisions, the probable outcomes can be identified using equilibrium concepts like the Nash equilibrium. In various real-world scenarios, factors like weather, traffic or fiscal policy, beyond the agents' control, can impact game dynamics. Often, the equilibrium observed doesn't align with the actual cost functions of the agents. This research proposes the use of Nash Fixed Point Networks, a new class of neural networks, capable of predicting game equilibria using context. Contextual factors can significantly affect games, like (often unseen by agents) traffic in a non-cooperative route-planning game. Our experiments, incorporating both generated and real-world data, showed advantages of NFP Networks over other methods when dealing with various types of games.

This study tackles the issue of assessing causal influences in cases where some variables involved in ensuring causal validity are incompletely known. For these situations, we develop tight limits on the causal influences by solving two intricate optimization problems. The derived limits automatically adapt to increasing numbers of unknown confounding variables, even when their dimensions grow exponentially. Moreover, our results remain valid even in the presence of vast amounts of high-dimensional data, prompting a discussion on their practical applicability in such scenarios.

Significant physical harm can be inflicted by subtle, long-lasting cyber assaults on industrial control systems. They often go undetected under normal operating conditions, making early detection by predictive models essential. In this research, a more efficient predictor for detecting attack effects on LTI systems in real-time is developed. A new method for estimating uncertainty in a single step ahead prediction using convex optimization is proposed. This approach relies solely on a system model, eliminating the need for data collection or control inputs. It also allows for straightforward monitoring of system states and input signals for attack detection. A driver system was used to test the predictor's real-time performance over a wide range of parameters. The results show that this approach has a significantly shorter processing time than previous methods, operating within milliseconds, allowing it to detect attacks in real-time.

A precise summary can be derived from lengthy written documents via deep learning models, but training is typically resource-intensive and necessitates substantial datasets, which can be time-consuming and costly to obtain. Considering these constraints, we introduce an unsupervised method for automatic summarization. This method is built upon a generation augmented interpretation scheme, where the key elements of a document are identified through a combination of sequence and graph models, then are subsequently used to generate a summary. This method is further enhanced by incorporating a novel graph-based approach that utilizes syntactic and semantic dependencies, resulting in improved performance on datasets comprising summaries written in Indian languages.

We establish the definition and certain attributes of S-rings of Krull type, in addition to examining the properties of such structures, particularly independent S-rings of type A. We calculate the injective dimension of a quotient category formed by modules over an independent S-ring of type A, with respect to a specified subcategory consisting of modules having trivial interactions with codivisorial modules.

The objective of this research was to identify and characterise potential substellar companions associated with five rapidly accelerating stars using data obtained through long-term radial velocity measurements. These stars were initially thought to have companions that could have formed through dynamical mean-motion resonances. However, our analysis focused on determining if a companion existed for each star and if so, what their mass and separation might be. As our analysis progressed, we recognized that the detected RV variations could be caused by non-circumstellar sources or fluctuations stemming from stellar activity. Consequently, our goal shifted to constraining the possible masses and separations of unseen companions, rather than directly detecting them. Our analysis lasted roughly five years and utilized for each star: Lyot curves, RV data, and images from 2.2m and 1.3m telescopes, as well as archival data including H-alpha and Ca H&K photometry from the Skymapper Telescope. Our findings indicate that the RV time variations of the star GJ 411A can be explained by stellar activity, whereas for GJ 406, GJ 269, GJ 208, and GJ 744, no conclusive evidence could be found. In addition, our analysis set theoretical lowest mass limits for any companion to these stars, ranging from 7 Jupiter masses. The system of GJ 411, on the other hand, does not seem to contain resonant multiple companions despite exhibiting an accelerating kinematics, which is consistent with our understanding

Recently, Variational Bayesian (VB) networks have gained popularity as a limited
edition of Bayesian Deep Neural Networks (B-DNNs), allowing for efficient
approximations of Bayesian inference through minimization of KL divergence.
However, the quality of VB network reconstructions depends heavily on data
quality, and such networks have not performed well in applications involving
image compression due to issues with existing VB networks' reconstruction
accuracy, particularly in cases where noise is present. In an effort to
significantly improve this limitation, we propose the Least Square VB
Autoencoder with Regularization, which utilizes a novel reconstruction loss
function. This loss function differs from the traditional VB loss and relies
heavily on regularization to mitigate overfitting in cases where training on
perfectly fitted data results in inaccurate predictions. By using this new
loss function, we achieve a considerable improvement in VB network
reconstruction, ultimately resulting in a 40.lem improvement over previous
reconstructions made using VB networks. Furthermore, our approach outperforms
other competing compression methods in terms of reconstruction accuracy
while maintaining efficient inference and encoding.

Smart home technology is gaining momentum, driven by Internet of Things (IoT) advancements. Yet, IoT applications are prone to security risks, which patients, children, and elderly people may particularly suffer from if their sensitive information is compromised. A secure smart home can significantly be enjoyed by these populations, which is why establishing a reliable monitoring system is of high importance. This paper presents a cutting-edge monitoring system designed for smart home devices and medical equipment, built on Private Block Chain technology and Location Based Services. The proposed approach uses mobile device GPS tracking, combined with a private blockchain, to monitor medical equipment or IoT devices at residential locations in real-time. The proposed system incorporates a new data verification and validation method within the private blockchain, providing a secure, decentralized solution. The performance of our location-based method was evaluated using various distance measures, including Euclidean, Manhattan, and Road Network Distance Routing (RNDR). Among these, RNDR showed better results, with location error rates of 12%, 18%, and 20% recorded at 95% of locations, compared to Euclidean and Manhattan methods, respectively.

A novel approach to quantizing log-likelihood ratio storage utilizing deep learning is presented. It was discovered that average L-values of QAM symbols consistently adhere to an ordered relationship, which facilitated the design of a deep autoencoder. This autoencoder simultaneously compresses and separately reconstructs L-values using a weighted loss function prioritizing accurate reconstruction of lower-magnitude inputs. The proposed method was demonstrated to rival the performance of state-of-the-art maximum mutual information quantization while reducing memory usage by at least 75%.

We have devised three new parameterized algorithms for identifying whether a directed graph can be represented in an upward planar layout. Specifically, we've developed a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the number of source vertices, an XP algorithm based on the tree-width, and a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the tree-width and the number of series-parallel structures. Our novel method combines the upward planarity constraints with the parameterized algorithms for series-parallel decomposition and tree-width. Interestingly, our research reveals that further investigation is needed to develop a fixed-parameter algorithm based solely on the number of series-parallel structures.

Crowdsourced image datasets, often marred by noise, pose a significant challenge for even the most sophisticated neural networks. This difficulty arises from class imbalance and uncertainties in labeling, issues that are particularly prevalent in datasets consisting of images of ancient Greek papyri such as AL-ALL and AL-PUB, which also encompasses the realm of digital humanities. This research proposes a novel method for addressing these problems in datasets compiled using crowdsourcing. This approach utilizes ensemble modeling to mitigate the effect of noise, a technique proven effective in dealing with the noise present in these datasets. Additionally, we describe a technique for capturing the distribution of data points, referred to as 'Human Softmax,' which reveals valuable insights into the crowdsource origin of the data points. Lastly, we demonstrate that leveraging measures of entropic uncertainty can facilitate data point reclassification in cases of class imbalance.

For semiflows with uniformly or nonuniformly expanding dynamics, which exhibit exponential decay in correlations, we can prove the exponential decay in the H\"older norm of the transfer operators acting on smooth observables.

A particular matrix known as a covering array has specific characteristics. It is made up of different symbols and certain sub-matrices must include each combination of those symbols a set number of times. The best, or smallest, such matrices are known as optimal, and if they have uniform distribution of those symbols across all columns they're also referred to as uniform. Historically, there have been limited optimal covering arrays, but a recent study has developed a method to produce an infinite set of them. This set includes covering arrays with a particular number of columns (d), a large number of rows (t), and a large number of symbols (t T). The study also found that a particular set of numbers can be used to determine if a given matrix is optimal, and this led to another set of numbers being classified as "good" based on their potential to produce optimal matrices. Finally, there are a few open questions left unanswered.

This paper examines a unique category of nonlocal games, denoted by $\mathcal{G}_\infty$, in which the imposter strategy always produces an identical outcome independent of the question being asked. Previously, researchers, led by Hirschfeld, proved that if the imposter strategy consistently produces the same outcome across all questions, it must have a certain average probability value $\le \frac{1}{2}$. This led to the discovery of a new, more robust definition of the $\mathcal{G}_\infty$ game class. Our research extends this by proving that if the imposter strategy is not perfectly certain in its response $\mathcal{G}_\infty$, it means the game's quantum value must be strictly limited to $\frac{1}{2}$. Our research further demonstrates that if the imposter strategy is not perfectly certain, the game's classical value must be strictly limited to $0$. Our research validates that if the imposter strategy is not perfectly certain, the game's quantum value must strictly be less than or equal to the classical value. Our research presents a new measurement tool to determine if a nonlocal game falls within the $\mathcal{G}_\infty$ class without relying on the computability of the density matrix. Our research presents an algorithmic method for determining if two elements within $SL(2,\mathbb{R})$ can combine to produce the $\mathcal{G}_\infty$ game
This study partially replicates the work by Soltani et al. who introduced EvoCrash, an automated tool for reproducing Java crashes through a guided genetic algorithm.

By utilizing sound wave velocity and absorption measurements in very strong magnetic fields, we have found a previously unobserved state transition in the interlocked vortex lattice structure of the doped material La$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$CuO$_4$. The discovered phase shift, occurring at high doping and magnetic field strengths, corresponds to a normal-to-square lattice structure transition. Ultrasonic measurement frequencies allowed us to identify this complex transition, where nearby interlocked lattice structures became out of sync, indicating a state transition triggered by a conventional elastic instability. These findings are corroborated by computational models, where a square lattice structure was shown to be more stable at higher doping levels than the interlocked composite structure.

Photons are valuable tools for understanding the properties of the quark-gluon plasma (QGP) created in high-energy nucleus-nucleus collisions (NNCOLs). Previous research focused on photon polarization in a static medium found that polarizations develop due to the medium's velocity field, and subsequent studies found that this effect can be used to investigate the medium's properties using the fluid-dynamic description of NNCOLs. Building on this, a theoretical study has been conducted to investigate how thermal photons interact with the medium's flow properties, and preliminary results have been found to be consistent with experimental data. Furthermore, this interaction is found to be influenced by viscosity, and researchers anticipate that this relationship will allow them to measure the QGP's viscosity using the fluid-dynamic description, effectively employing thermal photons as a "viscometer" for the QGP.

Our study centers on investigating regular magnetic orders composed of triangular and kagome lattices made up of spin-1/2, spin-1 and spin-3/2 particles without any external magnetic fields. Using a reliable numerical method, we resolved the Bethe-Ansatz equations and examined the strong-coupling limits in both cases. This enabled us to identify and distinguish various magnetic orderings, such as those called Néel, clock, ferrimagnetic, partial ferrimagnetic and spin liquid types. A particular focus of our research is on characterizing spin liquid states, particularly a type known as quantum spin liquid, within the strong-coupling limits of spin-1 and spin-3/2 systems. Furthermore, our calculations also revealed the critical behavior of the same systems, specifically regular quantum spin liquids, within the same parameter space. This research is set to provide fundamental insights into the interpretation of experimental data obtained from actual systems through the application of a well-established theoretical model.

Large data-driven companies have considered online controlled experiments (A/B Testing) a gold standard for several decades. Many companies use a standard framework that measures "average treatment effect" (ATE), but this approach has its limitations. One significant concern is controlling false discovery rates (FDR) when evaluating multiple hypotheses simultaneously, as past methods have struggled with the challenge of dependent data. In this research, we present a new framework (called T2D) designed to meet these challenges, providing robust and efficient results. Our method builds on past innovations that explored FDR control and uses a novel dependency-aware t-statistic (ta) that delivers stronger, more reliable results. Additionally, we leverage computational advancements that run in O(n) rather than the traditional quadratic time complexity, making it suitable for large-scale applications. Our method effectively detects dependent ATEs, providing significant improvements in power while effectively controlling FDR, especially in cases of very dependent data where previous methods have failed to meet FDR control. Additionally, we provide results and computations that are free from approximation as they are based on exact algorithms and we also provide a new version of the T2D method that uses computational improvements to run in linear time (O(n)) making it even more suitable for large-scale applications.

The foundational aspects of cosmological inflation are addressed. The derivation of equations governing the inflaton field, an introduction to slow-roll parameters, and a description of how inflationary perturbations correspond to cosmic microwave background temperature fluctuations are presented.

The CDF II Collaboration has made a precise measurement of the W boson mass which deviates from its predicted Standard Model value by 7$\sigma$. Although direct searches by the CDF II and ATLAS have set tight limits on low mass range rationals in 2HDM, this research explores the type-X 2HDM's potential to comply with both the W boson mass and muon's gyromagnetic ratio anomalies. Specifically, this model can satisfy both the observed anomalies and the CDF II search restrictions by introducing a minimal extension to the Standard Model.

Software developers who perform maintenance tasks encounter multiple change requests 
expressed by software engineers in different wording strategies, implying the same 
modification needs to be applied, leading to a difficulty in decision-making, as researchers have extensively investigated yet not fully solved. 
As a result, the task of concept location becomes more complicated due to varying 
sentence structures and semantic meanings. 
This study introduces a pioneering system named QUICKAR (Query Intelligent Reformulation 
for Finding Closely related KETs Using CROWD) to tackle the challenge of varying 
wording by reformulating inappropriate search queries based on relevant, in-domain context provided by developers, thus enhancing primary search query efficiency. 
Using crowdsourcing, we gathered a database of modification requests from actual development projects, including NLTK-suggested synonyms, anti-synonyms, and irrelevant terms for comparison purposes. 
By leveraging the reformulated queries from human experts via the crowd, we achieved an average improvement of 26.58% in system performance on an in-domain dataset. 
Additionally, we evaluated our approach on a dataset from maintenance practitioners and found that it outperformed two of the existing techniques, showing promising potential.

Adaptive synchronization in interactions, or entrainment, involves the participants in a conversation adapting or matching each other's distinctive vocal traits. To better grasp how people adapt to each other's communication style during conversations, it's necessary to analyze various acoustic characteristics and compare them through multiple metrics. However, traditional methods used for this purpose have several limitations, including the need for a large amount of labeled data and a specific categorization task. This paper explores a new unsupervised approach to assess entrainment using similarity distances that can be applied across different tasks and doesn't need to be modified. Specifically, we developed two new unsupervised metrics, dynamic spectral density similarity and temporal representation similarity, which measure acoustic characteristics in conversations at different levels. These metrics were implemented using deep neural networks and tested on established datasets, including two types of embedded training instructions and a set of recorded conversations about highly sensitive topics collected through telephone interviews. Our analysis shows that the proposed approach successfully identifies patterns of adaptive synchronization in conversations and that dynamic spectral density similarity tends to demonstrate more pronounced adaptive synchronization compared to temporal representation similarity. Moreover, our analysis reveals that the relationship between characteristics in conversations follows an irregular pattern, and that responses to initial statements in conversations are relatively consistent over time.

We've developed an open-source suite of web visualization tools tailored for
analyzing spectral and imaging data, which are being utilized in the second edition
of the RCSED galaxy energy distribution catalog (rcsed2.voxastro.org). To create
these tools, we employed Next.js, Tailwind CSS, and the Full Stack React front
end framework, ensuring they're accessible from anywhere and compatible with all
data formats. To display data, users can upload their own spectral or imaging
datasets or access those from the RCSED2 catalog. A web-based environment replaces
the traditional flat-text output of spectral fitting results in browser-based tools
like PySpecView, emulating the interactive experience of graphical interfaces like
Astropy or Python while maintaining cross-platform compatibility. Additionally,
we've incorporated a JSON-based data format for spectra, images, and galaxy data,
along with a data processing pipeline powered by Tornado, to ensure high-performance
processing and seamless data handling. To provide users with a seamless experience,
we've implemented advanced web capabilities, such as web Workers for intricate
computations and WebSockets for real-time feedback and two-way communication, in
conjunction with a database of known galaxies based on their characteristics. By
using this platform, users can not only visualize data but also share findings and
access a shared repository using QR codes, in addition to generating and
distributing pre-processed datasets in common formats. Furthermore, we've enabled

Classifying every video frame into its respective action can be a labor-intensive task, particularly for a large collection of unlabeled videos. There are significant challenges associated with identifying the duration and definition of each action. A new approach, referred to as Self-supervised Co-occurrence Action Parsing (SSCAP), tackles the problem by treating every video of a specific class as an original training dataset. SSCAP identifies actions and their occurrences without human intervention, reconstructs the duration of each action, and accurately classifies the action for every individual video frame. Experimental results on JHMDB-21, UCF101-24, and DGD-50 demonstrate SSCAP's superior performance on action recognition and segmentation tasks. Furthermore, our innovative method extends to semi-supervised learning by integrating labeled videos at different time points. Ultimately, every video frame is re-organized to match the defined actions, yielding impressive performance gains.

We explore the existence of seven hadronic molecular states consisting of $\bar D^{(*)} \Sigma_c^{(*)}$, create associated interpolating currents, and compute their masses, decay constants, and production rates through QCD sum rules. Utilizing current algebra, we then determine their relative production ratios in $\Lambda_b^0$ decays. The study also examines their decay properties and applies the Fierz rearrangement to analyze their ratios in the $J/\psi p$ mass spectrum.
