In this study, we investigate the Toeplitz algebras of specific classes of Toeplitz operators on the p-Fock space and the p-Bergman space with 1 < p < ∞.  Let BUC(ℂⁿ) and BUC(ℬ_ᵐ) represent collections of uniformly bounded and continuous functions on ℂⁿ and ℬ_ᵐ (ℂⁿ's unit ball) respectively.  On the p-Fock space, it is proven that the Toeplitz algebra, having translation-invariant, closed BUC(ℂⁿ) subalgebra symbols, can contain compact operators both with and without the closure operation applied.  On the p-Bergman space, a similar but more restrictive condition is required, necessitating the subalgebra symbols to be closed.  In both cases, the key to these findings revolves around the phenomenon where the zero set of such symbols may include an entire analytic subspace.  Consequently, the necessary linear operators can be efficiently constructed using the kernel representation of these operators.

Despite significant advancements in object detection, current methods have limitations in detecting diverse object categories due to the labor-intensive process of creating training data with bounding-box annotations. Recent open-vocabulary object detection methods have been developed to address this limitation by training on a set of base categories, enabling detection of unseen object types. However, their effectiveness is restricted by the relatively small number of base categories used for training. To mitigate this constraint, we present a technique to automatically produce pseudo annotations of diverse objects, including their bounding-box coordinates, through the combination of image captioning and box proposal algorithms. With these pseudo labels, we train a detection model, which, when combined with few initial annotations provided by interactive bounding-box feedback, significantly enhances its detection performance across diverse object categories. Experimental results on the COCO dataset validate the efficacy of this technique, with our method achieving mAP of 48.24 on the COCO 80 category dataset, 41.24 on the COCO 188 category dataset, and 33.87 on the COCO 5000 category dataset, with notably high performance across all categories evaluated. Furthermore, our method demonstrates generalizability to larger and more complex datasets, including the 10K category ImageNet dataset without any manual intervention, with mAP of 30.24, representing an encouraging first step towards unsupervised object detection.

A young B star in the Rho Ophiuchus cloud produces a significant H II region, which is surrounded by strong ionization and other physical effects on surrounding molecular gas.  This area is unique in that it allows the study of how star-irradiated material looks when it has not yet been ionized, providing a context in which to assess the impact of high-intensity starlight on interstellar material.  A comprehensive analysis of starlight as the primary source of radiation in this cloud reveals that this mechanism is responsible for the observed spectrum in the south-east of the cloud, with no evidence of other contributing radiation sources.  A detailed study of this irradiated material indicates that it is primarily composed of atomic hydrogen.  This hydrogen gas has a spatial distribution that corresponds to what might be expected if it were photoionized, but the velocity of this hydrogen does not match the expected distribution of a rotating accretion disk around the star.  This discrepancy suggests that this hydrogen is not simply an accumulation of material that has been photoionized, rather it may be in contact with high-intensity starlight.  A comparison of ionized and atomic hydrogen in Rho Ophiuchus reveals that the former is primarily concentrated in the centre of the system, with less intense ionization towards the periphery, while the latter is observed towards the south-east.  This distinction may be attributed to the role of self-absorption in determining the distribution of ionized hydrogen.  A

The remarkable achievements of Transformer models in natural language tasks have piqued the interest of computer vision experts to explore their potential applications in visual tasks. A notable benefit of Transformer models is their ability to capture complex dependencies within input sequences while facilitating parallel processing, an advantage over traditional recurrent networks. Unlike convolutional networks, Transformers rely on minimal inductive biases in their design, making them ideally suited for set-function applications. Moreover, their straightforward architecture allows image data to be represented as a fixed-size vector, similar to embedded input sequences, which can then be processed using a self-attention mechanism. This process enables modeling of global relationships within images, as well as capturing multiple scales of content, making it an attractive choice for various computer vision tasks. This review aims to provide an in-depth overview of the progress achieved by Transformer models in computer vision, specifically focusing on their applications in image classification, object detection, semantic segmentation, and video-based task implementations, including necessary modifications and differences in approach as compared to the standard Transformer architecture. By highlighting these advancements, this survey aims to identify potential research areas and investigate the benefits and limitations of adopting Transformer models in computer vision.

Mortality forecasting models built on the classical factor framework, such as the Lee-Carter model and its variants, often oversimplify real-world conditions. In response, authors have suggested incorporating elements from the Bayesian framework, which models factor loadings as uncertain. Both traditional and Bayesian models assume that factor loading relationships remain consistent over time. Contrary to this, contemporary research indicates that economic influences on mortality rates change over time. With this in mind, we develop a novel model that incorporates both historical trends and current economic conditions, while allowing factor loadings to adapt to changing circumstances. Our analysis verifies the effectiveness of this model in accurately forecasting mortality. Moreover, results demonstrate that incorporating this level of flexibility not only improves short-term forecasting but also positively impacts long-term forecasting and overall performance.

Reducing the cost of neural architecture search (NAS) by sharing weights across multiple child models has been an area of focus. Unfortunately, child models may suffer from interference, impacting their accuracy, due to the varying performance and data flows in top models. In this study, we: 1) Investigate the source and severity of interference, 2) Introduce an innovative data management strategy to minimize its impact, and 3) Improve the expressiveness of constant embeddings to reduce interference and minimize NAS's overall computational and memory requirements. Our proposed approaches are validated using the CHAIR framework on the CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and ImageNet datasets, where results show significant improvements - an average 1.9% higher top-1 accuracy can be achieved with 13% fewer samples, and the accuracy of child models in the final stages can be boosted by 2.8%. The source code is available at: https://github.com/huawei china/chair-iso.

Time series data in various scientific disciplines are analyzed and measured. One common technique to analyze these data points is to use multiple signal processing features that capture distinct characteristics, such as intensity, correlation, and shape, to summarize and represent individual time series in a meaningful way. This chapter's focus lies entirely within the R programming language, which enables it to handle both extraction and feature calculation alongside other necessary time series data preparation and analysis steps.
We identify concrete, infinitely precise criteria under which a proper geodesically complete CAT(0) space has a semistable fundamental group at its boundary.

Human-assisted Translation Quality Assessment (TQA) is an extensively utilized method that helps gauge machine translation efficiency, negotiate translation contracts, and evaluates human translator proficiency.  Despite its importance, little research exists using quantitative methods to determine TQA's reliability. In contrast, this investigation employs various statistical methods to assess the reliability of human translators. We utilize multiple indicators, such as translation accuracy, fluency, and thoroughness, to evaluate a translator's reliability. Different statistical techniques, including those for categorical and continuous data, are applied to corporate translation samples, with a focus on establishing the translator's, rather than the reviewer's, reliability. The study ultimately explores the challenges posed by TQA and discusses potential solutions in assessing translator reliability using statistical methods.

In random systems, the scattering matrix correlates incident wave patterns with internal distributions within a volume, and previously this correlation was leveraged to increase energy delivered to a target. This study determines a general set of constraints and formulas governing the eigenvalues and modes within any given geometry that optimize energy within a specific area within that geometry. These formulas are universally applicable, regardless of the system's characteristics or factors influencing it, and they predict that certain properties are necessary for optimal energy concentration, and that this concentration is possible regardless of how small the target size becomes.

We've found that using the same data and training methods, the key components of neural networks (so-called "lottery tickets") are often similar or even the same. This discovery raises the possibility that these optimized networks are merely variations of a limited set of ideas. By exploring the underlying structures of neural networks, we found that even without training, networks with significantly reduced capacity can still accurately classify complex image patterns. This suggests that these optimized networks are ultimately relying on a limited set of fundamental features to perform their tasks. This discovery has significant implications for the field of neural network research, as it challenges the long-held assumption that these complex models are necessary for performing complex tasks.

In lotteries with exponentially increasing payout levels, a smart player knows when 
to purchase tickets, how many to buy, and how many to hold, based on the current jackpot amount.
By utilizing a dynamic programming framework, a player can ensure the maximum possible return 
on investment is achieved, and by employing a backward-looking approach, they can adapt to 
changing jackpot sizes. Notably, a critical threshold for jackpot sizes exists below which it 
is not beneficial to participate, and beyond which a lucrative opportunity arises, and in 
this favorable regime, a specific ratio of tickets to jackpot sizes allows a player to 
secure a substantial return on investment.

The large-charge expansion technique opens up a new possibility for calculating critical properties of high-charge operators $\phi^Q$, where the charge $Q$ is fixed. For operators of a given charge, the mathematical structure of their critical properties can be determined by performing a series of calculations at the six-loop level, combining the results with an existing two-parameter ansatz. We utilize this approach to find the critical exponent of the six-loop $O(N)$ $\phi^Q$ operator, where $Q$ is an integer from 3 to 6, thereby allowing us to refine our understanding of the operator's behavior. We then derive the critical $O(N)$ vector self-coupling $\lambda$ function up to the six-loop level and use it to calculate the critical exponents of the $O(N)$ $\phi^N$ operator. We find that the results agree well with existing three-loop $\epsilon$ expansion calculations when $Q$ is equal to 3, 4, 5, or 6, although they do not match at $Q$ equal to 7.

Our research systematically explores the impact of novel electron-phonon coupling mechanisms on valley Hall transport in two-dimensional materials, particularly when driven by mid-infrared or optical phonons, through a non-equilibrium dynamics model. We find that in 2D materials, the valley Hall effect is highly resistant to the effect of these phonons to the extent that the carrier-phonon coupling remains relatively weak. However, when the 2D material is in a symmetrical valley state configuration and the electron-phonon coupling becomes significantly strong, it can cause a phase discrepancy of the valley-Hall current, either 180 degrees or 4 quarters, due to the effect of these phonons. Furthermore, our model reveals that this phenomenon can serve as a characteristic indicator of the presence of these phonons in 2D materials, also allowing us to calculate the size of the resulting orbital gap, which is seen to be proportional to the 2D strain and the size of the 2D material's valley-coupled units.

The VisDA 2022 Challenge seeks unsupervised domain adaptation for industrial waste sorting in semantic segmentation tasks, where we proposed the SIA_Adapt model. To tackle the challenge, we introduced three key methods: (1) a self-iteration attention module for reducing representation discrepancies, (2) patch-level unsupervised domain adaptation using high-resolution features, and (3) improving segmentation quality within sensitive industrial settings. Our approach resulted in first-place rankings in both baseline and robust tracks of the challenge.

t-SNE is a widely employed method for reducing high-dimensional data to lower-dimensional representations, particularly in data visualization. Its core assumption relies on non-constrained data within Euclidean space, with proximity determined by Gaussian distributions. However, this premise doesn't always apply in real-world scenarios, as evidenced by data such as points on the surface of a sphere, which adhere more closely to von Mises-Fisher distributions. In response, this study develops a novel vMF-SNE algorithm tailored for embedding spherical data efficiently. Utilizing an iterative procedure, it achieves more effective embeddings than the conventional t-SNE method, as highlighted through its performance on synthetic and actual medical imaging data sets, resulting in more informative visualizations and better overall results.

We investigate polaron properties in the two-dimensional Fermi polaron from both theoretical and numerical perspectives. An analytical diagrammatic method is developed to describe the decoupling of the many-body wave function in two dimensions. The results from this approach reveal that, at zero temperature, the duality between the polaron and the photon is characterized by two critical lengths: the light diffusion length and the gyromagnetic suppression length. When the duality parameter exceeds a certain critical value, the photon becomes completely screened, leaving behind a nearly pure polariton state, which exists across a wide range of parameters. The numerical calculations conducted in two dimensions differ significantly from one-dimensional and three-dimensional polaron studies where only one critical length (the quasiparticle decay length) or two lengths (the quasiparticle and photon decay lengths) are present respectively, which underscores the unique characteristics of the two-dimensional polaron system. Furthermore, the concept of "saturation non-thermal activation" is also explored in the context of two-dimensional polaron studies, which hold crucial implications for the study of two-dimensional systems across the ferromagnetic spin-exchange interaction, Bose-Einstein condensate and two-dimensional metals.

In this hybrid digital-analog approach to quantum computing, any quantum algorithm can be implemented without traditional two-qubit gates by utilizing an inherent, always-active connection between qubits. Building on this principle, our research explores how digital-analog simulation can be used to study fermionic systems, specifically the Fermi-Hubbard model, using a fermionic SWAP network and a method to correct distortions. Focusing on the effects of qubit connectivity and the distribution of interaction coefficients, as well as the precision of entanglement, our results indicate that an optimal qubit connectivity arrangement for simulating fermionic systems of any spin configuration can be determined without knowing the specific details of the system. Moreover, our research shows that digital-analog simulation can efficiently handle fermionic systems even when the effects of distortion are present.

Graph polynomials hold significant value due to their potential to develop algebraic formulas describing various graph characteristics and encoding multiple graph invariants through their evaluation processes. Certain graphs, including complete and bipartite structures, can be identified through matching polynomial properties and relationships with established polynomial sets. The chromatic polynomial evaluated at -1 reveals the count of a specific graph orientation type. This study focuses on a general theorem involving families of graphs, which can be characterized through polynomials with established linear recurrence relations. This finding provides numerous applications in characterizing similar graph types, and offers an alternative to using complex polynomial sets in favour of a simpler linear relationship approach. The work highlights the distinct capabilities of graph polynomials in describing various graph characteristics.

We derive an expression for the pullback of the Hitchin connection, extending from the moduli space of genus two curves to a 10-fold cover of a Teichmueller curve, which was first found by Veech. Subsequently, we develop an expression in terms of iterated integrals that describes the monodromy representation of this connection. Consequently, as a secondary result, we determine the quantum representations of a vast array of pseudo-Anosov elements in the genus two mapping class group.

Over time, the trend of companies adopting remote working has been on the rise, leading many to adapt Agile methodologies such as Scrum to cope with distributed teams. However, the global shift to fully remote working brought about by the COVID-19 pandemic was a unprecedented phenomenon. This research involves an empirical study involving multiple studies to explore the effects of remote working on Scrum project success. The investigation combines data from the RemoWork project, a German government initiative, along with academic journals to develop a comprehensive model. A theoretical framework for measuring remote working practices was developed and subsequently refined through a cross-disciplinary analysis of data. Additionally, the research's findings were confirmed through an empirical study involving 69 Scrum masters and 137 remote workers from German companies, who assessed the effect of various remote working practices on Scurum project success using multiple project success indicators. The research identified statistically significant correlations between multiple remote working practices and improved project outcomes. The findings were then incorporated into an operational model for achieving successful remote working in Scrum projects. The research's conclusions highlight the importance of adopting flexible working routines that balance personal and work-life conditions to ensure high project success rates.

The concept of dichotomous matrices serves as an expanded interpretation of Hermitian matrices, with newly formulated guidelines identifying which arrowhead matrices fit this classification. Furthermore, specific conditions were derived to ensure unitary irreducibility of these matrices, and their maximum orthonormal vector count was calculated in relation to boundary numerical range, a criterion used in classification. This research enabled a comprehensive matrix classification based on the aforementioned Gau-Wu numbers.

In a study using the ALICE detector at the LHC, scientists investigated the elliptical movement of electrons created when beauty particles decay at a specific point near the centre of a collision between lead nuclei at a high energy of 5.02 TeV. These electrons were observed within a narrow region and the researchers found a stronger movement in a particular direction during a collision that had an irregular shape. Their data matched predictions made by several computer models and showed that a stronger movement of these electrons, when compared to those created in a different type of collision, increased in line with what is expected to occur due to a greater elliptical movement of the collision itself.

In pursuit of breakthroughs in the simulation of 2D materials, we explore the application of algebraic topological methods that extend beyond traditional point-cloud topology used in spatialepidemiology. We focus on analyzing datasets based on a geographic divide, where regions are assigned color values. We introduce novel metrics based on stabilization techniques that address color changes rather than spatial distortions. These metrics are computed using the persistence diagrams of colored alpha-complexes. We demonstrate the effectiveness of these metrics with synthetic and real-world datasets.

This study examines the extremal gain of optimal power control over binary power control in networks with multiple interferers. In these networks, it's proven that the gain of optimal power control is directly proportional to $\log(K)$. Consequently, the optimal gain in such networks is always greater than that of binary power control by a factor of $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$. Moreover, it's found that binary power control can be considered as a suboptimal solution with a gain within $\log(\sqrt{K}+\epsilon)$ of optimal power control for any positive $\epsilon$. These findings are based on a new method of quantizing power levels using a single quantization step, which provides a simple and efficient characterization of such networks. This method was pioneered in a prior investigation by Tse and Bresler. Such a quantization approach is shown to effectively capture the inherent structural properties of such networks. As a result, it provides a computationally efficient method for designing precoders that perform near optimally at finite precision. In this study, it's discovered that the gain of optimal power control is always greater than that of binary power control by a factor of $\sqrt{K}$ and that the resulting precoders are at least as robust as those selected through binary power control. Auditing business processes often requires categorization of complex data.
Weighted bipartite graphs can efficiently represent transactions between
financial accounts, allowing us to apply methods from formal concept analysis.
The introduced methodology provides a transparent and scalable categorization
framework that handles uncertainty by subsuming imprecise values with the
Dempster-Shafer theory and orthogonal distances. The framework's capability
is demonstrated through an auditing scenario where money has been misplaced.

The Strauss process is a point process that weighs the probability of specific locations based on the distance between them and their overall count. We've found that traditional methods of calculating this probability, like the acceptance-reject method, are inefficient at certain distances. To solve this issue, we've created a new'stitching' technique that seamlessly connects Strauss process realizations of decreasing point counts, making acceptance-reject type algorithms more efficient. We've demonstrated that our stitching method works properly and has a reasonable expected computation time. Additionally, we've created a specialized algorithm tailored to the Poisson process, resulting in significantly faster computation for smaller'stitching' lengths.

In the context of the generalized uncertainty principle, modifications are identified in the Lorentz and Galilean transformations. The findings demonstrate that the generalized uncertainty principle's effects are more prominent at high speeds, as they become more pronounced in the Lorentz transformation than in the Galilean transformation. The underlying symmetry that gives rise to these transformations, in the form of the Lorentz transformation, is found to be broken at high speeds. The symmetry remains intact in the Galilean transformation. The number of symmetry generators that remain unchanged or unaccounted for within the generalized uncertainty principle's framework is found to be seven.

Multitasking scheduling in service industries has gained significant interest due to workers frequently transitioning between tasks. Building on Hall, Leung and Li's 2016 model for shared processing multitasking, this research extends the model to a more complex setting with parallel machines. Unlike the original model, where a set fraction of processing capacity is allocated to routine jobs, this extension allows for varying fractions of routine jobs' processing capacity to be assigned on each machine. The primary objectives remain the minimization of makespan and total completion time. Unfortunately, it's demonstrated that solving these problems optimally using polynomial time unless P=NP if machine ratios are fully adjustable. Conversely, it's possible to devise efficient solutions for machines with limited allocatable ratios or specific job ratio constraints.

A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on control system development for a one-legged hopping robot that jumps on a simply supported elastic foundation. This simulation model, which incorporates nonlinear characteristics, accurately represents the one-legged hop's dynamic behavior. The ground deformation model used in this simulation is based on nonlinear Hertzian contact dynamics. To develop stable and efficient control systems, two approaches are employed: linearized model predictive control and pseudo-inverse based quadratic programming. These methods demonstrate their effectiveness through various successful one-legged hopping trajectories on an elastic foundation. To validate the accuracy of the one-legged hop's dynamic model, the simulation results are compared to analytical solutions of nonlinear Hertzian contact dynamics. Additionally, experimental trials are conducted using a one-legged hop made from a single board and driven by a pitch-based actuation mechanism. This mechanism serves as an electro-mechanical system that mimics human hopping.

In the rapidly evolving landscape of Internet of Things (IoT) networks, periodic firmware updates are vital for maintaining optimal security and reliability. Given the trend towards implementing security measures via codified policies and decentralized network configurations, we assessed the performance of the latest mesh-network protocols – BPLC 1.1, BLT 10, and TPV3 – through 1200 hours of continuous testing. Our investigation involved a large-scale mesh network, analyzing firmware updates and signal strength readings from 2048 nodes. The results were evaluated on a daily and seasonal basis, utilizing real-world mesh networks in the United States, Canada, and Europe. Our comprehensive analysis focused on the time required for updates, signal strength variations, and inter-node connectivity, aiming to identify the best protocol for the CoAP-based mesh network.

To make the most out of the most effective human-level interactive graph search method, researchers have explored applying it to a wider range of problems than it was initially designed for. However, when searching for multiple targets at once, human-computer collaboration becomes significantly more complicated. A new interactive algorithm using oracle black-box and grey-box techniques has been developed to tackle this issue by scheduling human interaction in an optimal manner. A new model has been created to understand the performance limitations of this problem, which involves making multiple target retrieval more efficient despite the constraints of available budget and human participation. Through experiments conducted on both generated and real-world datasets, the algorithm's superiority over other approaches has been substantiated, providing a solution to a complex problem within optimal bounds.

The exploration of quantum machine learning has demonstrated the potential for
groundbreaking insights in both areas of research. Experimental findings indicate
that quantum computers could significantly outperform traditional machines in
certain machine learning tasks, although they may also be susceptible to
adversarial threats. These threats involve introducing small, manipulative
distortions to legitimate data that can cause a high level of confidence in
incorrect predictions by the quantum learning system. This study investigates
the universality of these threats in quantum classification systems, employing
examples based on real-life images and quantum matter phases. We discovered that
universally damaging instances exist both for quantum systems built upon
superconducting architecture and for systems using complex vectors with more
elements than their respective initial input. Moreover, our research reveals that
almost all samples had been incorrectly classified by the quantum learning
system when only a minimal disturbance was added to legitimate data. This study
also found that in some cases, attacks with zero added disturbance can still
mislead quantum classifiers. Our work provides the first universal examples of
adversarial examples for quantum classification methods. Furthermore, our study
offers the first universal examples of adversarial examples for quantum
classification methods that are induced by expected measurements rather than being
dependent on specific data. These results are encouraging for our ability to
detect and address adversarial attacks in quantum machine learning settings.

We examine Steklov eigenvalues in nearly spherical domains of three dimensions. 
Building on our earlier research, which demonstrated the differentiability 
of two-dimensional Robin eigenvalues with respect to domain changes, we 
obtain various consequences related to the Steklov eigenvalues. These 
include: the Steklov eigenvalues are highly sensitive to small boundary 
variations; their averages over all eigenvalues of a given size exhibit 
deterioration in boundary approximation; and we establish a limit relation 
for the lowest Steklov eigenvalue under Robin and Neumann boundary conditions.

Conformance checking focuses on comparing modeled process behavior to observed process behavior from actual event data. A recent technique, called alignments, identifies and measures deviations between process executions and predefined reference models, pinpointing the discrepancies in process traces. Notably, alignments require entire or initial segments of process runs from start to finish; this paper explores new methods to analyze partial process runs and assesses these methods with real-world event data.

Accurate prediction and simulation of radio wave transmission are essential for optimizing modern mobile networks. Existing propagation models are widely used, but they have significant limitations, as they are only applicable in specific scenarios and their accuracy declines rapidly as they encounter increasing uncertainties. In this research, a new method using deep convolutional neural networks significantly expands the scope of predictive models by leveraging real-time data measurement. Our study shows that this method's performance surpasses traditional models when predicting changes in unknown network patterns. Additionally, this method's predictive ability can be confidently extended to uncharted territories, even with limited corresponding data, and it effectively estimates signal loss caused by terrain features' altitude changes. With these capabilities, this method has the potential to optimize mobile network deployment while minimizing costs associated with physical site surveys.

A straightforward semantics is proposed for temporal planning. We define and formally establish the logic within the interactive theorem prover Isabelle/HOL, and then obtain a validation algorithm based on that semantics. By using a formal Isabelle/HOL proof, it is shown that the validation algorithm faithfully represents the developed semantics. We also demonstrate through practical experiments that the verification of our algorithm is useful.

Power system expansion planning models, used to integrate renewable resources, rely on complex optimization problems involving various economic and technical factors. These factors carry significant uncertainties, yet their impact on model accuracy is poorly understood. This study introduces a new approach to assess the sensitivity of power system models to specific assumptions. This method involves re-optimizing the model under alternative parameters and measuring the resulting differences in solutions. By applying this method to real-world power systems, we discovered significant variations in model outcomes, including substantial disparities in deployed renewable energy resources and total network investment costs, with up to 774% variation in costs occurring. Furthermore, our results indicate a high correlation between model accuracy and the ability to represent complex network interactions, with models failing to capture essential power system properties such as loop and branch flows. This study's findings highlight the limitations of current power system models and suggest opportunities for improvement through advanced optimization approaches or assumption adjustments that better reflect the intricacies of power systems.

This study establishes the global existence of classical solutions for the Vlasov-Poisson and the ionic Vlasov-Poisson models within confined areas, under specified boundary conditions that include a particular reflection scenario for the Vlasov equation.

When conducting software maintenance, developers typically receive numerous, loosely written requests for change, described using everyday language and involving relevant technical terms. The task requires identifying key terms related to the request's technical context, allowing developers to locate relevant sections in the source code and apply the desired changes. Unfortunately, developers often struggle to craft effective search terms for their tasks. This paper presents a new approach, STRICT, which uses machine learning and information retrieval to automatically determine suitable search terms based on a change request's description. The proposed method leverages a source code index and a corpus of software comments to generate search terms that effectively pinpoint relevant sections in the source code. Experiments on a dataset of request pairs demonstrate that STRICT outperforms baseline systems, successfully identifying 70.9% of concept locations and nearly doubling the accuracy of a previous search term extraction method.

Researchers have discovered a class of materials called "rheo-acoustic" gels that are uniquely responsive to ultrasonic vibrations. This breakthrough reveals that when subjected to these high-frequency sound waves, colloidal gels exhibit a profound reduction in rigidity. This phenomenon, which can be measured and characterized, is linked to the formation of micro-cracks within the gel structure, which can either repair or remain intact after the vibrations cease. Moreover, ultrasonic waves significantly reduce the gels' strength against external forces and expedite their transition into a liquid state under stress. Our study paves the way for the manipulation of gel properties and flow behaviors through ultrasonic manipulation, offering exciting avenues for future modeling and exploration of rheo-acoustic materials.

This research paper explores the validity of the Collatz conjecture for a certain set of odd sequences with an infinite number of elements, which is then generalized to encompass all positive odd integers. By applying the principle of mathematical induction, this extended set is used to prove the conjecture. A second verification of the conjecture via mathematical induction is also presented in section 9. Consequently, the conjecture is validated through a duplicate approach. The paper concludes by offering two algorithms written in GNU Octave code, which are designed to evaluate the credibility of the conjecture for specific numbers. The first algorithm represents a re-statement of the Collatz conjecture function, whereas the second generates a new Collatz function, which is then checked using the first algorithm for a sequence of numbers and the number of steps required to reach one as per the conjecture.

To effectively organize digital collections and facilitate targeted searching within a particular field, precise categorization of document subjects is crucial. Specifically, classifying academic papers into core areas or subfields enables focused retrieval and pinpointing relevant content. Nevertheless, manually assigning classification categories is a time-consuming and labor-intensive process, making it a pressing issue for large research institutions and databases, including the pre-print archive arXiv, which faces this challenge due to the rapid influx of new content. In an attempt to develop an automated subject classification system for scientific documents, we have explored the connection between academic disciplines and core areas or subfields within specific fields, which is rooted in mathematical entities and their associated knowledge graphs. By leveraging this foundation, we have created a Mathematical Entity Linking (MEL) task that seeks to identify and extract relevant mathematical concepts from a given paper's abstract. Our proposed framework not only provides a practical starting point for subject classification but also enables further advancement by utilizing the extracted mathematical entities to infer paper categories. To our knowledge, this is the first initiative that combines the mathematical knowledge graph and MEL to tackle the subject classification challenge.

To guarantee matching among all agents, the Deferred Acceptance algorithm traditionally demands complete and ranked preference lists from each party. However, studies show that stable matchings are found even with shorter, albeit incomplete, preference lists, thus sparking curiosity as to why and how agents should optimize these lists to maximize matching coverage. Researchers have introduced a metric, called proposal history, which tracks the likelihood that each agent will be matched with another, if they were to initiate or respond to a proposal. Utilizing this metric, the current paper develops an offline and online strategy for determining which agents should make which proposals during the matching process. These schemes are proven to outperform random choices and achieve a better guarantee, specifically at least an $\Omega(d^{-1/2})$ improvement in matching coverage probability for large and growing preference list lengths, where $d$ denotes the number of interactions involved. Furthermore, the algorithms can be applied to various and complex preference structures, including those involving complete lists and complete graphs. The proposed schemes are evaluated on a range of these scenarios and found to significantly outperform random choices. The best-performing algorithms are shown to approach optimal performance, specifically getting close to matching coverage probability of $\Omega(d^{-3/2})$ on complex preference lists. The results are even more impressive when applied to more complex scenarios such as complex preference structures. The experiments confirm the results and show how the algorithms can be applied to very complex scenarios such as employer-worker, student-alumni and group-date problems. The

Current evaluation metrics for summarization models are inadequate, as they are
highly unreliable in assessing human quality and limit the variety of generated
summaries. To overcome these shortcomings, a new evaluation metric called
SummScore has been developed. This innovative approach utilizes a CrossEncoder
to compare the semantic meaning of original text and summaries, thus preventing
bias against diverse summary formats. The Cross-Encoder, pre-trained on text-matching tasks, effectively captures nuanced semantic differences between summaries.
Furthermore, SummScore encompasses four distinct sub-models assessing Coherence,
Consistency, Fluency, and Relevance, which are combined to form the final score.
To achieve compact and real-world processing performance, the final score is
derived from ensembling these individual scores and a temperature transformation.
The results of our experiments demonstrate SummScore's superior performance in
conforming to human assessment standards.

A new method for extracting a sparse signal from cross-related data is presented. This type of correlation is common in fields such as optics and seismic analysis, but the additional dimension creates an inverse problem bottleneck as the number of related data points quadratically increases. To overcome this, a new scheme is offered which uses a specific pattern of connections. This pattern, revealed in the paper, has significant implications for signal recovery algorithms. Notably, a fast recovery method can be leveraged, which only needs to collect half the amount of data points compared to traditional methods, yet it still yields nearly identical results. This breakthrough is supported by a mathematical proof. Furthermore, an experiment is conducted to verify the method's efficacy, demonstrating its ability to recover a signal accurately even when there are disturbances present.

The conventional approach to 3D object detection, where camera and LiDAR data are combined, is no longer tenable in realistic scenarios due to its vulnerability to LiDAR malfunctions. This has restricted the use of these models in practical autonomous driving applications. Our novel technique, called BEVFusion, represents a significant improvement in robustness by leveraging a more accurate spatial structure of LiDAR and camera data. It achieves this through the integration of cross-modal feature fusion within a multi-level BEV representation. Because BEVFusion no longer relies on LiDAR data, it can function effectively even when camera and LiDAR sensors are mismatched. Our experimental results confirm the superior performance and greater resistance to LiDAR malfunctions of our technique compared to existing models.

We are reassessing the significance of thermal fluctuations in incompressible fluid turbulence and proposing a theoretical model where these fluctuations can maintain turbulence in a stable state. This model is based on the idea that as turbulence is contained within a specific volume of fluid, it becomes isolated from external influences, and the resulting energy levels remain stable. The energy levels within this closed system are contingent on the system's finite size and thereby subject to fluctuations due to thermal effects. The fluctuations arise from the idea that the energy transfer between different scales within the turbulence occurs continuously, and the resulting emittance is proportional to the fourth power of the fluid's angular frequency and the temperature. The measurement of this emittance, previously known as the 'dissipation range brownian motion,' has been challenging due to the minuscule scale of the turbulence's dissipation range. The study of this phenomenon presents a significant problem due to the limitations of current instrumentation and the constraints of working with extremely small particle sizes. The estimated thermal decay rates provide an essential benchmark for evaluating the feasibility of future experiments.

Previous studies on laser propagation through a heated fluid employed simplified thermal conductivity and convective heat transfer assumptions, leading to inaccurate predictions. This study presents an in-depth numerical analysis that accurately simulates the thermal behavior of the fluid and its impact on laser interaction phenomena. The study examines the diffracted beam in the far field produced by a laser passing through a heated fluid and identifies key features. The study further explores the behavior of the incident laser as it interacts with the heated fluid and identifies distinct spatial and temporal patterns resulting from diffraction, deflection, and laser energy loss due to absorption and scattering. The study provides a comprehensive understanding of the underlying physical mechanisms, allowing for accurate interpretation of observed patterns in the far field.

Discussions among developers encompass a variety of interactions, including in-person conversations and online comments, which are beneficial to label as relevant to software design for documentation and improvement purposes. This is made possible through a process known as design mining, which applies machine learning to categorize discussions as pertaining to design. However, design mining discussions are subject to variability, which might impact the performance of the model. This paper proposes a method to assess the stability of design mining models by analyzing the differences in predictions made by the model when given slightly altered versions of the discussion text. Analyzing the correlations among features, the model's predictions, and the labels revealed the reasons behind the model's stability. Experiments with four datasets and multiple discussion segments demonstrated the effectiveness and importance of specific semantic features, and further revealed that datasets with more consistent design-related discussions tend to yield more stable design mining models.

This paper presents a novel evaluation engine for big stream and data processing pipelines called H-STREAM. It integrates stream processing operators as cloud-based micro-services to facilitate the analysis of near-real-time data streams. These micro-services are dynamically configured based on specific service-level agreements and resource availability of the hosting platform. We illustrate the effectiveness of H-STREAM through a comparative study of processing parallel data streams and demonstrate its superiority over existing techniques, such as Stratosphere and Apache Flink. Furthermore, H-STREAM is scheduled using an extended version of the MOCHA compiler, ensuring efficient deployment of micro-services on cloud platforms.

The hunt for Top and Bottom companions is a key area of study for both the ATLAS and CMS experiments, as their single production offers considerable detection possibilities. Though past research mainly focused on the resonant production mode of these hypothetical particles, new findings have uncovered a diverse and complex phenomenology associated with the non-resonant diagrams at narrow widths. In this research, we thoroughly examine the influence of the non-resonant diagrams on the single production topologies of Top and Bottom companions and their subsequent decays to W bosons and various quarks. Through numerical calculations and table-based presentations, we compare the relative strengths of the non-resonant and resonant diagrammatic contributions and provide guidelines for accurately representing these diagrams in experimental analyses.

A recent breakthrough in translating English to SPARQL using neural machine translation (NMT) models holds great promise for automating SPARQL query generation, but these models have a major limitation: they can only handle queries based on knowledge that was learned during training. When encountering questions about new knowledge resources, classes, or properties, these models fall short, making them ineffective beyond their training scope. Leveraging the success achieved in other areas of natural language processing, we developed an innovative approach that involves introducing a 'copy mechanism' to neural SPARQL translation (NeSPARQL) models. By enabling the models to draw on the question's abstract syntax tree, this approach facilitates the transfer of essential elements, such as pre-existing knowledge resources, classes, or properties, thereby enhancing the models' ability to handle queries that involve novel elements. Experimental results confirm that the NeSPARQL model performs significantly better than its basis, leading to an overall improvement of 11% in question answering accuracy when evaluated on datasets that were outside the training dataset.

This work reveals the flaws in utilizing citations as a basis for evaluating researchers and introduces a novel model for a more effective evaluation system.
One significant advantage of this new approach is that it produces comparable rankings to those based on citations with significantly less noise.
Moreover, it offers additional benefits that have been elusive to existing citation-based methods: 
  (a) It can rank both researchers and journals equally well, providing equal insight into both aspects, 
  (b) It can automatically detect both notable and unnotable work with high confidence, 
  (c) It can offer the ability to analyze past contributions and predict future performance, 
  (d) It can evaluate diverse fields and remain adaptable to different domains.
Our proposed method relies on high-quality journal labels obtained through a straightforward, low-effort process and uses a simple supervised learning model trained on selected keywords.
Evaluations on a comprehensive dataset of over 1.5 million papers from the past 115 years and 195,000 papers from the past ten years show that it significantly improves upon existing evaluation methods with several key advantages.

Advanced learning methods can address longstanding control challenges, but the complex neural networks used pose significant analysis difficulties regarding the safety of control systems. Fortunately, recent research has introduced methods for analyzing and verifying the complex control systems. This tutorial synthesizes and introduces techniques for verifying the robustness of neural networks that originated in related fields. These techniques are further applied to establish guarantees for systems that combine neural networks and control feedback loops. Ultimately, these tools facilitate the analysis of safe control systems and support deep reinforcement learning with robustness guarantees.

This study builds upon three significant lines of research related to dissimilarity-based clustering and integrates them into a unified framework that provides a principled and flexible method for performing clustering tasks. These research lines involve using functorial clustering, addressing clustering problems with variables that contain redundant information, and developing methods to handle overlapping clusters in a clustering hierarchy. By combining these insights, we develop innovative approaches to measure dissimilarity between variables and between clusters, as well as techniques to handle overlapping clusters. We establish theoretical connections between these methods and demonstrate their practical utility under realistic assumptions about real-world data. Additionally, we apply these techniques to a diverse set of real-world datasets, including a massive collection of DNA sequences associated with diseases.

Tensor completion has become a crucial technique for recovering incomplete visual data and its applications are highly relevant to real-world tasks such as image and video filling. However, existing methods primarily focus on recovering finished visual content and often struggle with processing streaming video, whose frames need to be processed in a sequential manner. Moreover, these methods typically require accessing the entire video dataset beforehand, which contradicts the streaming video scenario where only current or past frames can be accessed. This paper proposes a new approach called Patch Tracking-based Streaming Tensor Completion (PISVC) for filling in missing video streaming information. First, it develops a universal model using tensor rings that incorporates both low-rank and coherent information, and leverages patch matching for tracking moving objects across video frames. Additionally, it designs an efficient algorithm with computational complexity sub-linearly related to the number of video frames, making it suitable for processing streaming video. PISVC is validated on various visual tasks including video filling, past video reconstruction, and live video filling, and it significantly outperforms existing methods in these tasks.

It is demonstrated that except in three specific instances, the conjugacy classes of classical Weyl groups $W(B_{n})$, $W(D_{n})$, and $W(A_{n})$ where $n\geq 3$, do not correspond to Nichols algebras. The exceptions occur in the $n=2$ cases for $W(B_{2})$ and $W(A_{2})$. The proof relies on preliminary analysis that uses the Poincar\'e polynomial technique and the study of the Poincar\'e polynomial of the diagram of a pre-Nichols algebra obtained from a graph with the edge weights $\pm 1$, $\pm 2$, and $\pm 3$. This study also yields a polynomial bound for the number of 2-generated elements in a finite nilpotent algebra.

Three-dimensional rotating turbulent flows, characterized by an $l^{-5/3}$ power law in wave length, have been observed in various numerical studies. This "enstrophy containing" turbulence was initially interpreted as being similar to nonrotating, three-dimensional turbulent flow. However, such interpretations neglect the fundamental differences between even- and odd-mode wave numbers resulting from the preservation of angular momentum in rotating systems. This work focuses on even-mode turbulence, demonstrating that it too exhibits an $l^{-5/3}$ power law. Notably, when fourth-order finite difference methods are employed in global domain projections, even-mode energies become dominated by small-scale processes, following a $l^{-5/3}$ power law. This suggests even-mode turbulence is likely to be close to fully developed, and potentially consistent with inertial wave turbulence.

Researchers have introduced various forms of iterative graph normalization to enhance node feature representation in graph neural networks (GNNs), which relies on simplifying graph structure by removing influential nodes through maximum weight independent sets (MWIS). Although graph normalization integrates two complex problems - graph convolution and MWIS - that require distinct solutions, most advancements in this area overlook these challenges or apply generic methods that don't consistently deliver optimal results. Our research addresses these limitations by combining iterative normalization with a specific type of MWIS that uses iterative antimonotonic projections based on a submodular function, thereby guaranteeing better convergence and precision. We also develop a method to simplify graph structure while minimizing computational requirements by leveraging the similarity between graph labels and graph structure, which allows us to determine the optimal label sparseness and graph structure. Our proposed method, Label-Scaled Graph Normalization, demonstrates superior performance on various benchmark datasets, resulting in faster label assignment and more efficient graph structure simplification.

This research studies the impact of a magnetic field on electrically modulated single-layer graphene, aiming to understand the effect of modulation on the transport properties. We focus on one energy band at a time and account for both the modulated and k-space averaging effects. Our calculations confirm that the modulated effect is equivalent to a change in carrier type, indicating that our theoretical framework is valid. We observe that in samples with a p-type character, the modulated effect enhances the magnetic field's influence on transport properties. Conversely, in samples with a n-type character, the modulated effect suppresses the magnetic field's effect. Additionally, our analysis shows that the modulated effect leads to a change in thermodynamic properties, and these results are unaffected by the sample's geometric configuration or modulation method.

Recent monitoring over a period of five years involving regular spectral observations of the CR Dra system has yielded several key findings. This includes the discovery of a persistent, low-frequency radio emission characteristic that is most likely attributed to magnetospheric activity. The CR Dra system, comprising a binary pair of flare stars, has been continuously observed in radio waves for over forty years, with the current observations revealing a consistent, low-frequency radio emission that co-exists with occasional bursts. This is in contrast to the typical high-frequency gyrosynchrotron radiation associated with flares. The observed low-frequency radiation is believed to be a result of electron-cyclotron maser emission that operates within magnetospheric magnetic loop structures.

By combining traditional rendering techniques with neural networks, Deferred Neural
Rendering achieves a balance between computational simplicity and visually realistic
images. Extending DNR to use skinned meshes for rendering dynamic objects would
significantly expand its potential applications. However, doing so requires accounting
for unmodeled mesh deformations and potential misalignments, which can otherwise
jeopardize the rendering pipeline. To address these challenges for realistic virtual
human avatars, we developed Articulated Neural Rendering, a new framework that
extends DNR. In experiments and user evaluations, ANR consistently outperformed not
only DNR but also other avatar creation methods, demonstrating its superior
image quality and flexibility to render avatars at high frame rates.

Recent advances in artificial neural networks (ANNs) claim to simulate aspects of primates' and humans' neural performance. However, these ANNs primarily rely on basic visual characteristics when performing object recognition tasks, unlike humans. Additionally, ANNs are hindered by unusual or misleading input, whereas humans' learning of abstract patterns allows them to withstand extreme visual distortions. We propose a set of image transformation methods rooted in neurophysiological research, applying them to human visual performance and ANNs to evaluate their limits. The results demonstrate a notable disparity between humans and these ANNs in withstanding such transformations. We further explore the feasibility of improving ANNs by leveraging these transformation data, although limitations remain due to the inherent discrepancies between humans and these networks.

The connection between the Askey-Wilson algebra and both the SU(2) Chern-Simons theory, along with its relationship to the Reshetikhin-Turaev link invariant, which uses quantum algebra $U_q(\mathfrak{su}_2)$, is examined in this exploration. Certain tangles, including non-autonomous versions of the Alexander and Hopf tangles, can be utilized to define a basis for the space of cycle operators in the SU(2) Chern-Simons theory. Furthermore, a basis for the Askey-Wilson algebra can also be established using tangles with analogous properties to their non-autonomous counterparts, along with their trivalent vertices and a cycle. It is discovered that cycle operators, along with their trivalent vertices and a cycle, have a correlation with the generators of the cycle operators in the Reshetikhin-Turaev construction which involves the $U_q(\mathfr{su}_2)$ quantum algebra. This relationship can be utilized to establish that the cycle operators in the Reshetikhin-Turaev construction, along with their trivalent vertices and a cycle, are closed under the action of the $E$-generator of the Askey-Wilson algebra. This exploration may lead to a relationship between the cycle operators in both the SU(2) Chern-Simons theory and the Reshetikhin-Turaev construction, along with their trivalent vertices and a cycle, along with their generators.

Our study presents computational findings based on a novel trimer-cluster quantum Monte Carlo simulation approach, which accounts for quantum fluctuations in a class of two-dimensional frustrated antiferromagnets that form a network of closely-connected triangles. Specifically, we examined a weakly-connected hexagon lattice hosting the Kitaev-Clay-Kaplan-Moessner-Sherman model as an exemplary case, where nearby sites interact in a long-range manner. Our analysis focuses on the effect of inter-cluster bonds on the spin liquid's properties, particularly its response to increasing connectivity within the system. At a intermediate level of connection, our results reveal a significant shift towards an unconventional topological phase, where the spin liquid transitions from a non-trivial state with gapped boundaries to a non-topological state with gapped bulk and boundaries. Moreover, the theoretical framework's predictive capabilities are compared to recent experimental data obtained from a related compound, FeSe.

Pre-trained language models, exemplified by GPT-3, have exhibited an unexpected capability for zero-shot learning in various tasks without explicit training, likely resulting from their broad conditioning on diverse data and promptings. To better understand this phenomenon, we gathered a substantial dataset of 435 prompts and descriptions from the internet documenting the capabilities of language models, including specific examples of their training datasets, tasks, and applications. We then used this dataset in conjunction with prompt learning to meta-train a subset of large language models, initially in a few-shot capacity and subsequently as a few-shot adapter module to be attached to a wide-range of large language models. We discovered that our adapted language models demonstrated notable enhancements in zero-shot learning tasks, with a 13-point increase in accuracy, thereby enabling a unified framework for zero-shot, few-shot, and weak-shot learning. Furthermore, our framework is designed to facilitate weak-shot learning across diverse domains and extension with ease.

In depth research into the likelihood and characteristics of a first-order electroweak phase transition in the context of the $Z_3$-invariant NMSSM has been conducted. By analyzing the constraints from the Observed Higgs boson mass, data from LHC, dark matter searches and other parameters from physics, we determined the suitable parameter space for this specific model. Furthermore, we utilized numerical methods to investigate the likelihood and characteristics of early universe electroweak phase transitions within this model's remaining possibilities. Key indicators include the ratio of relic density and energy release during the phase transition were identified and studied. Results show that a substantial portion of model's parameter space is capable of meeting the requirements for successful electroweak phase transition as well as dark matter searches. Additionally, we found that the phase transitions that occur in this model are typically slow, appearing more plausible compared to other models that may involve the disappearance of the standard model's global $U_1$ symmetry. Such a scenario also reduces the possibility of detecting gravitational waves during these events. Ultimately, these predictions will allow for evaluation of the model's validity based on the results from ongoing and future searches for gravitational waves in the early universe.

We introduce novel approaches for visually and statistically identifying reliable redshifts through measurements of spectral or model spectra in the submillimeter waveband. Our approach consists of a 2-dimensional grid of predicted submillimeter optical depth shapes as a function of redshift, allowing us to synthesize observed submillimeter spectra. This methodology, dubbed High-z Sudoku, incorporates observed optical depths from other nearby objects, such as millimeter or submillimeter galaxies, that have previously been measured. Our approach leverages the similarities in submillimeter spectral shapes at high redshifts and reduces uncertainty by defining a 2-dimensional grid of predicted spectra to identify potential matches. Using a statistical measure, we identify two strong candidates for submillimeter redshifts, 4.889 for Herschel's brightest submillimeter galaxy and 5.698 for Herschel's second brightest submillimeter galaxy. Furthermore, we found that the statistical method had a 75% success rate in its initial application to a subset of millimeter wave galaxy spectra. Our approach effectively identifies reliable redshifts, and we apply it to the Simulated Herschel Atlas to find robust submillimeter redshifts in excess of 6. Our results demonstrate that the combination of very large optical depths and intense dust emission in the jet of AMPS_0143C are challenging for standard model spectra in the observed submillimeter range. Our approach, and its associated data and code, are made publicly available for consistent

This research uses large-scale matrix-product state simulations to determine the dynamical spin structure factor of the $J_{1}-J_{2}$ Heisenberg model on a triangular lattice, specifically for $S=1/2$ quantum spins. The simulated temperature range is 0.0 to 0.8 times the nearest-neighbor exchange energy $J_1$. The findings indicate that at low temperatures, $J_{1}$ forms an up-up-down spin arrangement of antiferromagnetic vectors along the primals direction that softens in the presence of $J_{2}$. However, above the spin order's temperature limit, $J_{2}$ introduces a distinct feature in the structure factor that distinguishes it from the $J_{1}$ Heisenberg model's magnetic liquid phase, which is otherwise present above the same temperature limit in both scenarios. The research also notes that a nearby $J_{2}$ range of approximately 0.19 to 0.185 leads to the formation of an up-down-up spin arrangement of antiferromagnetic vectors along the primals direction that softens in the structure factor. The research also applies a $J_{2}$$\rightarrow$0 limit to analyze the primary spin arrangement's spin order. The research also notes that a nearby $J_{2}$$\rightarrow$0 limit to analyze the primary spin arrangement's spin order. The research's results support up-up-down and up-down-up spin arrangements along the prim

The study explores lattice cutoff effects on the phase transition in $SU(3)-$Higgs theory across four dimensions and their implications on the geometric structure of the gauge group. By analyzing the Hot Deconfinement transition through various observables and by computing a key non-perturbative quantity called the Polyakov sum correlation, researchers can evaluate the interplay between the Higgs mechanism and Deconfinement. These findings not only clarify lattice artifacts but also provide insights into the thermal properties of actual particles, distinguishing between a scenario where Deconfinement remains a well-defined phenomenon in $SU(N)$ gauge theories with an embedded $SU(M)$ subgroup, and one where it transitions smoothly into a $Z_N$ symmetry breaking phenomenon.

Cr$_2$Al exhibits a tetragonal structure similar to Mn$_2$Au and is of interest in the study of antiferromagnetic spintronics due to its in-plane N\'{e}el vector degeneracy. This study focuses on growing Cr$_2$Al crystals and examining its magnetic properties as a function of orientation. Using neutron diffraction and simulations, the research finds that Cr$_2$Al has a magnetic ordering identical to Mn$_2$Au and is likely to provide new insights into spintronics through comparison with MoSi$_2$-type structure materials. The results from various measurements and simulations confirm that the system exhibits a single ordering phase transition, no spin canting, and an in-plane N\'{e}el vector temperature of $634 \pm 2$ K. The findings of this research match well with predictions made using simulations and further support the system's unique characteristics.

A new kinetic model, the $\sigma$-model, is proposed to simplify the complex calculations associated with Boltzmann's collision operator in rarefied monatomic gas simulations. Specifically, this model adjusts collision frequency based on velocity, influenced by a singular parameter $\sigma$, which represents the size of molecules. When $\sigma$ is set to zero, the model simplifies to the classic Boltzmann equation, but for non-zero $\sigma$, the model captures the influence of a gas's potential interaction while maintaining the solution space and time evolution of the Boltzmann equation. Furthermore, the model's collision frequency is constrained by an upper bound that corresponds to the maximum value of the physical collision frequency. Additionally, a regularized Boltzmann model is derived, which addresses the non-differentiable aspect arising from $\sigma$ and improves the model's convergence. The model's applicability and performance are validated through comparisons with exact solutions to model problems under Knudsen and Boussinesq conditions, as well as through simulations of real gas flows, which highlight the dependence of rarefied gas flow behavior on varying intermolecular potentials, contrasting with the uniform flow behavior in isotropic gases.

Voice assistant applications, such as Alexa, rely on models called parsers that can translate natural language into a logical format. However, current parser models are limited because they are trained on small sets of examples, which doesn't allow them to learn about the world. We've developed a new parser that can learn from limited data and understand natural language more effectively. In our experiments, this parser outperformed existing models when trained with only a few hundred examples, while its ability to reason with what it learns also showed significant improvement.

The Electron-Ion Collider's future will involve utilizing electron-proton and electron-nucleus collisions to thoroughly investigate the fundamental components of matter. To determine crucial information, precise measurements of heavy quarks formed at these high-energy interactions are vital. To obtain this information, cutting-edge forward detectors must provide accurate and detailed data. Design work for one such forward detector, the Forward Silicon Tracker, is in progress, focusing on employing advanced silicon technologies that enable fine spatial and temporal resolution, thus enhancing our understanding of matter formation in the most extreme conditions. Details about the development and integration of these advanced detector technologies and forward detectors for the Electron-Ion Collider will be shared.

A new generation of space telescopes, including the Neil Gehrels James Webb Space Telescope and the Arcus mission, are designed to investigate the observability of active galactic nuclei (AGN) in the soft X-ray band. These observations have the potential to reveal new insights into the physical characteristics of low-intermediate mass AGN that cannot be explained by current X-ray variability models. We analyze observations of a low-mass AGN, the galaxy M81*, made by the Neutron star INdependent X-ray (NIX) on the Suzaku satellite. Although the Suzaku data appear to show variability in the form of a rapid, hour-long fluctuation, this phenomenon must be treated with caution due to the limitations of the instrument. Using the Astralopy software, we conducted simulated independent observations of the source using a suitable X-ray instrument. Our results suggest that the observed variability is likely an artifact of the instrument rather than real, and indicate that the AGN in M81 exhibits complex, short-timescale behavior characterized by a rapid rise and fall lasting less than an hour. These findings demonstrate the importance of interpreting apparent rapid variability in low-mass AGN with caution due to the potential for spurious effects. They also highlight the potential of upcoming space missions to investigate this behavior in more detail.

The existence of magnetic fields in stars has long sparked debate about their influence on the atmospheres of stars. Our research provides new evidence from spectropolarimetric analysis on how the strength of a magnetic field in HD58260, a magnetic star, decreases as you move higher in its atmosphere. The results suggest that the outer atmosphere has a magnetic field roughly one-third as strong as its inner layers. The increased flow of high-energy particles in magnetic fields near these stars may explain their surrounding magnetospheres and the high-energy phenomena observed in their high-energy radiation. Our findings also highlight the challenge of directly measuring magnetic fields in the outer layers of these stars due to their low-average polarization in emission lines and the need for polarization measurements from multiple lines.

A link exists between a Dunkl operator over a field with two elements and a first derivative, 
exemplified through its equivalence to an operator set representing one-dimensional oscillator motion.
This equivalence holds in that the operator translates the classical Hermite polynomials into the generalized Hermite polynomials.

Using ALMA's H30α (231.90 GHz) observations of the metal-poor dwarf galaxy NGC 5253, we estimate the galaxy's star formation rate (SFR) and assess the reliability of other SFR measurement techniques. Based on these observations, the galaxy's photoionizing photon production rate and SFR (in units of mass per year) are calculated to be 1.03±0.03 and 0.53±0.16 respectively. The SFR derived from the 70 μm flux is 0.58±0.25, which is 1.09 times the value obtained from Hα+[(ion III] flux, 0.53±0.16). The 24 μm SFR (1.17±0.45) is 2.2 times the H30α SFR (0.53±0.16), indicating significant overestimation. The proposed new technique to correct for overestimation uses a SFR-to/24 μm flux ratio of 0.53/1.17 and adjusts the 24 μm SFR by dividing it by this ratio, which would yield a more accurate SFR. We demonstrate that two continuous minimal actions of the infinite dihedral group on an infinite compact Hausdorff space can be orbit equivalent if and only if they are conjugate, provided the group in question remains unchanged. However, this equivalency breaks down when considering other virtually cyclic groups like the direct product of the integer group and a non-abelian finite simple group, especially when these are used instead of the infinite dihedral group.

We analyze the statistical approximation of the $L^2$-operator defined as $P(X\in\cdot)$ where $\mathcal{X}$ is a Polish space, $\mathcal{Y}$ is a Hilbert space and $X$ is a $\mathcal{X}$-valued random variable. We establish that this operator can be approximated in several senses using finite-rank and continuous functions. We also explore how these different approximations relate to change-of-measure problems. Notably, this work provides the first known rates of convergence for $P(X\in\cdot)$ in the $\mathcal{L}^p$-norm for $p>2$ within the context of nonparametric statistical inference. Moreover, this study reveals that none of these approximations converge at a rate greater than $n^{1/d}$, regardless of the sample size. We support these findings using various methods, including empirical approximation trees, regression and kernel-based techniques and regularized lattice approximations. We also examine the challenging $p=1$ and $p=2$ limits, considering change-of-metric and Radon-Nikodym derivations. These involve introducing innovative solutions, including the construction of first-order and second-order approximation trees.
