Designing effective state observers for nonlinear epidemic models presents significant challenges. This difficulty stems from the inherent nonlinearity of these systems, which often follows the law of mass action and is governed by the SIR model. In this paper, a state observer is created for the SIR model, which not only accounts for nonlinearity but also takes into consideration external influences such as time-varying infection rates and initial conditions. This design focuses on developing an observer that accurately estimates the state by minimizing a discrete error measure. Furthermore, we propose and implement an artificial neural network (ANN) to replace the nonlinear dynamics of the SIR model, which also allows us to estimate the infection rate directly. Additionally, we discuss the relevance of our work to high-dimensional epidemic models, which often result in an algebraic Riccati equation with a resulting positive lower bound on the error of estimation.

The consideration of temporal contexts within knowledge graph embeddings presents an opportunity to enhance link prediction accuracy. However, existing static models that disregard time-related factors may still demonstrate competence in this link prediction task. In this research, a novel approach is proposed that combines the predictive capabilities of both temporal and static models to achieve superior performance. Specifically, two novel approaches - TPE and CPE - that translate static embeddings into temporal predictions via different methods to estimate neighbor scores, have been devised. Our empirical evaluation on four knowledge graphs reveals that both TPE and CPE achieve significant performance improvements over static models in link prediction tasks. Furthermore, the TPE strategy significantly surpasses state-of-the-art temporal KEEPMODEL performance while also showcasing superior computational efficiency.

Research driven by ultrafast dynamics in materials science, particularly when combined with spatial properties, is gaining significant traction. Despite existing ring oscillators for this purpose, they lack the capability to handle high energies efficiently due to their inherent limitations. In contrast, gigahertz-resonant VCSELs offer a powerful alternative for generating intense, short pulses. Although they offer a powerful approach, there has been a lack of in-depth understanding regarding their inner workings as ligth-based devices. In this study, we provide a comprehensive mathematical framework for interpreting the inner dynamics of these devices, including their spatial and temporal behavior, particularly during Kerr-lens mode-locking. In addition to this framework, we also developed a novel approach for predicting the stability of these devices based on their inherent properties. In order to validate this newly developed approach, we performed a series of experiments that examined the frequency of oscillations, pulse intensity, and spectral properties of these devices. In conclusion, our new mathematical approach provides a powerful tool for deep learning in biology, physics, and materials science, including spatial optics and resonant oscillator design.

Several optimistic assumptions prevalent in federated learning literature are often unachievable in real-world scenarios. To counter this, an asynchronous framework provides a more realistic setting for testing federated learning's reliability. This setup reflects varying amounts of non-IID data across participants as well as heterogeneous client engagement influenced by computational and battery limitations. Additionally, the framework accommodates delayed client-server communication. To alleviate the high communication overhead associated with asynchronous online federated learning (AOOFL), we employed a novel approach involving partial data sharing for feature gradient transmission among participants. This strategy was then verified and improved upon through comparative experiments involving a synthetic dataset and real-world ambient sound datasets. Results showed that when both online and offline updates were allowed, a solution could be reached with lower communication frequency and fewer training samples per participant, as observed in the case of an online incremental learning setup. Furthermore, when only offline updates were permitted, a solution could be reached with reduced communication frequency, increased client engagement, and fewer training samples per participant, as observed in the case of an offline federated learning (OFLL) setup. Notably, the proposed AOIFL approach successfully integrated ideas from both AOOFL and OFLL and demonstrated significant reductions in communication frequency, a more balanced distribution of computational resources among participants, faster convergence and lower communication overhead.

To improve the efficiency of thin-film silicon solar cells with limited light absorption, researchers investigate a back reflector with a nanostructured, three-dimensional photonic band gap crystal made from silicon that can easily be integrated into the existing thin film. Using the scattering matrix method, the absorption in single-layer and multilayer systems is calculated. The results show that compared to a flat interface, 2D periodic structures only offer a limited increase in absorption, about 20-30%, while 3D photonic band gap structures can enhance absorption by a significantly higher amount, up to 1000%. Due to their compactness and simplicity, these 3D structures have great potential for application in high-efficiency thin-film silicon solar cells.

We have derived a set of holomorphic functions, denoted by $\beta_{\lambda,\mu} (s)$, which, when the absolute value of $s$ tends to infinity in the right half-plane, behave similarly to iterated exponentials. These functions are linked to nested exponentials through a useful functional equation and have a series expansion that converges within a certain region of the complex plane. By using this expansion, we can study the dynamics of the function $f(x) = \beta_{\lambda,\mu} (2x)$ on the unit disk and develop asymptotic solutions to the tetration equation, thereby broadening the existing solutions by adding new, more complex cases. Additionally, we have demonstrated that the resulting hybrid asymptotics for $\lambda=0$ reduce to a traditional multiscale analysis, illustrating its inclusion in this particular scenario.

We have developed a novel method of constructing high-dimensional expanders by utilizing covered expander graphs. Specifically, starting with a covered expander graph $G$ and a bipartite expander $H$, we create a high-dimensional expander from their product $G \times H$. This product can be seen as a cover of an $n$-dimensional torus, resulting in a high-dimensional expander. This method allows us to construct a high-dimensional expander with spectral gap of $0.9999$ in poly($\log n$) dimensions, and it also enables the construction of a high-dimensional expander over finite fields with any degree of $d \geq 2$, by taking the product of multiple graphs. Additionally, we can construct a high-dimensional expander with spectral gap $0.9999$ in $2^{O(\sqrt{\log n})}$ dimensions, and in doing so, we resolve a problem first posed by Kaufman and Oppenheim of finding a high-dimensional expander explicitly constructible from a random symmetric matrix.

Researchers investigated the crystal and magnetic characteristics of the single-crystal, hexagonal GdInO3 through an integrated approach. A centered honeycomb structure comprising triangular and honeycomb sublattices was confirmed for this material. The former supports antiferromagnetic (AF) ordering within the triangular sublattice, whereas the latter exhibits ferromagnetic ordering that is subsequently canceled out by opposing sublattices. Magnetic property measurements on GdInO3 revealed two phase transitions, occurring at 9 K and 4 K, respectively. These transitions are attributed to the simultaneous ordering of triangular and honeycomb sublattices at 9 K, and the ordering of the triangular sublattice at 4 K. The low-temperature magnetization exhibits anisotropy, increasing in magnitude with a field of up to 20 kOe. An estimated effective magnetic moment per Gd3+ ion was calculated as 7.39 \mu_B, in agreement with the values for anisotropic or isotropic Gd3+ ions. A magnetically simple monodomain sample was found to be the cause for the alignment along the c-axis in the zero-field cooling process. Furthermore, the theoretical study of magnetic properties for a simplified model comprising a triangular and honeycomb sublattice revealed a possible explanation for experimental results, indicating that the material under investigation is a type II antiferromagnetic compound that becomes easily magnetized at temperatures below 9 K.

The application of graph embedding for predicting links in large networks has shown remarkable success across various domains, however, this method's efficacy largely depends on the availability of ample data. When dealing with sparse networks, this approach tends to lead to suboptimal results as they are based on the quantity of available data. In an attempt to overcome this limitation, this study proposes a novel graph embedding framework called Structural Structural Nearest Edges (SSNE). This framework defines node similarities solely based on the quantity of shared nearby edges and their shared common neighbors, which is well-suited for sparse networks. SSNE leverages the advantages of both shared edge quantities and shared common neighbors to achieve optimal performance. Additionally, SSNE incorporates an innovative technique that dynamically adjusts the level of shared common neighbors' impact according to the quantity of local structural similarities, thus enhancing overall performance. Experiments conducted on six real-world sparse networks demonstrate that SSNE outperforms existing embedding frameworks in predicting links. Furthermore, this study also analyzes and discusses the optimal quantity of shared edges and common neighbors that contribute to strong connections between nodes within the studied networks.

A low-cost water jet process is employed to achieve a 6mm deep silicon etch, overcoming a fundamental limitation and enabling the creation of a deep atomic vapor cell. Although initial attempts resulted in partially blocked vapor channels due to misaligned jets, clever rearrangement of the process and deep silicon beams yield deep cells of up to 6mm, necessary for supporting multiple hyperfine levels of cesium. To fine-tune the cell's temperature, a self-regulating thermoelectric controller is used, maintaining temperatures between 90-110°C. At the European Microelectronics and Photonics System Design and Simulation Congress, a deep silicon cell was demonstrated, allowing for a 110kHz linewidth. To further optimize the cell, researchers are now optimizing its design to increase the overlap between the cell's and laser beams.

We evaluate the precision of a recently proposed nonlinear interference model for a wide range of dual-polarization 4D formats, exhibiting an average disparity with split-step Fourier simulations of no more than 0.1 dB.

Preemptive wildfire detection is critical for minimizing ecological harm and human loss. Recent advances in Deep Learning have led to several fusion techniques for inferring invisible infrared imagery of wildfires using visible and infrared satellite images. In this research, we introduce FIRe-GAN, a novel method that uses a Generative Adversarial Network to estimate wildfire emissions from combined infrared-visible images. Unlike previous techniques, FIRe-GAN operates directly on low-dimensionality satellite images and employs a highly efficient and interactive training process. When evaluated using the Wildfire Satellite Imagery 2021 dataset, our model achieved top-notch results with the mIoU metric, requiring approximately 0.164 seconds of inference time on an NVIDIA GPU and showcasing significantly faster training convergence than preceding methods.

Early detection and treatment of depression is essential to prevent severe repercussions, making the utilization of multiple detection methods necessary, particularly when they do not rely on physical examinations.  Observing and analyzing an individual's social media behavior can aid in identifying depression, especially given its immense popularity.  Nevertheless, the majority of social media content is subject to change over time since platforms and user habits evolve rapidly.  In this research, a dataset containing English social media posts that demonstrate varying degrees of depression was compiled and analyzed, incorporating data collection, statistical analysis, and machine learning methods to test its merit.  The created dataset categorized 12 types of depression symptoms, applied supervised learning algorithms to classify posts based on depression indicators, and performed extensive statistical analysis to assess its worth, using performance metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score.  The findings indicate that deep learning methods utilizing the entire text can effectively identify depression symptoms, while also demonstrating the value of the created dataset for future studies on depression detection.

We have developed a stochastic model of of COVID-19, which incorporates
non-pharmaceutical interventions such as social distancing, limited healthcare
capacity, and probabilistic transmission and mortality. The stochastic model is
grounded in a standard compartmental structure, with a particular focus on the
number of free beds in hospitals, making it well-suled for tracking real-world
outbreaks where resources may become scarce due to high infection or mortality
rates. We have provided the necessary mathematical rationale for the model by
establishing a natural transformation from the stochastic model to a partial
differential equation, which describes the probabilistic distribution over time
of infected individuals. Additionally, we have proven an expansion that provides
a smooth transition from a deterministic model, where all individuals within a
compartment are uniform, to a more realistic scenario. The feasibility and
accuracy of the model have been validated through a comparison of numerical
simulations of the model to actual COVID-19 data from Michigan, yielding a
remarkably accurate representation of the past as well as predicted outcomes for
the present and near-future.

The ISGMR and a $K = 0$ component of the ISGQR in severely deformed nuclei exhibit a strong interrelation, manifesting as a distinctive characteristic in the isoscalar monopole (IS0) and quadrupole (IS2) strength distributions, respectively. This interrelation is primarily attributed to the coupling between the IS0 and IS2 states. In the present study, this coupling is included in calculations using the self-consistent RPA approach, utilizing the Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov mean-field framework as its base. Results for IS0 strength distributions in nuclei $^{24}$Mg and $^{28}$Si indicate that the inclusion of IS0$-\beta$-$K=2-$-$IS2$ coupling leads to a significant downward shift in the ISGMR centroid energy compared to that predicted by the SK3-RPA calculation, which neglects this coupling. Consequently, the SK3-RPA calculation falls short of achieving agreement with experimental data. Conversely, the SK3-RPA+$\Delta$IS0-$\beta$-$K=2-$-$IS2$ scheme yields isotropic strength distributions that closely align with the experimental data and further demonstrates that the IS0$-\beta$-$K=2-$-$IS2$ coupling has a negligible effect on the ISGMR energy, which is in line with the observations in the SK3-RPA calculation. A study on stick-slip dynamics and the convergence of motion paths in systems governed by Coulomb friction is conducted. The existence of a universally accessible and attractive region, near an equilibrium state, is confirmed through analytical means. Theoretical findings reveal that the system can only converge asymptotically, involving multiple sequences of stick-slip cycles, regardless of the starting conditions. Numerical simulations validate the theoretical models through diverse examples of convergence.

A novel reinforcement learning method based on the actor-critic type has been developed to tackle portfolio hedging challenges for a variety of financial securities and derivatives using historical data only. Key aspects of this approach involve leveraging various derivative types such as forwards, futures, options, and taking into account factors such as trading costs, liquidity constraints and other frictions. This algorithm can effectively handle portfolios of any nature and features continuous action and state spaces with a risk-adjusted objective. Most notably, the model allows for optimal hedging without the need for additional training in diverse initial conditions, thereby saving significant processing resources. Furthermore, theoretical analysis of the Bellman equation confirms the existence of feasible solutions and highlights the connection to our previously established Deep Hedging framework.

In today's commercial recommender systems, sequential models play a crucial role. These models predict the items users are most likely to engage with by analyzing their previous platform interactions. Despite their importance, many of these models struggle to grasp the underlying motivations driving users' actions online, making intent modeling vital for user understanding and optimal long-term engagement. We've developed a novel approach to probabilistically model user intent using variational autoencoders and inferred latent variables from user behavior signals. Our approach then adjusts the recommendation pipeline to optimize recommendations for each inferred user motivation. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach by achieving a substantial relative enhancement in recall for all levels of user intentions.

The reducible double confluent Heun equation stands out for its distinctive feature of being a special case of a Fuchsian equation with a singular point of the first kind. Due to its unique characteristic of an unfixed precursor equation, it presents a particular challenge in terms of classification within the framework of the Painlev\'e equations. In this study, a Fuchsian equation with a singular point of the first kind and two moving singular points is introduced, and the corresponding uncoupling process is described. The distances between these moving singular points are found to be determinative of the unfolding process, specifically reducing to the DCH equation under a specific set of conditions. The analysis is then extended to a Frobenius integrable equation with a non-resonant singularity of the first kind, and the corresponding unfolding process is also described.

Low-rank matrix recovery issues with complex high-dimensional data are ubiquitous in statistical and machine learning domains. This research investigates the fundamental recovery boundaries for a wide range of such problems. We specifically address the problem of estimating a matrix of rank one from observations with differing Gaussian noise levels across various submatrices. We derive exact formulas for the expected reconstruction error and discuss the relationship between these results and previous work on the topic. These findings are achieved through an innovative method that combines spectral analysis of the combined matrix with stochastic geometry concepts. This approach is highly adaptable to a variety of matrix recovery problems, including the case of overlapping or orthonormal submatrices. They are, however, limited to scenarios with differing Gaussian noise levels, as indicated in the paper.

In this research, we examine the vibrational spectrum of a constrained ring, taking note of its distinct properties that defy symmetry expectations inherent to topological models. A unique characteristic arises due to 2nd-order exceptional points, where an otherwise trivial band structure becomes topologically complex at higher energy levels. Absence of traditional symmetry in the model allows the emergence of fractional boundary states in the system. Moreover, another key aspect of the bulk-boundary correspondence can manifest at zero energy level, caused by an exotic $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ fractional boundary state which is unrelated to any inherent symmetry.

We introduce the semi-inclusive Lepton Flavour Universality ratio $R_\Sigma$ to verify electron-to-muon universality in the $b\to s\ell^+\ell^-$ process at $e^+e^-$ B-meson facilities. This combined observable enhances our capacity to detect potential violations of short distance origin Lepton Flavour Universality, all while retaining a straightforward theoretical explanation if a deviation from its predicted Standard Model value, $R_\Sigma^{\rm SM}=1$, is observed.

This study presents a novel approach to designing distributed output-feedback controllers for interconnected systems with constrained agent interactions. Each agent's controller is autonomously configured based on its locally available data, leading to a decentralized design. Importantly, our approach can maintain stability even in the face of dynamic network reconfigurations, without requiring adjustments from other agents, thus ensuring seamless integration of new members and efficient controller upkeep. This robust design is enabled by leveraging Bass' algorithm to compute stabilizing controller gains through distributed solutions to Lyapunov equations.

We've developed a COVID-19 diagnosis framework that employs CT scan image scans to identify patients and use BERT for natural language processing, both of which involve a secondary classification stage. Initially, we trained a classification model for CT scan images, which achieved a 0.7951 AUC score. Additionally, we presented a novel approach for leveraging CT scan images and patient demographics in conjunction with BERT. Notably, when using only clinical features within a two-stage classification model, we attained an ROI classification accuracy of 0.9131 AUC and 0.8422 AUC for COVID-19 classification. We found that using certain clinical features alone is sufficient to diagnose COVID-19 with remarkable precision.

Network science is the multidisciplinary study of intricate systems, which can be represented as interconnected networks consisting of nodes and edges with assorted attributes. These seemingly straightforward structures conceal an extraordinary depth of complexity due to their capability to encapsulate a wide array of real-world phenomena, encompassing chemical reactions, biological pathways, social connections, and other intricate relationships. Mastering network science necessitates the mastery of various graphical representations, computational tools, and fundamental concepts applied to various types of graphs. To streamline this process, this document aims to provide an comprehensive roadmap to the fundamental knowledge and techniques of network science. Each section is designed to offer a thorough understanding of the underlying graph theory and associated concepts, while also delving into more advanced topics to explore specific interests. To ensure maximum effectiveness, this atlas seeks to provide accessible and relevant explanations to a range of specialized topics, from the study of planar networks to the application of network science in medicine, while offering a glimpse into the broader spectrum of applicable fields.

The study of eco-evolutionary dynamics is being hampered by a limited focus on the significant influence of deep-time, long-term ecological and evolutionary processes that are difficult to model numerically. By separating these processes into three distinct domains - millennial to tens of thousand years, long term (~100,000 years) - researchers can better understand their interactions and modulators, such as climate change, genetic variation, and non-genetic inheritance. Drawing from paleoclimate studies, phylogeny, and taxonomic classification, this review explores the complex interplay between these domains and proposes a new framework for understanding and predicting eco-evolutionary patterns, from rapid changes to deep-time processes.

A recently established benchmark called SUPERB drives research into learning speech representations by comparing various speech models with minimal adjustments to improve downstream performance. By showing that self-supervised speech models can be made resilient to adversarial changes through the enhancement of their initial training, SUPERB promotes the development of improved speech representations. However, the challenge remains to create effective adversarial transformations that can reveal the limitations of these speech models. This study investigates the potential of SUPERB to identify and mitigate these limitations by introducing a method that generates new adversarial transformations through clustering, which in turn helps to improve the speech models' robustness to these changes. The results show that these speech models become more resistant to the adversarial transformations generated in this study and outperform non-adversarially trained models (SUPERB) in a range of tasks. Additionally, the research shows that these speech models can be modified with minimal adjustments to become more effective in improving downstream speech understanding. The research suggests that these speech models can be made more robust to the adversarial transformations generated in this study and outperform non-adversarially trained models (SUPERB) in a range of tasks.

Our research focuses on the underlying structure of Automated Market Makers (AMMs), 
a prevalent form of blockchain-based, decentralized exchanges. 
We reveal that the order processing mechanism results in token value diminishment for liquidity providers, 
and show that this token degradation can be interpreted as a stochastic process. 
Our analysis also reveals that a key AMM model is akin to a popular financial option model.
We make two primary contributions - we discover that AMM models featuring substantial token value diminishment possess limited trading advantages,
and provide guidelines for achieving optimal liquidity provision compensation.
Furthermore, our findings also offer potential applications in token valuation and the forecasting of token issuance costs.

A new analytical framework, referred to as Sensitivity Analysis, evaluates how conclusions based on incomplete data can be affected by uncertain prerequisites. We apply this approach to the typical scenario where participants either drop out or skip measurements, focusing on changes in dataset interpretation rather than raw data collection. Our framework relies on Bayesian inference combined with the E-value method for objective interpretation. We demonstrate the implementation of this approach through novel Bayesian networks and inference algorithms tailored for high-dimensional datasets. Furthermore, case studies on biological and health sciences datasets show how the proposed method effectively identifies crucial missing data patterns, allows for the quantification of bias resulting from those patterns, and identifies potential hidden relationships between variables.

This study concludes a comprehensive categorization of $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-symmetries within the larger framework of the extended quantum plane $\mathbb{C}_q\big[x^{\pm 1},y^{\pm 1}\big]$. In contrast to the more commonly analyzed non-degenerate quantum plane $\mathbb{C}_q\big[x^{-1},x,y^{\pm 1}\big)$, our findings reveal an unexpectedly high number of $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-symmetries within the settings of both the positive and negative degeneracies. Specifically, we found that the number of symmetries in the positive degeneracy case exceeds expectations by half, while an unexpectedly high number of symmetries also exists in the negative degeneracy case. Furthermore, our analysis sheds light on the underlying structure of the respective symmetry groups, revealing a consistent pattern of generators in the degenerate symmetries. We also present an accompanying inversion network in the context of the extended quantum plane. In addition, corresponding results for the extended Yangian algebra $Y(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$, as well as its specialized version $Y(\mathrm{SL}_2)$, are derived in conjunction with the established results for their respective extended forms. The integration of Artificial Intelligence techniques and improved information systems within Internet of Vehicles (IoVs) has yielded substantial benefits, albeit with heightened risks of security breaches and compromised privacy. As IoVs technology continues to evolve, there's growing interest in privacy preservation methodologies that adapt to these changes. Federated Learning has shown promise in safeguarding IoVs data and reducing communication security risks, whereas Blockchain technology presents possibilities for secure and verifiable data management. Considering the promising potential of combining Blockchain and Federated Learning, there's still a lack of comprehensive reviews on their applications in IoVs settings, making it challenging for researchers to stay updated on the latest developments in this area. To address this gap, our paper conducts a systematic literature review to investigate the applications of Blockchain-Enabled Federated Learning in IoVs, exploring their underlying challenges, technical applications, and future trends. Through a comprehensive survey of 22 primary studies that employed Blockchain-Enabled Federated Learning in IoVs, we're better equipped to understand the existing challenges, identify key gaps, and pinpoint opportunities for future research in this field.

The ALICE experiment has recorded the $p_\mathrm{T}$ distribution of D meson production, including both prompt and non-prompt (formed in beauty-hadron decays), in proton-proton collisions at 5.02 TeV, and focused on data with an integrated luminosity of approximately 19.3 nb^-1. D mesons were identified through their decays into different hadronic combinations, such as $\mathrm{D^0 \to K^-\pi^+}$ and $\mathrm{D_s^+\to \phi\pi^+\to K^-K^+\pi^+}$ and their conjugates, and were detected within a rapidity range of -1 < $y_{\mathrm{CM}}$ < 1. The cross sections for both non-prompt and prompt D meson production were calculated based on these measurements and then compared with various theoretical models, including those from PYTHIA 8, EPML2, and FASTMC 2.0. The production cross sections for both D mesons increased with proton-proton collision energy, and the production rates for medium-effect-corrected non-prompt D mesons showed a higher value than expected under the assumption of no medium effects, at intermediate transverse momenta (2 < $p_\mathrm{T}$ < 16 GeV/$c$).

The escalating demand for bigger cooling systems to support increasingly larger numbers of cryogenic qubits in quantum computing applications is prompting innovation.
Through the National Quantum Initiative and Department of Energy's support, our work at the Superconducting Quantum Materials and Systems Center at Fermilab aims to create a 2-meter diameter by approximately 1.5-meter tall experimental space capable of achieving extremely low millikelvin temperatures using a novel cryogenic platform. 
This cutting-edge cryogenic platform, founded on superconducting radiofrequency technology typically used in accelerator cavities, is designed to support three-dimensional superconducting qubit structures. This document outlines the baseline specifications and key features of the newly conceived platform.

Previous research indicates a high prevalence of misused crypto APIs in Java and C, but similar studies for other languages have been absent, with one notable exception - a study conducted on professional developers in Python revealed a lower incidence of insecure code for crypto-related tasks. This led to the investigation of whether this result would hold true in real-world scenarios and among broader segments of developers. A large-scale analysis of open source code in Python ecosystems showed that a sizeable proportion of crypto-related code in popular libraries is flawed due to unmet dependencies, but when considering active projects only, the percentage significantly drops, with only 5% potentially vulnerable code being detected upon examining the crypto APIs usage, as defined by NIST guidelines and existing security guidelines. This study is the first to assess crypto APIs usage in Python, a language with a significant and active developer base.

This paper presents an effective approach for locating fixed three-dimensional objects within large-scale metropolitan landscapes using an aggregation strategy for substantial amounts of two-dimensional image data, yielding significantly enhanced precision and robustness. A decentralized decision-making framework forms the foundation of this method, facilitating its capacity to handle large-scale data sets in a distributed and parallel manner. Evaluating this method with extensive image collections, encompassing nearly 400,000 images across 40 square kilometers of New York City and San Francisco, demonstrates its capacity to accurately reconstruct three-dimensional coordinates of objects, such as streetlights. Furthermore, the approach is shown to progressively improve in performance over time as the amount of collected data increases.

We address the challenge of deconvolving sparse signals within seismic reflection inversion to retrieve the subsurface reflection coefficients with high resolution. Our model uses a synthesis-based sparse method that utilizes both L1 and L2 norms, offering a middle ground between resolution and denoising. To enhance the model's ability to handle an increased number of zero coefficients, we introduce an adjustable number of combinations of grouped coefficients and apply the Chambolle-Pock algorithm to iteratively minimize the total cost function, ultimately achieving state-of-the-art performance in sparse seismic reflection inversion.

This article investigates the semigroups of composition operators on BMOA-type spaces, specifically on BMOA_p and its analogue VMOA_p. BMOA_p is a part of the BMOA family, which includes BMOA as a special case when p equals 1. VMOA_p, on the other hand, is a subspace within BMOA_p. Our focus lies on exploring the maximum subspace by letting p vary between 1 and positive infinity, which leads us to the selection of VMOA_p as our area of study. We establish some significant criteria to determine the membership of an integral operator in the semigroup of composition operators from BMOA_p to BMOA_p, thereby providing several concrete operator criteria in this regard. We further extend our research to linear sectorial operators and investigate some important issues related to the Kuramochi-Tamura condition, which is a critical factor in deciding whether a semigroup is compact or not. Our research ultimately leads us to the conclusion that the Kuramochi-Tamura condition is not only necessary but also sufficient for establishing the compactness of the semigroup of integral operators from BMOA_p to BMOA_p.

Understanding universal properties of a critical quantum spin chain model requires identifying key components of conformal field theory, notably the coefficients of operator product expansion, which describe operator fusion. Research suggests that these coefficients can be computed using wavefunction overlaps of low-energy states in the spin chain. We have demonstrated that central charge, conformal dimensions, and operator product expansion coefficients are encoded in wavefunction overlaps, accompanied by universal corrections that rely on cyclic orbifold CFT content. This approach allows for numerical computation of all conformally primary field scaling dimensions and central charge using finite-size systems, resolving unresolved universal finite-size corrections. Additionally, this method resolves the long-standing scaling dimension discrepancy for the Haagerup model, a critical spin-1/2 chain with interacting boundaries.

Automated part-of-speech (POS) annotation is a crucial task for linguistics and natural language processing, typically addressed through machine learning. Although accurate, models often produce perfect solutions, predicting unknown tags for unknown texts is not feasible. This poses a significant challenge when working with ancient texts, as limited data prevents mass classification. A proposed solution is employing deep neural networks for set-valued prediction, allowing the identification of a tag set relevant to the given text. Experimental results on corpora from German and English demonstrate a high likelihood of correct tags being included in the prediction set, particularly for texts yet to be analyzed.

This research focuses on developing a method for determining if a non-smooth function is compatible on a given set, and if so, calculating its derivative in a specific type of geometry known as symplectic. A particular class of non-smooth function is that which consists of a collection of smooth functions whose gradients do not all point in the same direction. An example of such a function is a piecewise smooth function, where different components are defined on separate subspaces of symplectic spaces. It is demonstrated that this non-smooth function is compatible on a given set precisely when the sums of its component functions' gradients over specific tangent spaces satisfy a particular condition. Furthermore, it is shown that if a non-smooth function meets this condition, calculating its derivative is a straightforward process. As a result, it can be used to prove traditional integrability theorems for smooth functions, and it provides a method for determining if a non-smooth function is compatible and calculating its derivative in a way that generalizes Hamilton-Jacobi theory.

As self-driving cars and autonomous vehicles have undergone substantial improvement, they now require integration with urban infrastructure, including traffic signals, signage, and designated lanes. Unlike vehicles, signs and other urban features aren't manufactured and have inherent purpose-specific designs. When a new level of autonomous capability is reached, where vehicles can ask locations for needs, like the most efficient route or collision-free paths, these objects become relevant. However, current systems can't translate human understanding into precise digital language on their own. We suggest an automated system that translates a city's needs into a machine-readable format and provides a way for a user to input the requirements verbally. We tested this approach with a voice-controlled interface and achieved successful specifications without additional human input.

Our research presents an innovative technique for accelerating variational quantum algorithms based on hidden inverse methods. This approach incorporates inverse operations of quantum gates that have a high likelihood of causing errors. By applying the hidden inverse method to the variational quantum eigensolver algorithm, we observed a substantial improvement in its convergence rate. In addition, our experiments with physical devices under real-world conditions proved the effectiveness of this method in reducing errors triggered by noise in quantum gate operations. The outcomes of our studies indicate that applying the hidden inverse method to an appropriate subset of quantum gate operations can accelerate the convergence of the variational quantum eigensolver algorithm.

In a general category $\mathbb E$, taking the image of a preorder under a certain operation might result in a larger preorder. We investigate when this property holds for categories with certain characteristics, such as being regular or having specific types of monomorphisms. In these categories, taking the image of a preorder gives us a unique equivalence relation, unique up to equivalence. When the preorder is already an equivalence relation, the result is also unique, giving us a condition for equivalence relations that is not necessarily true in all cases. We also look at when taking the image of a monomorphism in these categories results in an epimorphism and explore some examples.

Using a joint multivariate spatial model based on the work of Heffernan and Tawn, the relationship between satellite wind speed data, wave height observations, and extreme weather patterns is examined in the North East Atlantic between 2007-2018. A template-based approach is used to compare and combine wind and wave data from satellites and historical forecasts. Analysis involves standardizing data via a scaling method to eliminate the effect of mean wind speeds, and a non-linear connection between wind, wave, and weather patterns is discovered, with significant impacts of wind speeds exceeding 55 knots and significant covariances between wind and wave patterns.

Recently, Contrasting pre-trained image and text embeddings through Visual-Language Pre-training has received significant interest due to its capacity to learn transferable visual representations. Nevertheless, its performance is limited by semantic inconsistencies between the training and target datasets. To optimize visual representation extraction, we introduce a new technique that refines VT-CLIP by utilizing easy-to-hard filtering and learning multiple visual features from diverse, easily-to-hard semantic sources. Case studies validate that visual representations can be effectively transferable across scenarios with distinct semantics. We implement this approach with and without supervision and employ additional techniques to enhance data utilization, achieving state-of-the-art results on multiple tasks such as image-classification, cross-domain and zero-shot retrieval, and zero-shot classification, while surpassing the best available CLIP models without requiring task-specific training.

To enhance the accuracy of computational models plagued by noisy data and parameters, this study addresses the issue of reducing error in a linear system affected by uncertainty. By building upon Etter and Ying's '20 elliptic operator shifting, we extend this concept to a more broadly applicable setting. For any matrix pair with a certain relationship, we develop a shifting mechanism that reduces error in a linear system. In several scenarios, such as noisy data and parameters in physics, our method involves transferring the uncertain matrix to a comparable but simpler matrix, utilizing a rotation technique. Experimentation with a realistic example from superconductivity has demonstrated the efficacy of this approach, as shifting the uncertain matrix to an identity matrix led to a significant improvement in accuracy. Furthermore, we derive a mathematical upper limit for our method in any matrix pair with a certain relationship, thereby providing a standardized framework for error reduction.

We calculate the slices and the stable slices of integral suspensions of the
one-dimensional quaternionic Eilenberg-Mac Lane spectrum, based on the complex
polynomial ring. Additionally, we use this calculation to further understand
the homotopy quotients by the quaternionic groups. Our method of calculation
is grounded in the use of linear compact groups. As a direct application, we
determine the thinness of the relevant Eilenberg-Mac Lane spectrum. Another
outcome of this study is the derivation of an intrinsic description of the
category of sequential spectra which is relevant for quaternionic homotopy theory.

Given a Noetherian local ring with a specific prime characteristic and its primary ideal in terms of an $\mathfrak{m}$-primary parameter, we establish criteria for $F$-rationality based on the Tight Hilbert Function and the Tight Hilbert Coefficients of that ring. We then provide a controlling example for $F$-finitely generated modules in relation to Hilbert-Samuel functions, offering a comprehensive understanding and extension of existing concepts and models. Additionally, we demonstrate the inapplicability of Goresky-MacPherson's compactly supported cohomology for certain rings.

The application of machine learning in image-based diagnostics and therapies is gaining momentum, thanks to advanced deep learning techniques that can be trained and fine-tuned with large datasets. However, to be used directly in clinical settings, the outputs need to be standardized and conform to specific rules set by international organizations such as the DICOM standards. The difficulty in interpreting results using standard methods has been a significant hurdle for the 'radiation oncology' and'molecular imaging' research communities, but a new issue with widely applicable standards and a sample implementation is now available. The proposed library, highdicom, automates the process of writing standard annotation and model output files in DICOM format, making it possible to create custom workflows and process directories full of DICOM files using command-line interfaces and Python code. The library provides a flexible solution that allows for the standardization of diverse machine learning methods and modalities while keeping the code highly modular and extensible. The highdicom toolkit offers a natural extension to the capabilities of the dicompyler2 library, which was primarily focused on creating DICOM files from pathology and microscopy data. Although highdicom maintains the same spirit and goals, it expands the scope to include any machine learning model that generates spatial data such as segmentation maps, prediction arrays, and qualification scores associated with medical image files. The highdicom library is now actively used by multiple research and clinical projects to standardize their output and facilitate the evaluation and interpretation of machine learning model outputs in medical

We have expressed the Noether current of general relativity using a finite parameter deformation. When the parameter deformation is substantial enough to alter the topology of the manifold, the Noether current's charge evaluates the surface term of the Einstein-Hilbert action, hinting at a connection between black hole entropy and the Noether current's charge. As an example, we calculated the surface term for Schwarzschild and Mielke metrics, corroborating the value of black hole entropy derived from the Hawking-Negro formula. Furthermore, applying Virasoro algebra to the improved volume-energy-momentum tensor of general relativity yields a Virasoro algebra for semi-classical general relativity, providing a possible connection to holographic gravity.

In recent times, deep learning models have been effectively utilized for categorizing DNA sequences based on various tasks. A major challenge often arises due to the lengthy and variable nature of these DNA sequences. In our current research, a sequence-to-sequence autoencoder model is applied in an unsupervised manner to derive a standardized, fixed-dimensional latent representation for long and variable DNA sequences. The resulting latent representation is then evaluated for a supervised task - splice site classification - both qualitatively and quantitatively. The quantitative assessment was conducted under two distinct conditions. The results demonstrate the efficacy of using these learned representations as features or prior information in related tasks like splice site classification. Furthermore, through qualitative analysis using Integrated Gradients, significant DNA sequence signatures contributing to classification accuracy are identified, which align closely with existing knowledge in the field.

The manner in which the surface of materials is terminated has significant implications for their physical characteristics and can potentially alter a material's phase transition. To explore this, researchers examined the metal-insulator transitions in V$_2$O$_3$ films with different surface terminations. The study found that the metal-insulator transition in these films is contingent upon the type of surface termination - being tunable with terminal layers being oxygen-rich but fixed and correlated with the presence of a vapor phase epoxide layer when the terminal layers are vapor phase growth-induced and not oxygen-rich. Furthermore, the findings indicate that the metal-insulator transition in these films is accompanied by changes in the interface electronic structure and is made accessible for manipulation through the use of surface termination. The study also demonstrated that the interface electronic structure can be manipulated through the use of different terminations to produce correlated interface electronic states that capture the essence of the metal-insulator transition. The research also highlights that the metal-insulator transition in these films is accompanied by the presence of correlated interface electronic states that form in the gap or the conduction band. The study proposes that the metal-insulator transition could be potentially altered by introducing these correlated interface electronic states and also highlights that these electronic states could be used to induce a correlated phase transition that is metal-insulator like. The study was conducted through a combination of x-ray diffraction, x-ray photoemission, x-ray absorption, and transmission electron microscopy and transmission electron microscopy analysis. A new, systematic method referred to as the Clebsch canonization has been proposed to convert Lie-Poisson equations into corresponding Hamiltonian systems on the space of algebraic varieties, utilizing representative Clebsch maps. This method applies specifically to Lie-Poisson systems possessing an $su(N)$ algebra, resulting in systems equivalent to the Heisenberg spin chain and the nonlinear Schrodinger model.

The team has completed a comprehensive analysis of microlensing planets identified by the KMTNet AnomalyFinder in 2018, resulting in 9 newly identified and 8 previously known planets in the sub-prime field. Out of these 9 new planets, 6 were clearly found to have a planetary nature, with the remaining 3 requiring further examination due to uncertainties. Together with our sub-prime field's microlensing planets, there are now 19 known planets in the direction of the LMC, which is nearly double the initial count. The data also show that microlensing planets are significantly more common than expected to have a high mass ratio for their size. On the other hand, planets that are massive but short in duration are found to be less common than expected according to other studies. The data also show that many of the 2018 microlensing planets with long timescales tend to have a small mass relative to their size. This finding is consistent with those observed with other studies, which found similar results with strong gravitational pulls from their hosts, indicating a possible common universal law. All of the data gathered so far on microlensing planets, including those with varying levels of brightness, indicate that planets that are significantly smaller than Earth are the most common to exist. This finding is consistent with those observed with other studies, which found similar results, indicating that most planets to exist are likely to be significantly smaller than Earth. This information is found to be useful for future

To address a category of optimal control issues for partial differential equations where standard approaches fail, a new method of characterizing conserved quantities for invariant set control is introduced without requiring an estimate on the cost of trajectory tracking. This method bypasses the necessity for explicit trajectory tracking cost estimation, hence it can be applied to a broader range of equations. This paper utilizes the new approach to investigate the parameters influencing the conserved quantities of the 1D compressible Navier-Stokes equation.

This paper investigates the application of machine learning algorithms, including Random Forest and XG Boost, to predict non-performing loans based on a dataset from an Egyptian bank. Tenfold cross-validation methods are employed to assess the performance of the trained models, utilizing evaluation metrics such as accuracy, precision, and F1 score. Specifically, 80% of the data is used for training and 20% for testing, with random sampling to ensure representation. The models' performance is evaluated using metrics like macro F1 score, precision, and recall. Notably, our results reveal that XG Boost achieves higher accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score compared to Random Forest. The models' predicted classifications are then analyzed to determine feature importance. Consequently, models identified clients with loans who defaulted as having high interest rates, prolonged repayment periods, and substantial collateral values.

The connections between the chromatic symmetric functions of specific Dyck paths, originally discovered by Stanley and later expanded on by Shareshian-Wachs in their $q$-analogue, are crucial in their associations with Hessenberg varieties, diagonal harmonics, and LLT polynomials. Notably, for the so-called abelian Dyck paths, an unexpected relationship was also discovered in relation to the placement of non-attacking rooks on certain Hessenberg shapes. In this study, it has been proven that the $q$-chromatic symmetric functions of Dyck paths possess a particular decomposition in terms of a limited set of elementary and anti-symmetric polynomials, based on the number of ascents in the path. This development offers new insights into the structure of the abelian Dyck paths in relation to both q-NSF and NSF, and also provides an alternative, more simplified expression for the placement of non-attacking rooks on specific Hessenberg shapes, both in the maximum and limiting cases of $q$. These findings also reveal a novel invariance property under a specific operation, and also in the reduced and 'whitened' versions of the q-NSF and NSF. Along the way, novel and general explanations are given for specific seeming coincidences, including the associations between the $q$-NSF and NSF, and also in the context of the abelian Dyck paths in relation to both the placements of rooks on H

Deep learning models, specifically Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs), have been successful in image classification tasks but have limitations when dealing with 3D objects, mainly due to their 2D-based approach. To overcome this, different 3D-to-2D techniques have been explored, and among them, orientation convolutional networks (OCNs) stand out as a straightforward method that incorporates orientation information into standard 2D CNNs. In this paper, we investigate several essential aspects of OCNs that have not been fully analyzed before, including how local spatial contexts, dataset sizes, and specific problem types impact performance variation. Our findings reveal significant performance fluctuations dependent on spatial context size and problem type, with significantly improved results when considering larger spatial contexts in some cases. Additionally, we find that increased dataset sizes lead to more consistent results across different data sets. Our findings contribute to a better comprehension of the limitations and opportunities presented by incorporating orientation information in CNNs.

Using a novel relative trace formula, we investigate linear periods on $GL_{2n}$ that are modulated by a character. The key elements in this process involve establishing the relative fundamental lemma and the transfer of orbital integrals. Coupled with the spectral isolation technique pioneered by Beuzart-Plessis--Liu--Zhang--Zhu, we derive comparisons of the elliptic aspects of the involved relative trace formulas, ultimately yielding novel outcomes that extend Waldspurger's theorem to the scenario where n is equal to 1.

We develop a systematic method to study the impact of mass on the pole mass in comparison to short-distance masses like the $\overline{\mathrm{MS}}$ mass for a heavy quark, specifically with an emphasis on the top quark, through virtual loop insertions from heavier quarks. Our method adheres to heavy quark symmetry constraints, allowing us to decompose and gradually remove the effects of lighter massive quarks as well as the intervening momentum regions, all while accurately controlling high-order asymptotic behavior. By employing this method, we investigate the asymptotic behavior of massive flavor contributions and calculate fourth-order quark mass corrections, eventually determining that mass corrections for mass values up to 400 GeV and asymptotic Borel parameters are relatively stable, thus justifying the use of a constant approximation for such mass values. Our standard-model calculation, when performed in the pole mass or using PK masses, reveals a slight discrepancy of about 70 MeV or less between these masses, with agreement at the two-loop level and negligible differences at the one-loop level. Ultimately, we derive a tree-level relation between the top quark pole mass and the PK masses, both in the standard model and its effective field theory, both containing less than 70 MeV uncertainty.

Given a graph $G$ and a subset $R$ of its vertices $V(G)$ with $|R| = k$, we define $d_R(G)$ as the minimum degree of $G$'s subgraph induced by $R$.  For $1 \leq k < \infty$, and $\epsilon > 0$, we investigate the possibility of coloring $G$_'s subset $R$ with $k$ distinct colors in a sequence, where each color used is at most $\epsilon$ more frequently than the previous one.  This is achieved in a sequence where each color used is at most $\epsilon$ more frequently than the previous one.  This is a refinement of the Erdos-Faraday conjecture, which predicts two-colorability for such a subgraph under the same conditions, when $G$ is 2-regular.  This is a more restricted version of the original problem, which applies to 2-regular graphs. We establish a precise relationship between L^p to L^q contraction inequalities in weighted Bergman spaces over the unit disk. This connection, expressed as a Banach space theorem, includes the original hypercontractive inequality proved by Branges and a more restrictive inequality developed by Branges and Levin, with our proof providing a third approach distinct from previous methodologies.

Currently, the most trusted diagnostic tool for COVID-19 is RT-PCR, which
takes several days and sometimes produces incorrect results. Computed Tomography
scans can provide valuable assistance with COVID-19 diagnosis, although they expose
patients to a significant amount of radiation, which can be detrimental to those
requiring multiple scans. To address this issue, we analyzed a large dataset consisting
of low-dose and standard-dose CT scans to determine if low-dose scans, which use a
fraction of the standard dose radiation, can produce comparable diagnostic results
without compromising accuracy. Using 1883 pairs of low-dose and standard-dose scans,
we trained a complex neural network that can automatically identify COVID-19
characteristics in these scans and produce a diagnosis. By comparing our findings
to those obtained from standard-dose scans, we discovered that low-dose scans can deliver
a diagnosis that is just as reliable, though slightly less precise. Furthermore,
we successfully trained the network using data from two distinct populations and
tested it on unknown data, which shows that our model is resilient to different
data sets and not influenced by bias.

As numerous satellite constellations in the low-Earth orbit region are scheduled to launch, effectively managing their deployment in this orbit region to avoid collisions and satisfy regulatory requirements is of high importance. An efficient strategy for managing their deployment is achieved by tracking the spatial occupancy of each satellite constellation, which is defined in this paper. Defined in this paper is a metric for space occupancy, along with an algorithm for calculating it. This metric enables accurate identification of collision risks and helps reduce tensions surrounding "de-orbit" requirements, set forth by regulatory bodies, to minimize costs associated with revising satellite constellation configurations. The space occupancy metric is, along with its corresponding algorithm, validated through simulation in three stages: construction, initial operation, and ongoing operation. The space occupancy algorithm is further optimized for efficient real-time operation by being implemented in a just-in-time compiled language. The simulation demonstrates a 4.5-fold reduction in computational time when using the proposed algorithm.

To generate top-quality quadrilateral meshes on complex computer-aided design (CAD) models efficiently, we propose an integrated solution that combines mesh optimization techniques with constraints on mesh characteristics. Our approach involves dividing the mesh into basic units called macroquads, which are then optimized using a flexible and adaptable framework that also supports varying quad mesh topologies. Key features of our method include its ability to seamlessly integrate input entity-based constraints, simultaneously optimize macroquad properties and mesh topology, and generate high-quality meshes with optimal characteristics. We achieved these goals through the development of two optimization problems that are solved jointly by an integer linear programming (ILP) technique. We showcase the effectiveness of our approach by providing extensive simulation results on various CAD models, which demonstrate its capacity for accurate mesh optimization.

Pearson's correlation coefficient is frequently employed as a measure of association in statistical analysis. The strength of evidence for linear correlation is often evaluated using a hypothesis test, resulting in a p-value. Under certain data transformations and assuming normal distribution of a data set, a t-statistic provides an exact p-value; otherwise, the result is an approximation. The p-value can be estimated by analyzing how a sample correlation coefficient behaves under different permutations of the data. Although such estimates may rely on approximations of distribution moments, an inductive approach in this paper offers a precise formula for expressing sample correlation distribution moments in terms of data set characteristics, thereby allowing for more accurate estimates.

We detail the reasoning behind implementing a quantum S-matrix framework for tackling classical gravitational scattering between two bodies. Furthermore, a method is briefly discussed for computing black hole metrics across multiple spatial dimensions.

We investigate the two- or three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations with no-body forces and study the behavior of solutions in various space and functional analysis settings, specifically in critical L^q-based Sobolev and Besov spaces from Q_n^p to Q_n^q. Our main focus is the local stabilization of flows using finite dimensional feedback controls that act locally within the domain. Our approach relies on leveraging moment map formulations, Lie group techniques, and geometric analysis to derive suitable feedback laws, which can then be applied to various combinations of spaces from Q_n^p to Q_n^q with p< q < 2p < q < 2+ε. Moreover, we construct specific localized feedback laws that are highly localized and have compact support, and we provide precise estimates and upper bounds for the associated C^k and L^r norms for any k, r in (0, +∞). Our analysis allows for highly localized controls while maintaining precise estimates and uniform boundedness of solutions even in critical spaces. Our approach employs cutting-edge localization and scaling techniques in conjunction with Lie group analysis, Lie group integration, and Lie group integration methods. Our approach is general enough to cover diverse combinations of spaces from Q_n^p to Q_n^q with p< q < 2+ε. Our analysis reveals that highly localized controls can be used to stabilize Navier-Stokes flows while maintaining precise estimates and uniform boundedness of solutions even in critical spaces. Language learning dictionaries can facilitate vocabulary acquisition by supplying 
word definitions, although conventional dictionaries may struggle with 
capturing word meanings that vary across specific contexts. A potential solution 
is introduced in this study: the LitMind Dictionary, an online dictionary platform 
accessible through a web interface. It can automatically produce a definition 
based on user-provided words and surrounding context. Furthermore, LMD's data 
coverage has been expanded to approximately 400 million pairs of words and their 
environmental contexts through data extraction from Wikipedia, PMC, and ArXiv. 
Beyond this, LMD's knowledge base is continuously updated by leveraging a 
unified processing method for handling sentences, as well as correcting any 
errors encountered in its data by applying a robust correction algorithm that 
stems from a sequence-to-sequence-based approach. Finally, LMD's source code has 
been released under an open-source license, enabling the platform to be easily 
accessed by the public.

The growing interest in transparent AI has led to an increase in research on explainable recommendation systems. Among these, post-hoc methods have been identified as the most practical solutions for intricate models that operate as "black-boxes." A recently introduced model, LIME-RS, which combines local feature-based explanations with an influence score method, offers improved transparency. Nevertheless, an empirical examination of its performance is still required. In this context, we investigate how consistently LIME-RS works across different types of recommendation datasets and models, and whether it accurately highlights essential features. Through experiments using various datasets and models, we discovered that modifying the sampling process, specifically by increasing the number of instances sampled, significantly improves the consistency of feature presence across multiple evaluations. Surprisingly, even with this adjustment, LIME-RS tends to prioritize item attributes over user attributes as key factors. While an enhanced understanding of the model was achieved, the outcome is considered somewhat limited due to the constraints of the LIME method, particularly with regards to the inability to offer local explanations for complex models as efficiently as simpler ones.

Quantum devices based on superconducting properties may be effectively produced
using semiconductor-superconductor hybrids, made with materials like InAs quantum
wells. The surface of these InAs quantum wells has a low work function that creates
a significant barrier hindering the flow of carriers. Our investigation of the
energy-level alignment at the InAs/GaAs interface Pinning of the Fermi level in
InAs/GaAs(001) near-surface quantum wells reveals that pinning occurs very close
to the surface,.4 nm to the interface, also consistent with a vacuum-level
alignment in the InAs monolayer. This understanding of the Fermi level pinning at
the surface is crucial for developing efficient SCLC devices in the field of
superconductivity and for thoroughly examining quantum-confinement effects within
InAs quantum wells.

Research has shown that certain distributional assumptions are required to guarantee the reliable learning of arbitrary concepts using local queries or membership queries. Our investigation introduces a new class of hypotheses - shadow hypotheses - that enables the reliable learning of any concept within a predefined boundary, utilizing only local queries or a single membership query. Additionally, we show that if the underlying class of hypotheses possesses a bounded description size, then a specific model can effectively identify an equivalent shadow hypothesis by only asking a polynomial number of local questions. This finding is particularly significant as it abolishes the necessity for the delicate management of accuracy and noise tolerance in the learning process. Furthermore, we can further expand this result by integrating it with existing frameworks for handling noisy data. Ultimately, we can conclude that the use of local questions is particularly valuable in learning theories where shadow hypotheses are common, such as in the context of PAC learning for DNF formulas.

Our previous research significantly sped up Sinkhorn iteration by taking advantage of a kernel matrix's inherent properties, transforming its $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$ complexity to $\mathcal{O}(n)$ efficiency. This paper delves deeper into kernel matrix characteristics by defining and applying two pivotal concepts, Lower Collinear Triangular (LCT) and Upper Collinear Triangular (UCT), which ensure the matrix's diagonal and anti-diagonal elements are parallel. This property motivates an novel UCT factorization algorithm, an in-place matrix factorization that saves extra storage by overwriting existing matrix elements, but only for specific LCT matrices, now termed as Strongly Lower Collinear Triangular (SLCT). This algorithm leverages the matrix's structural properties to achieve a $\mathcal{O}(n)$ time complexity for the factorization for any SLCT matrix, and demonstrates its widespread applicability. Moreover, we prove that an optimal solution to the optimal transport problem can be precisely calculated using a linear time approach if the kernel matrix in question is an SLCT. This finding inspires a faster Sinkhorn algorithm, now running in linear time, by utilizing the UCT factorization algorithm, reducing the computational complexity from the traditional $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$ complexity to an $\mathcal{O}(n)$ efficiency. Comprehensive numerical tests were conducted to verify that our faster Sinkhorn algorithm, when paired with earlier advancements captured in Fast Sinkhorn I, results in remarkably faster

Young stars emitting intense X-ray and UV radiation can greatly impact their planetary atmospheres, causing them to lose heat and gain helium rapidly. Observations by the Telemetry Spectrograph and Analyser (TESA) on James Webb Space Telescope have documented the AU Mic system, consisting of a binary star paired with two planets, in the far-UV range. However, TESA's data collected over three periods spanning 90 days were affected by dust, flares, and varying levels of dust, making it necessary to use different calibration methods for accurate analysis. It has been determined that AU Mic is either a low activity or quiescent star in its flares, displaying an increase in far-UV by a factor of around 3. Moreover, in one specific flare, panchromatic radiation increases of about two orders of magnitude were observed, comparable to those seen in other young stars, and lasting for roughly an hour. Planetary atmospheres surrounding AU Mic b and c, detected through transit analysis, appear to be small in terms of scale with critical pressures at around 5-obar and a minimum radius of 1.15 RJ, and they are non-magnetic, based on observed non-reversed temperature curves. Moreover, in one specific scenario, the effects from flare radiation could potentially cause atmospheric losses for AU Mic b and c similar to those seen in exoplanets, specifically those related to photoevaporation.

We've developed a new method to calculate the friction caused by radiation that affects the paths of particles moving through a medium with resistance. We used this method to calculate the impact of this friction on the trajectories of photons and electrons in a medium with a similar amount of resistance as copper, and our results match previous findings on the effects of such friction on photons. We've found that extremely high-energy electrons may live for only exponentially small periods of time due to radiation-induced friction, which could have significant implications for certain high-energy particle phenomena.

In the context of an unevenly distributed classification problem, most popular classifiers are known to favor larger groups, and the nearest neighbor classifier is not immune to this phenomenon. This issue is addressed in a newly proposed statistical framework for the nearest neighbor classification method, which handles datasets where the majority classes outweigh minority ones. Initially developed for binary classification problems, this method is extended to accommodate multiple classes. Unlike existing over-sampling techniques that involve generating fake data points, this method achieves replicable results by sidestepping pseudo observation generation. Moreover, this method has demonstrated Bayesian risk consistency when subjected to relevant conditions and showcases its efficacy through its application on selected simulated and real-world datasets, showcasing its accuracy and reliability.

We employ data from the SkyMapper -- Optical Sky Survey to explore the demographics of ultra-bright, distant quasars above a specific threshold of 10^46 erg s^-1. By utilizing a purpose-built quasar candidate pipeline, we identify 57 new quasars in the vicinity of the Cosmological Inverse Tangent, consisting of 49 with high signal-to-noise spectra and 8 with incomplete spectra information. We supplement our findings with an examination of the quasar luminosity function at redshifts of 4.5 to 5.5, particularly focusing on the densest region of space, and we discover that our comprehensive study now covers 93% of the known territory. We establish that the dense cluster of quasars is significantly overpopulated with high-redshift quasars and we predict a very rapid, exponential decline in the number of these quasars at redshifts above 6. However, due to their extreme rarity, we predict their decline will be very gradual below redshift 3. By closely examining the observed and predicted distributions, we determine that the density of these extremely luminous objects changes very little from redshift 5.5 to 4.5, suggesting that their extremely rapid, massive growth occurs across a very narrow time frame of about 500 million years.

We have successfully observed the charge-tunneling phenomenon occurring between a quantum dot and a superconducting island using a technique that employs radio-frequency sensing. Our approach has allowed us to distinguish between different types of tunneling events, specifically those driven by individual particles as well as by pairs of particles called Cooper pairs. The combination of individual and paired tunneling events gives rise to a unique pattern that varies according to the quantum dot's energetic alignment relative to the superconductor's gap, and this phenomenon persists even when the quantum dot is in a non-equilibrium state. The discovery of a distinct sensing signal that fluctuates in accordance with the quantum dot's charging states has provided unambiguous evidence for the existence of paired tunneling events, and our research has revealed that these paired events can be identified through their regular periodic pattern of occurrence. The precise characteristics of these paired tunneling events are found to be in agreement with theoretical predictions, and our research has established that by employing a sensing method, it is possible to directly observe the individual and paired tunneling events that occur between a quantum dot and a superconductor.

Our research explores the contraction behavior of specific types of shockwaves in systems of equations, particularly those that conserve quantities, given the presence of a convex "stability" function. To expand upon existing work, we introduce a new metric that can accommodate spatial variations and use it to establish conditions under which shockwaves in a broader class of systems, such as fluid flow equations, will behave predictably. These conditions are more restrictive than existing metrics, however, particularly in systems where the stability function is not strongly convex, like in models involving rigid rotation, where additional restrictions on the flow's velocity are necessary to ensure predictable shockwave behavior.

We explore novel view generation -- the challenge of generating distant, unseen views by virtually navigating a given image -- through a new, promising approach. Our contribution is DiffDreamer, an unsupervised system that synthesizes novel long-distance views by simulating camera movements and training on internet-sourced nature scene images alone. Our results confirm that conditioned diffusion models excel at extending long scenes while accurately maintaining both detailed and overall consistency, surpassing prior methods based on GANs.

Many complex systems feature networks where interactions between diverse agents combine simple local rules to create complex emergent behaviors. While recent research has found connections between network structure and the underlying dynamic processes, detecting random complex patterns remains a pressing challenge. We develop a new, straightforward method grounded in mathematical techniques to discover and manage complex patterns that arise on large-scale networks, even without prior knowledge of their structure. This approach identifies underlying dynamics by analyzing a collection of snapshots representing network states over time. By applying operator-theoretic methods, it converts complex patterns into a linear format, facilitating model predictive control. We show that our proposed method simplifies a complex problem typically difficult to solve in large networks, transforming it into a more tractable and efficient optimization problem with a reduced number of variables.

The dynamics of a liquid film on a fiber heavily depend on the boundary conditions at the liquid-solid interface. This understanding has led to a theoretical model that uses the axisymmetric Stokes equations to examine the effect of liquid-solid slip on a film coated on a fiber undergoing the Rayleigh-Plateau instability. The new theoretical model reveals that slip leads to a higher rate of instability and a more complex evolution of the film coating. The theoretical model has been validated through numerical simulations using the finite element method and has also considered the effect of liquid-solid drawdown and corner formation, and compared it with previous experiments and other theoretical models.

We investigate the temporal Lipschitz stability for solutions of the Hunter-Saxton equation, focusing on $\alpha$-dissipative solutions with $\alpha$ a constant in the interval $[0,1]$. We introduce and study the properties of metrics both in the Lagrangian and Eulerian frameworks to determine Lipschitz stability within those systems.

Our study investigates the use of robotic ultrasound scanning for scoliosis assessment via ultrasound, through vertebral ring apophysis detection, via ultrasound. We compared the detection accuracy of robotic scanning with that of manual scanning in 60 patients, using 6 degrees of freedom and 3 degrees of freedom ultrasound systems. Robotic and manual scanning were performed simultaneously by two different operators. We found that the robotic scanning technique yielded reliable results, in terms of vertebral ring apophysis detection, across multiple operators. Specifically, the mean standard deviation for robotic scanning was 2.71 mm, and 2.94 mm for the two operators respectively.
