Moreover, robotic scanning demonstrated detection levels comparable to those of manual scanning, with mean standard deviations of 2.71 mm and 2.94 mm respectively showing slightly greater variation from the mean for both manual and robotic scanning results. These results suggest that robotic scanning is a viable alternative to manual scanning for scoliosis assessment, via ultrasound, and may ultimately lead to the development of a fully automated ultrasound system.

This paper introduces an innovative method for duration modelling in statistical parametric speech synthesis by training a recurrent model to generate phone transition probabilities frame-by-frame. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on specific distribution types and mean durations for synthesis, this new approach can model any distribution on non-negative integers. We explore a median-based output generation strategy, which offers advantages such as being more representative, controllable, and efficient. This method's potential to model synthesis durations is also assessed. Evaluations on two English neutral accent corpora reveal that our approach surpasses a comparable baseline in terms of both word accuracy and duration accuracy. Additionally, building on the longest repeating context in a dataset allows our model to achieve significant increases in synthesis speed and memory efficiency, respectively.

Identifying online hate speech is increasingly critical due to its capacity to inflict emotional and psychological harm on minority groups. A recent study from TU Berlin's research team analyzed the performance of different Natural Language Processing models on subtasks one and two of the 2021 Indo-European language shared task, which focused on detecting hate speech and derogatory content. Our team assessed the effectiveness of models that rely on word and character-based recurrent neural networks and those employing transfer learning via BERT, all of which utilized shared text classifiers. It was discovered that models employing transfer learning outperformed others across both tasks.

Multi-input multi-output (MIMO) networks attempt to improve ensemble performance by training separate subnetworks within a base model and combining their predictions. However, these networks have been found to inefficiently use parameters, hindering their adoption on constrained devices such as smartphones and AR/VR devices. This study suggests that a key issue with current MIMO frameworks lies in how they allow subnetworks to learn and share features. In response, we introduce an innovative 'unmixing' procedure for MIMO networks to facilitate shared feature learning among subnetworks. Our preliminary results demonstrate the efficacy of this modification, yielding feature sharing and better performance in smaller network configurations.

This study undertakes a comprehensive analysis of existing historical document image datasets, encompassing texts written in ancient languages such as Latin, Greek, and the Mongolian script, as well as other languages including English, French, German, and Italian. These datasets are classified based on documents, pages, layouts, and individual lines. The survey presents a total of 35 datasets, meticulously excerpted from a wide array of journals and conferences. The datasets are evaluated in terms of their shortcomings, offering insights that could inform the creation of new datasets. The study provides a systematic overview of a previously unexplored topic, making it a cornerstone for future research and offering the first comprehensive compilation of a specific field.

Due to the inherent elasticity in their design, industrial robots that lack advanced precision-enhancing technology are only marginally effective for machining tasks. Besides issues related to structure, temperature, and support bearings, the primary factor behind positional discrepancies between their drives and actual axes is caused by variations in the length of the drive shaft acoustically coupled with actuator motors. To mitigate positional discrepancies, a novel method utilizing two position sensors - mounted on the same shaft - is presented to improve precision in robot positioning. Derivatives of the difference between sensor readings are used to model and compensate for discrepancies between the robot's physical axis and its equivalent model, achieving compensation through a feedforward control method. Furthermore, a decentralized flatness-based controller is introduced to stabilize the multi-variable system, ensuring it remains stable in the face of disturbances. Consequently, the proposed solution provides improved precision in robot positioning, particularly when acted upon by actuator torque rather than position control. Furthermore, this position-based method offers considerable computational advantages over existing approaches compared in the results section.

This study introduces Multiple State Analysis, defining it as a new approach for
investigating life-long health trajectories leading to a specific adverse
outcome like myocardial infarction. MSDA offers a novel methodology for
examining the effects of concurrent health conditions on future health risks.
Using data from a large cohort of individuals who experienced a myocardial
infarction in the Netherlands, researchers from the Generation R prospective
cohort study found that, prior to the infarction, these individuals were more
likely than the general population to have suffered from neurological disorders,
such as dementia and stroke, as well as other health problems, including
hypertension, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and other conditions.
Notably, patients who experienced certain health problems before the
infarction were at a higher risk of subsequent major cardiovascular events.
These results highlight the value of predicting and monitoring for potential
health threats beyond initial myocardial infarction, illustrating the use of
MSDA to identify new targets for prevention efforts.

One widely accepted method for evaluating electronic properties of extended, disordered materials like thin films and nanostructures involves integrating non-periodic components over their surface. Standard approaches that treat the electronic density as a smooth, global distribution often fail to accurately account for interactions with surfaces, interfaces, and other boundary regions. This inaccuracies may manifest as apparent self-interactions or unphysical transfers of density across these boundaries. A more precise method is proposed here, which divides the electronic density into localized regions centered on surface sites, allowing for accurate interactions between the density and surface-related potentials. This scheme features efficient and computationally economical variants for both two-dimensional and three-dimensional systems. Its effectiveness is demonstrated by accurate evaluations of electronic properties, including work functions and charge densities, especially in cases where density is strongly coupled with surface potentials. Compared to other methods, it exhibits improved precision and efficiency, particularly at scaling lengths comparable to the radius of an atomic van der Waals domain. Its performance is further validated by accurately reproducing the experimentally and theoretically determined density decays observed at oxide and graphite surfaces. This method has the potential to replace older, approximation-based approaches for many types of materials and interfaces, and may also be adapted to describe the flow of energy across boundaries.

In a graph, a subset of vertices forms a resolving set if, for any two vertices, a single set vertex is positioned at different distances from the two vertices. The problem of finding a resolving set of size at most k, called the Metric Dimension problem, has been a subject of research since the 1970s. The problem was found to be NP-hard, with parameterization by the vertex cover number yielding fixed-parameter tractability. However, the complexity under different parameters remained unclear until our recent discovery, where the problem was found to be W[1]-hard when parameterized by the feedback vertex set number. Additionally, we found that parameterization by the vertex cover number results in the problem not admitting a polynomial kernel unless a significant assumption holds. While the problem remains open under the vertex cover number, we found fixed-parameter tractability when parameterizing the problem by distance to cluster or co-cluster.

Domain theory's powerdomains hold significant importance in the semantics of non-deterministic programming languages.  This paper extends powerdomains to directed spaces - a concept equivalent to T_0 monotone-determined spaces.  Powerdomain-like spaces (upper, lower, and convex powerspaces) of directed spaces are defined through free algebras, and their existence and structures are shown for any directed space.  Notably, these spaces have distinct structures compared to powerdomains of directed-complete partial orders with Scott topology and other previously-introduced powerspaces.  The upper, lower, and convex powerspaces have one-to-one correspondence with Scott and Hoare powerspaces when the directed space is directed-complete.  The structures of powerspaces of directed spaces were found through the exploration of abstract algebraic structures defined by powerdomain axioms, and a characterization of powerspaces of directed spaces using Tarski-like operators was also provided.  The investigation into powerspaces of directed spaces led to the extension of powerdomain axioms and the definition of a new algebraic structure - the subdownset system, which enables working with subspaces of partial orders as subdownsets.  The subdownset system has the potential to be applied to further investigations of powerspaces of arbitrary subspaces and of spaces with types in programming languages with dependent types.

Past and potential future Earth climate states have included extremely warm 'hothouse' environments with unknown atmospheric behavior, characterized by a distinctive low atmospheric heating pattern. In contrast to typical cooling effects, 'hothouse' climates are distinguished by a blocked window region for water vapor, which has led to theories of resulting temperature inversions and altered cloud formations. Prior climate modeling has failed to capture the low atmospheric heating effects and resulting cloud formations accurately, leading to a significant gap in understanding 'hothouse' climate dynamics. In the context of a model atmosphere with radiative forcing, this study investigates the effects of water vapor interactions on atmospheric and cloud phenomena in 'hothouse' environments. In particular, the study finds that 'hothouse' climates are characterized by a periodic cycle of high cloud formations, deluges of precipitation, and associated atmospheric responses. In the lower atmosphere, this includes the development of baroclinic waves and resulting midlatitude cloud formations, while in the upper atmosphere, the waves lead to altered jet stream configurations and further changes in cloud formations. Notably, the water vapor feedback associated with these climate phenomena increases the likelihood of heavy precipitation events, which in turn influence the atmospheric response to changes in parameters like CO2 concentration.

We've established an inverse Penrose transform for self-dual Yang-Mills theory and its spin-off variants in a flat space environment. The spin-off variants involve Yang-Mills theory coupled with a single higher-spin field that meets specific self-duality conditions. By implementing the inverse Penrose transform, we've determined that these higher-spin extensions of self-dual Yang-Mills theory can be represented as complex, higher-order systems, each involving at least four distinct complex variables. When we refine these systems to a three-dimensional null curve, the resulting equations of motion become intricately interconnected. For instance, one variant involves an equation that is inherent in another, while an even more advanced variant introduces an extra self-duality constraint. We've further observed that these higher-order systems exhibit immense gauge invariance, offering considerable freedom to simplify these systems while yielding equivalent physical results.

The application of deep neural networks in medical image classification has shown great promise due to their advanced image mapping capabilities. Despite this, current deep learning-based methods face significant challenges arising from noisy real-world labels, particularly in situations where quality control over the data is limited. In order to overcome these issues, an unsupervised learning method is proposed that actively identifies and rectifies problematic noisy real-world labels. By leveraging Bayesian statistics, the proposed algorithm distinguishes between noisy and high-confidence labels for each specific image, after which it incorporates an attention-based mechanism to dynamically distribute learning emphasis towards clean labels associated with noisy images. Experimental evaluations conducted using four diverse and publicly available medical image datasets show the proposed approach to significantly outperform state-of-the-art methods in handling varying levels of noisy real-world labels.

Consider a unit cube, $Q_n$, in $n$-dimensional space and a function space, $C(Q_n)$, consisting of continuous functions from $Q_n$ to $\mathbb{R}$. Define the norm of a function as its maximum absolute value over $Q_n$. Let $\Pi_1\left(\mathbb{R}^n\right)$ be the set of polynomials of degree at most one, i.e., linear functions on $\mathbb{R}^n$. An interpolation projector $P$ is introduced that maps functions from $C(Q_n)$ to linear functions on $\mathbb{R}^n$, using nodes within $Q_n$. When the number of nodes is an Hadamard number, a non-degenerate simplex can be formed with vertices at $Q_n$. Various methods will be discussed for establishing upper bounds for the norm of $P$ in the form $\|P\|_{Q_n} \leq c \sqrt{n}$ for the corresponding interpolation projector $P$. Here, $c$ is a constant dependent solely on the type of interpolation used. Furthermore, a lower bound of $\frac{\sqrt{n}}{4}$ will be derived for the constant $c$ in this context.

A correlated random walk (CRW) is derived from the Grover matrix, the evolution matrix of the Grover walk on a graph G, and an explicit formula is given for the characteristic polynomial of the CRW's transition probability matrix, utilising a determinant expression related to the graph's generalized weighted zeta function. This is exemplified in the cases of regular polygons, hexagonal rings, and American football-shaped carbon nanotubes.

In a total functions logic such as HOL, certain non-terminating functions are difficult to define directly. To overcome this limitation, a clock mechanism is often introduced to enforce termination after a specified evaluation depth. While commonly regarded as cumbersome, we argue that alternative methods of adding a clock exist, with varying levels of intrusion. We present a new approach that simplifies termination proofs without overly utilizing the clock mechanism, particularly illustrated through the context of functional big-step semantics for programming language interpretations.

The accuracy of models predicting the spatial arrangement of instantaneously occurring wall-bound flows is heavily reliant on the geometric characteristics of the representative structures they employ. However, identifying the 3-D geometric characteristics of the numerous, rapidly moving, and ambiguously visible coherent flow structures present in wall-bound flows has long been a challenge. This study suggests the effective prediction of these structures through a data-driven approach that leverages the simultaneous measurement of flow and structure dynamics. By focusing on the critical elements driving rotation in these flows, the study develops an instance-based model to geometrically identify and characterize the pivotal structures in wall-bound flows. This instance-based approach is highly adaptable, applicable to various flow types, and only requires knowledge of a few pivotal elements for determination of the structures in question. As such, it significantly simplifies the existing process of modeling instantaneously occurring flow structures, thereby improving the accuracy of 3-D models. This technique is demonstrated to be effective in modeling flows around complex shapes and in diverse situations, such as turbulent flows with oscillating patterns and under the influence of surface irregularities.

This study demonstrates the presence of self-dual (topological) solitons within a modified baby Skyrme model that incorporates Born-Infeld terms governed by Maxwell's equations. The model in question does not contain any gauge fields but instead interacts with two-component scalar fields, which owe a certain allegiance to Noether conserved charges as their symmetry is realized. By demonstrating that the model in question possesses non-trivial Poincaré symmetry, despite not being part of chiral models, we are able to derive the related Ward identities. We then proceed to solve the model's equations, yielding solitons that possess a topological characteristic with an associated index determined by a mapping of the compact three-dimensional space to a one-dimensional sphere. The solitons' energy, which grows logarithmically with increasing radius, along with its angular momentum, which grows linearly with radial distance, are also quantified.

For a three-dimensional Weyl semimetal model in a magnetic field, where each unit cell has an orbital magnetic flux of $p/q$ with $0\le p \le q-1$, we studied its phase diagram under minimal crystalline symmetry. The results show the existence of various phases: phases containing multiple Weyl nodes with surface Fermi arcs; a Chern insulating phase featuring gapless surface states despite bulk gapping; a unique phase combining gapped, topologically non-trivial bands with nodeless surface states through which charge is not carried. Additionally, this phase was found to exhibit pseudo-time reversal symmetry breaking due to its topological characteristics; it resembles a known model, the respiratory complex, which facilitates efficient oxygen uptake; and it suggests gapped surfaces in certain three-dimensional topological insulators when exposed to a strong magnetic field.

This research paper introduces an advanced optical nanoantenna design, consisting of a hybrid silicon nanoring coupled with a localised assembly of quantum dots, which together constitute an efficient source of unidirectional photons when coupled with optical excitation. The structure features a narrow 10-nanometer gap separating a gold mirror from the nanoring and quantum dots, enabling efficient interaction between the quantum dots and the hybrid antenna. The resulting increase in scattering efficiency allows for a significant reduction in the required excitation intensity to cause radiative emission from the quantum dots. The antenna's performance characteristics can be further optimised by adjusting its geometric dimensions to achieve complementary enhancements of scattering and excitonic interactions. Notably, this novel nanoantenna design may potentially enable the observation of non-linear optical phenomena associated with very low-intensity light emission.

Mechanical screening, a widely recognized phenomenon, is observed in various materials where particles of different sizes repel one another. In the case of granular screens, a thicker layer of larger particles exert a greater force on smaller particles compared to thinner layers, exceeding the force required to displace a single large particle. We have conducted an in-depth study on the mechanical screening in granular matter by analyzing a system consisting of spherical particles of two different sizes pressed against a stationary wall. Our findings indicate the occurrence of mechanical screening, revealing that larger particles exert a stronger collective push on smaller particles. We have also identified unique characteristics in the system, where forcing smaller particles together can actually increase the overall pressure against the larger particles against the wall, a phenomenon known as "meddling counterpressure". Our research combines both experimental and computational components, where we utilize molecular dynamics simulations to confirm that considering individual particle interactions is sufficient to explain our observations, thus validating a fundamental assumption in theoretical studies of mechanical screening.

Utilizing first-principles calculations, the electronic characteristics of silicene, enhanced with a single manganese atom and surrounded by a boron nitride substrate, are analyzed, with results compared to those of manganese doped silicene in the vacuum. From magnetization calculations, it is found that only four molecules exhibit ferromagnetic behavior, while the remaining show ferro-orbital ordering. In contrast to the vacuum's N\'eel-type ferromagnetic state, manganese decorated silicene exhibits antiferromagnetic behavior when in contact with the boron nitride substrate, albeit with significantly reduced magnetization. Band structure calculations reveal that manganese decorated silicene on boron nitride maintains its metallic properties, yet displays notable differences in the Band Gap at M (BG_M) energy, as well as in the density of states at the Fermi level, compared to vacuum decorated silicene.

The Sgr A East radio source is situated approximately 27 parsecs from the center of the Milky Way and is thought to represent either a young supernova remnant or a massive star cluster located within the central bulge of the galaxy. In this study, we consider the possibility that Sgr A East is actually the remnant of a supernova that occurred within a dense environment of the galaxy's central star cluster, Ossert. Our simulation of the supernova's expansion takes into account the significant impact of the surrounding cluster's density on the remnant's expansion dynamics, particularly during the early stages of the supernova's evolution. This effect differs substantially when compared to a supernova that occurs within an environment with uniform density. The Sgr A East remnant's age of 1000-1500 years is consistent with a supernova that occurred in Ossert and is also consistent with X-ray and gamma-ray observations of the remnant, which indicate an age of 1000 years. Our model predicts that Sgr A East will continue expanding and merging with nearby clouds within the next 50000 years, potentially incorporating up to 30 cubic parsecs of material during this time. Our simulation also predicts that Sgr A East will continue to expand and grow in both north-south dimensions while its east-west dimension will either diminish or grow, depending on whether it merges with the dense Gazgoule cloud.

In multi-class text classification, we're faced with an ultimate decision: either we've got too few data samples and not enough to make an accurate prediction, or we've got a ton of data, but it's so noisy that it's rendering our models useless. This paper delves into this conundrum by examining various techniques that create artificial representations of our data. These methods are widely recognized for their ability to improve classification accuracy, but they've never been thoroughly tested for text data sets. To rectify this, we've conducted an extensive review of the most popular data augmentation techniques used for text classification tasks and we've put them through their paces on a selection of renowned text classification data sets. The outcome? Enhanced performance across the board when using class imbalance correction, but a notable exception where the original distribution of our data set is preserved – in this case, we've seen a significant improvement over standard preprocessing methods that don't account for class weight imbalance.

This study examines how local online news in the U.S. responded to the COVID-19 pandemic from January 2020 to October 2020. During this period, coverage by individual news sources showed patterns consistent with a time interval that coincided with the pandemic's progression. When comparing the quantity of local news coverage with COVID-related cases and deaths across different states, a significant correlation was established. However, state-specific analyses revealed that local news coverage was more closely associated with COVID cases than with COVID deaths. Furthermore, local news coverage was found to be more extensive in states that experienced more COVID cases. These state-specific findings were linked to differing audience levels, which indicated that local news coverage was more comprehensive in states that had a larger population or a significant number of potential news recipients. Moreover, local news coverage was found to be more extensive in cities that boasted a higher circulation of print newspapers.

Smoothed particle hydrodynamics possesses innate conservation capabilities, which are safeguarded by integrators that accurately track key variables like position, velocity, and mass over time. However, preserving angular momentum is a more intricate process due to the cumulative effects of discrete sampling and the complexities of high-order momentum calculations. By leveraging the principles of gyroscopy, a SPH integrator is developed that guarantees the conservation of angular momentum in a step-by-step manner, which when combined with the accurate time-stepping approach, results in seamless and consistent angular momentum preservation across all methods of quadrature and boundary integration, irrespective of the order of momentum calculations, and which also adapts to rotating frames of reference with a simple correction that affects only the quadrature scheme, thereby facilitating efficient numerical simulations at high order.

Numerical studies have been conducted on the $Q^2$ dependence of several measurable quantities within the $e \vec {p} \to e \vec {p}$ process, where $e$ is polarized and $p$ is also tagged with polarization. Calculations were carried out using two methods: first with relativistic independent fields from an earlier work and then with relativistic perturbation theory. Results were also obtained from the Bag model and from $QCD$ with $2$ loop calculations from the $DREsidue$ program. We examined STT, specific to the final proton only, in $e \vec {p} \to e \vec {p}$ and found, surprisingly, that it does not vanish even at high $Q^2$. This indicates that there are contributions from the time component of the $Z$ exchange and also from the twist-2 $\{g_{1}^{p}, h_{1}^{p}\}$ FFs, manifesting in $Q^2 \times $STT of the final proton. Using $QCD$ with $2$ loop calculations from the $DREsidue$ program, $Q^2 \times $STT of the final proton shows significant similarities with an independent fields calculation from an earlier work. $Q^2 \times $STT of the final proton shows significant contrasts with a relativistic perturbation theory calculation. Also, using $Q^2 \times $

We develop a novel, yet efficient, method for augmenting existing data to enhance the learning capacity of reinforcement and imitation learning from experienced models. The policy cloning approach, a fundamental component of various learning techniques, is our focus, as it scales up the rate of knowledge acquisition and accelerates the learning process. By introducing noisy target outputs as artificially generated data, we promote the model to accurately reproduce these values, ultimately achieving improved generalization performance using reduced available data. We experiment with this novel technique within the GRL framework and examine its application in both behavioral cloning and general reinforcement learning, demonstrating that it stacks favorably against prior methods in a range of established baseline tasks.

A comprehensive analysis of the creation of two Higgs bosons ($hh$) paired with a vector boson ($W$ or $Z$) using a massive dataset of 139 inverse femtobarns of proton collisions at a 13 TeV energy has been carried out utilizing the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider. By examining the resulting events in various exclusive final states with jets, which are categorized based on two, three, or four distinct regions, no significant excess above predicted background interference was discovered over the applicable range of Higgs boson pair masses between 350 and 450 GeV, yielding observed and expected upper limits of 0.87 and 0.80 times the predicted cross-section of the standard model for each of these masses, with an associated uncertainty. These results further supplement a previously published search in 2018.

Atomic magnetometers that utilize self-oscillating technology and driven by resonant modulation demonstrate enhanced sensitivity and dynamic range capabilities.
This technology, in conjunction with phase-coherent feedback from modulation, enables the production of strong sidebands within atomic energy levels, leading to maser-like behavior, particularly in cesium atoms, where detection of extremely small magnetic fields has become possible.

For K3 surfaces with an automorphism having a Siegel disk, the associated Picard number falls between $0$ and $18$ and must be an even integer. Conversely, applying the technique of hypergeometric groups, K3 surface automorphisms possessing Siegel disks can be constructed to demonstrate all conceivable Picard numbers through the identification and computation of relevant algebraic numbers derived from Lefschetz-type formulas and their corresponding residues.

A supergravity unified framework neutralino is proposed as a plausible candidate for dark matter, where a long-lived neutralino decays into the hidden sector's lightest supersymmetric particle, exceeding the age of the universe. We introduce an extension to the MSSM/SUGRA model with a $U(1)_{X_1} \times U(1)_{X_2}$ hidden sector gauge sector, where the hidden sector neutralino is lighter than its visible counterpart, leading to a loop-suppressed radiative decay process. The computation demonstrates that the visible sector neutralino can decay with a lifetime greater than the age of the universe. The detectability of this scenario lies in the indirect observation of a signature decay product and direct detection of the neutralino in the form of events occurring at the same time, simultaneously satisfying experimental constraints, resulting in a gamma ray spectrum characterized by an energy-dependent non-thermal excess at energies around the decay energy, increasing towards higher energies due to a thermal peak in the spectrum. The hidden sector neutralino is likely to be the lightest supersymmetric particle, making it resistant to direct detection, whereas its presence can be inferred through its indirect effects on the visible sector neutralino's relic density. The proposed model is compatible with various experimental bounds and its features enable a natural realization of dark matter with a long-lived neutralino as a decay product, characterized by an increasing gamma ray excess with energy, potentially detectable through future gamma ray observations at space-based instruments like the

The main contributors to the theory of parametric integer partitioning, a complex field of study, have made significant breakthroughs in finding efficient algorithms for solving certain problems within it under certain conditions. Despite these advances, developing efficient algorithms for the key problem of finding a polynomial approximation in genus was an unresolved issue until now, with previous methods only able to achieve linear time complexity. This paper introduces a new algorithm that runs in linear time and is able to approximate the genus of any given dense graph accurately.

A stochastic Newton algorithm for distributed convex optimization tasks is proposed, which utilizes individual machine capabilities to calculate gradient and Hessian-vector products for the same shared objective between communication intervals, significantly minimizing required communication rounds. Convergence analysis and performance preservation are demonstrated for quasi-self-concordant objectives like logistic regression, backed by empirical results.

Our approach to training a neural network to identify hate-speech in Hindi and Bengali is outlined in this work. We investigate the viability of leveraging transfer learning for these languages due to their shared origin, which lends them a degree of similarity. Our experiment's implementation on low-powered hardware yields results that hold up against those of more costly models, a noteworthy finding. Additionally, given the limited training data and our unfamiliarity with these languages, our study represents an attempt to decipher languages often shrouded in mystery.

In nuclear and particle physics, being able to identify the direction of nuclear recoils is a significant advantage. This capability, achievable at low energies, could help verify that a dark matter signal originates from space, surpass the neutrino floor, or distinguish between various neutrino sources. With sufficient readout detail, such as when employing micro-pattern gaseous detectors, Time Projection Chambers can allow directional recoil detection. The main issue with these detectors is identifying and eliminating background electron recoils triggered by gamma rays from radioactive substances within the detector and surroundings. We created new indicators that can tell electron and nuclear recoils apart at keV-level energies by using simulated ionization topologies. Our simulation shows that these indicators perform significantly better than the traditionally used dE/dx discriminant, offering up to three times greater differentiation. Additionally, these new indicators remain effective even at lower spatial resolutions while maintaining some extra discrimination benefit when the spatial detail improves.

A comprehensive analysis of commercial driving behavior requires considering various personal characteristics and environmental influences that vehicle sensors may not be able to detect. For a more accurate and fair evaluation of drivers, it is crucial to incorporate additional information about their behaviors, assessed by experts, alongside sensor data. However, relying solely on expert assessment is insufficient as it is impractical and costly to collect extensive expert input. Therefore, machine learning models are necessary to create a more robust and efficient decision-support tool that can learn when to trust experts and sensor data, and when to consult them. This study involves developing such a model, utilizing a large dataset that combines driver and passenger behavior footage, along with driver feedback and domain expert assessments, collected via built-in vehicle cameras, driver feedback, and subsequent employee reviews. Our model effectively moderates expert and sensor inputs to create a more comprehensive decision-making tool that maximizes fairness, efficiency, and user satisfaction.

This paper reports on the findings from the 2022 Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) challenge.
The competition highlighted an underinvestigated area in Optical Character Recognition (OCR) technology: accurately reading previously unseen text in real-world scenarios. As such, a benchmark was established to measure OOV performance and the difference in recognition quality between previously seen and never seen characters. For the first time, the OOV challenge brought together a community of researchers from the OCR field to develop more sophisticated algorithms that can adapt to unseen characters quickly and efficiently. The OOV challenge sparked a wide range of innovative solutions and the majority of participants shared their results through published papers. The challenge also brought together a collection of 13 diverse datasets that featured script varieties such as Asian languages, languages with non-Latin alphabets, and languages with significant variation in vocabulary, including languages with large dictionaries. These diverse datasets were used to test a range of tasks including data augmentation, character-level training, and automatic text correction in a single system. The OOV challenge also brought to the forefront a community-level approach to tackle the long-standing issue of never-seen characters in OCR technology. The success of the OOV challenge has paved the way for a community-wide approach to tackle the issue of never-seen characters in OCR technology in a more collaborative and inclusive manner. The results and information from the OOV challenge can be found at the official challenge website located at https://outofvocab.github.io/.

Random fields in mathematical physics play a major role in understanding the characteristics of a system's probabilistic behavior in small and correlated samples. These fields are particularly relevant in physical systems with disorders, where their properties need to be described in terms of complex geometric patterns. To tackle this, a new approach is introduced that utilizes geometric concepts to analyze the dynamics of random fields, including their connection to random motions within complex structures. This methodology is employed to investigate the geodesic curves in the statistical manifolds of these fields, with specific applications to the study of Brownian motion on these curves. Ultimately, this framework is used to derive geometric interpretations of and a link between random field correlations and the Ricci curvature of the underlying structure. These findings are illustrated through a collection of relevant examples.
In our research, we conduct experiments on Rayleigh-Taylor Instability by introducing a controlled disturbance through magnetic levitation technology.

For a cuspidal Hecke eigenform $F$ attached to the symplectic group $Sp_n(Z)$ and a Dirichlet character $\chi$, we examine the standard twisted L-function, $L(s,F,\chi,St)$, and show that its algebraic component at critical point $m$ has bounded denominators as $\chi$ changes. This work refines a previous finding of Boecherer. A similar result also holds for the product of Hecke L-functions of primitive forms from the special linear group $SL_2(Z)$.

In a tight binding model using the non-equilibrium Green's functions formalism, researchers explored how spin-dependent transport behaves in armchair graphene nanoribbons with ferromagnetic gate control. The investigation delved into conductance and spin polarization oscillations caused by varying barrier heights, which can be regulated with gate voltages, in addition to analyzing the effects of varying widths on the band gap and contact nature. The results show spin polarization oscillates more intensely in nanoribbons with wider band gaps compared to graphene nanoribbons with the same hopping parameters. The differing band gaps lead to varying energy band alignments, resulting in normal, Andreev, and quasi-normal conductance states. The spin polarization also exhibits a greater variation in low energy regimes, where the band gap is larger. These properties make these structures suitable for spin-based electronic devices.

This paper presents proofs of Korovkin theorem analogues in the realm of weakly nonlinear, monotone operators applied to multi-variable Banach lattices of functions. Our study encompasses the almost everywhere convergence, convergence in measure, and $L^{p}$-norm convergence. The discussion is supplemented by several examples that demonstrate the theoretical findings.

A graph on n vertices is called pancyclic if it contains a cycle of every possible length from 3 to n. In 1972, Erdos demonstrated that a graph on n vertices with n larger than 4k to the fourth power and an independence number of k will always contain all cycles. After his findings, he suggested the independence number squared value should also be sufficient for this, later proven otherwise by subsequent results and further improved upon by the presented work which now shows that there exists a constant c, that n being larger than ck to the 7/3 power guarantees a pancyclic structure.

The trajectory of light particles created in gold-gold, ruthenium-ruthenium, and zirconium-zirconium collisions at a specific energy level of 200 GeV has been studied in this research. This study utilized the CLVisc model to examine the development of uneven energy density, pressure variations, and radial movement along a specific axis, finding significant relationships among these elements. By comparing data on specific particles to laboratory collisions, researchers discovered that an initial medium imbalance is a primary driver of light particles' trajectory. The uneven initial medium creates opposite forces depending on impact point and rapidity direction, causing a negative relationship between QGP flow and rapidity, which in turn influences directed flow characteristics. Furthermore, the investigation showed that the nuclear shape has little to no effect on the directed flow behavior of light particles.

The adaptive spectral Koopman method was designed to solve complex autonomous dynamical systems that serve as the groundwork for numerous applications across diverse scientific and engineering fields. However, the Koopman formulation introduces an issue with a time-dependent tensor that requires expensive computation in high-dimensional spaces. This limitation severely restricts the method's usability for systems with high dimensionalities. To overcome this problem, we developed the sparse-grid-based adaptive spectral Koopman method (SKM) by incorporating Smolyak's technique to break down high-dimensional tensor computations into more manageable tensor components of lower dimensions. Furthermore, we employed the tensor train adaptation scheme to dynamically adjust the tensor-structured data to accommodate rapidly changing systems. By combining these two techniques, SKM significantly reduces computational complexity while preserving accuracy. This method's efficacy was demonstrated through numerical simulations of two complex systems: the Mackey-Glass time series and the solar surface magnetogram.

This review provides an overview of quantum mechanics history with a specific focus on addressing the theoretical difficulties in explaining ionization within the framework of quantum mechanics. The fundamental principles of resonance theory are then explored, and the exterior complex scaling method for extracting resonance parameters through the Schrodinger equation are comprehensively explained. The nonHermitian operator formulation is also a notably straightforward and comprehensive approach to tackle the topic, and in this review, it is applied to describe resonance states in atoms and molecules subjected to extreme electromagnetic environments.

The Sinkhorn algorithm remains a widely-used solution to the Schrödinger problem. While it's well-documented that this algorithm converges when a solution exists, a linear convergence rate is achieved only if both the solution and the reference coupling have the same support. Considering that structured stochastic processes may result in degenerate situations where the solution does not exist, research demonstrates that even in such situations, the Sinkhorn algorithm leads to two specific points of convergence. Crucially, these limiting points enable the calculation of a solution to a more relaxed version of the original problem. The relaxed version can be thought of as the result of replacing the original problem's marginal constraints with marginal penalizations in a related problem. As a result of these findings, a new theoretical framework has been established that connects the original problem to this related relaxation, allowing for the quantification of a gap between them. Additionally, numerical experiments illustrate a substantial improvement in the ability to find a solution to the original problem when starting from a reference coupling with a marginal constraint relaxation, compared to using unregularized data without marginal constraints.

The ATLAS experiment at the LHC recorded data of 257 pb-1 in proton-proton collisions at a 5.02 TeV centre-of-mass energy in 2017, which is utilized to determine the t¯t cross-section. The measurement involves both dilepton and single-lepton t¯t final states and yields a combined result. The calculated t¯t cross-section has a total uncertainty of 3.9% and amounts to 67.5 pb, which corresponds to 0.9 pb (statistical) ± 2.3 pb (syst. error) ± 1.1 pb (lumi.) ± 0.2 pb (beam). This outcome is consistent with theoretical quantum chromodynamic predictions and offers constraints on the proton's parton distribution functions at large Bjorken-x.

It's logical to assume that the characteristics of a surrounding system or environment would influence the behavior of its core element. Researchers have recently explored this relationship in the context of central spin models, specifically when interacting with a hyperfine-tuned nucleus, to comprehend the phenomenon of spin flip relaxation. This study reveals the distinct stages of localization during a spin relaxation process that occurs due to an irregularly fluctuating environment. Our investigation specifically focuses on a central spin model coupled to a hyperfine-tuned nucleus in an applied magnetic field, and we analyze the model's response to various types of environmental fluctuations. We have identified and described two distinct forms of localization - an initial form associated with relaxation triggered by fluctuations and a later form resulting from self-interference within the central spin model. Additionally, our study shows that the duration and intensity of these forms of localization vary significantly in response to different types of environmental fluctuations. This distinction becomes particularly apparent when comparing the model's response to correlated versus uncorrelated fluctuations and to fluctuations following a Lorentzian and a power-law decay.

The conditions on $A$, $B$, $p$, $b$, and $c$ are specified that guarantee 
${u}_{p,b,c}(z)$ meets the requirement ${u}_{p,b,c}(z) \prec (1+Az)/(1+Bz)$. This yields conditions 
for $(-4\kappa/c)({u}_{p,b,c}(z)-1)$, $c \neq 0$, to be close to 1 in a part of the complex plane 
and for ${u}_{p,b,c}(z)$ to be close to 1 in a part of the complex plane when $c = 0$. 
The conditions are more extensive than those for ${u}_{p,b,c}(z)$ to be within the Janowski class.

Urban settings are known to benefit economically and socially due to their diversity of physical and social interactions, which also contribute to community resilience. However, COVID-19-related mobility restrictions significantly reduced urban face-to-face interactions, prompting concerns about their lasting social effects. To explore these changes, this study uses a vast dataset containing one million anonymized users in four major US cities, spanning pre-pandemic to post-pandemic periods. By examining users' diversity of encounters, it reveals a significant decline in urban diversity of encounters during the pandemic. Furthermore, it finds that individuals who adhered to pandemic guidelines experienced a decrease in their income diversity of encounters. Ultimately, this research implies that urban diversification of encounters may be temporary, as cities return to normal after the pandemic, but only if there is a return to pre-pandemic social patterns.

This research project focuses on the advancement of a nonlinear field-split
preconditioner comprising two stages to expedite convergence of complex two-phase
fluid dynamics and transport within diverse porous media. A proposed algorithm,
Field-Split BDDC, offers an efficient method to split domains and communicate data
between individual sub-domains, ultimately facilitating faster convergence rates.
Through in-depth analysis, our approach outperforms alternative preconditioners
such as the Linear Schur Complement and Balanced Nearest Neighbor preconditioners
by achieving significantly reduced convergence times with increasingly complex
models, specifically up to 4.7 times faster convergence rates. This research's
impact is further highlighted by demonstrating its relevance to realistic models
of oil reservoir simulation.

The property of chirality exists ubiquitously in various sizes of geometric patterns - ranging from organic life forms to DNA and proteins - across different scales. Chiral matter responds to chiral light with specific polarization properties that allow for the identification and separation of enantiomers within molecular pairs. Developing an optical cavity capable of efficiently interacting with one chiral form of a molecule while rejecting its opposite form is a highly sought-after application in various fields. We successfully designed and created a chiral optical cavity that only supports waves with a specific polarization, effectively excluding the opposing polarization state. As a result, this allows for enhanced interactions between this polarization state and chiral matter, while suppressing the opposite polarization, opening up potential applications in emerald city construction and high-precision measurements of chirality.

This paper examines the connection between Jackiw-Teitelboim gravity on anti de-Sitter spaces and a semi-classical limit of two-dimensional string theory, with c less than 1. We observe that the world-sheet theory of this string theory, comprising a space-like Liouville CFT and a time-like non-rational CFT, exhibits actions and partition functions matching those of the JT gravity model. This match, significantly influenced by boundary actions, extends to annulus amplitudes. We explore this connection further by demonstrating that the boundary of the JT gravity model is associated with a non-rational CFT possessing a specific operator algebra. This property reveals that the JT gravity model possesses an inherent, string-theoretic interpretation of boundary actions and partition functions.

A spacetime distortion, or warp bubble, generated by the Alcubierre metric can enable massive objects to achieve global speeds faster than light. This phenomenon arises due to the spacetime contraction occurring in the region behind the warp bubble, necessitating an enormous amount of exotic matter to sustain it. In 2017, a proposal was made to achieve similar warp bubble effects using ordinary matter under specific conditions, through the Generalized Einstein's Field Equations. This proposal was further refined to ordinary matter in this paper, applying the birkhoff theorem, which reveals that ordinary matter is able to sustain the warp drive configuration in the presence of the cosmological constant without requiring exotic matter. However, this outcome comes with the restriction that pressure must surpass density in ordinary matter.

As urban cities' aging underground infrastructure systems require growing upkeep, cities are faced with the challenge of coordinating maintenance, predicting and resolving issues, and fulfilling their goal of becoming smart cities due to limited infrastructure data availability. To alleviate this issue, cities need a unified approach to collect, organize, provide, and use infrastructure data across various applications. To address this problem, we introduce GUIDES, a framework for coordinating maintenance and data dissemination in underground infrastructure systems, encompassing APIs and web services, and specific implementations for sewer infrastructure. Our solutions allow for efficient data dissemination to various applications using different queries, resulting in reduced data storage needs and improved efficiency. We evaluated GUIDES's effectiveness in maintaining infrastructure data databases and providing seamless access to users, and our extensive case studies demonstrate GUIDES's potential for smart cities realization.

To analyze the center-of-mass motion of hundreds of $^9$Be$^+$ ions, arranged in a two-dimensional Wigner crystal, we utilized the interaction between optical dipoles and the ions' spin, enabling the characterization of their transverse movement. This was done by comparing the experimentally measured effects on spin dephasing with theoretical predictions, resulting in accurate estimations of temperature levels consistent with the ions' initial cooling processes. The experimentally determined temperatures, including both peak and average temperatures, were found to be in good agreement with the expected outcomes. The study's results are notable as they demonstrate that the interaction between optical dipoles can be utilized to examine the thermal behavior of complex ion structures, providing a potential method for evaluating motional-state distributions and mode temperatures. The experiment also set boundaries on the rate at which these ions experience external heating, matching theoretical expectations for the effects of systematic vibrations, though it remains possible that some unseen form of noise contributes to this bound.

TERS is an essential technique for analyzing surfaces with subnanometer resolution. Yet, accurately simulating specific TERS signals is computationally difficult. Our innovative method combines the primary factors driving TERS signals, which are electromagnetic interactions between a Tip and a sample, and chemical bonding between the Tip and the sample. This approach, rooted in first-principles quantum mechanics, allows us to assess various factors in detailed simulations. These encompass radial and angular distributions of signals, distinct optical properties of TERS, and distinct chemical interactions between TERS components. This new framework replaces previous approximations, which relied on the non-equivalent 'electrodynamic' approximation and the classical van der Waals model. In our study, we demonstrated that the van der Waals model underestimates the intensity of specific Raman signals by as much as an order of magnitude. Conversely, the 'electrodynamical' correction has a minimal impact on Raman signals but is crucial for other types of electromagnetic signals. Our simulations also highlight the considerable impact of specific chemical interactions on Raman signals, particularly when compared to van der Waals interactions. This new framework enables us to thoroughly examine and predict the underlying mechanisms of TERS, contributing to a deeper comprehension of this technique. Furthermore, the methodology employed here can be used to develop a general strategy for the interpretation and prediction of various local spectroscopic methods.

We used the 64-m Sardinia Radio Telescope to study the emission of nearby galaxies in the K band. Our goal was to identify magnetic dust emission common to cosmic microwave background observations, known as Anomalous Microwave Emission. We obtained Sardinia Radio Telescope data alongside previously collected ALMA and ATCA data, and our findings indicate that two galaxies, Mrk 348 and NGC 2798, showed no signs of AME. When we compared our non-thermal radio flux estimates to the values obtained using ATCA and ALMA, we found them to be comparable. However, we did notice that our Sardinia Radio Telescope data yielded lower levels of variability in the non-thermal radio flux relative to the values obtained with ATCA and ALMA. This is attributed to differences in resolution and dynamic range.

Ammonium sulfate's seemingly uncomplicated ferroelectric transition in spite of its widespread use, is actually the result of a complex series of events involving structural changes within the material. Initially, the ammonium ions' orientation in the material triggers a phase transition that leads to discrepancies in the way the material's crystal lattice expands when heated. Eventually, these discrepancies cause a significant increase in entropy associated with the material's transition. Researchers discovered a complex series of events involved in the material's transition through high-resolution imaging and computational modeling and this understanding has implications for the development of more efficient temperature-sensitive materials.

In probabilistic learning, organisms sometimes opt for a less than optimal strategy known as probability-matching, which means choosing options based on their reward probabilities, as opposed to the optimal strategy, maximization, which involves consistently selecting the option with the highest reward.  Despite years of study, the factors leading to probability-matching are still unclear and an interesting aspect is the similarity between this and maximization at a brain level.  We provide evidence that explains a part of the likelihood-matching phenomenon and also shows that an individual's tendency to likelihood-multiply, which is a step towards learning, is similar to their tendency to maximize expectations of reward.  We found that people who demonstrate a strong maximization phenotype are more likely to have a stronger brain signal at the ventral tegmental area in response to positive outcomes.  We found this to be the case whether or not the participants received a variable reward, which suggests that the ventral tegmental area's response to positive outcomes contributes to phenotypic differences in probability-matching.

A proposed Witting configuration, with a different complexity of 40 rays, could reformulate the Penrose model for spin-3/2 systems based on a dodecahedron's geometry, to explain quantum entanglement and contextuality. An alternative setup, using 120 rays and 30 triangles from a simplified E8 complex, might offer a more comprehensive understanding of these quantum phenomena. We describe both arrangements and suggest that they could lead to new Penrose-like models, which might help us experimentally study the mentioned quantum principles.

The continuous Fréchet distance c-approximate near neighbor problem involves precomputing a data structure that efficiently finds closest polygonal curves within a certain radius from query curves, considering an approximation factor for potential inaccuracies. This study primarily investigates this problem using time series curves, providing comprehensive analysis for the first time with rigorous lower and upper bounds. Specifically, it develops a novel algorithm combining the Rabin-Kreps-Welch distance and quantization techniques, achieving significant results including logarithmic query times, linear storage, and logarithmic preprocessing costs. In contrast, it also establishes strict lower bounds based on existing computational limitations, taking into account the complexity of comparisons involved.

To mitigate systematic measurement errors on quantum computers, current methods employ counteractive postprocessing techniques known as measurement error mitigation (MEM). A key limitation of these techniques is the tradeoff between scalability and validity: methods that handle large datasets effectively can only guarantee the presence of certain errors, whereas those that work with specific error types are not suitable for large-scale experiments. To address this challenge, researchers introduced the scalable measurement error mitigation (SMEM) scheme, an iterative approach that unfolds the measurement distribution, upscaling it with each iteration to tackle an increasingly wide range of errors. It's claimed that SMEM can mitigate a wide range of errors, specifically up to $2^n - 2$ error types for any given $n$-qubit system, without relying on assumptions about specific error conditions. Furthermore, it's claimed that SMEM can outperform current methods in terms of both scalability and compatibility, with prospects for efficient implementation within existing quantum software. An experimental implementation on superconducting quantum processors showed that SMEM could correctly compute two-qubit correlation functions even with multiple noisy qubits, achieving a high fidelity of around 95%. Notably, researchers demonstrated SMEM's ability to correct a specific type of noise on a specialized processor, using 12 qubits, which is an advancement over existing methods. They also explored the potential for partial measurement to accelerate computations, a feature closely related to variational quantum algorithms.

When humans operate robot arms, it is frequently necessary for the robot to interpret their intentions and adjust its movement to accomplish the task efficiently. However, if the robot inaccurately interprets the human's goals, its movement may conflict with their original understanding, resulting in a communication breakdown. In particular studies examining synergetic control found that explicit negotiation of task objectives is needed to prevent such communication conflicts. Within a pick-and-place task, our research discovered that utilizing a simple task-convention-based method enabled shared control and resulted in an effective exchange of control between human and robot, while encouraging new learning and improving the quality of the robot's action execution. Furthermore, the convention also facilitated detection of the human's intended goals, thus providing valuable feedback to inform robotic system design and promoting an effective collaborative user experience.

For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, an effective mapping system that automatically constructs and maintains a spatial map of their surroundings is crucial, taking into account that the actual environment may significantly diverge from their anticipated setting. Traditional mapping techniques often assume a predictable environment, which can result in poor performance or failure in unfamiliar settings. Given that existing information on the environment's layout typically diminishes over time due to changing locations, an autonomous system requires a map that combines both local and global spatial data, alongside an understanding of how these components interact. Notably, purely metric representations of these maps fail to provide sufficient insight into the global structure, whereas topological maps, focusing on spatial relationships, are better suited for adaptive navigation in unfamiliar environments. Nonetheless, existing topological maps are incapable of supporting global planning, prompting our proposal of a new hierarchical topological map representation (HITMAP). HITMAP addresses these limitations in several ways. Firstly, it divides the map into manageable sections, allowing for efficient updates in the face of spatial uncertainty. Secondly, it introduces a global graph, representing the layout of the environment as a whole, thus facilitating global understanding and planning, not bound by local spatial data limitations. Thirdly, it integrates a metric graph, incorporating estimates of distances and connectivity between landmarks, thereby providing a more precise representation of the environment's layout. HITMAP has been implemented as a component of an existing navigation system, with results demonstrating HITMAP's capability to construct and maintain a usable map, showcasing its

Research focuses on developing two-dimensional zero-complementary array code sets with desirable properties such as unity amplitude and zero cross-correlation values, which can be applied to two-dimensional linear codes and systems, including 2-D biorthogonal codes. A new method is proposed to create such code sets, starting with inter-group complementary code sets, and a specific example is given in this context. The given example includes 16x16 size arrays, consisting of 16x4 partial codes, and 16x12 complete codes, along with 225 zero cross-correlation values. Additionally, 16x16 size arrays, comprising 16x8 partial codes, and 16x8 zero cross-correlation values, are constructed using this method. Furthermore, a general formula derived from this construction is valid within the scope of Boolean algebra.

Computed Tomography (CT) is extensively utilized in both engineering and medical fields for creating detailed images of internal structures within various subjects and objects. Since most X-ray sources emit X-rays of multiple energy levels, which interact with materials at varying rates, the process of reconstructing images from a few energy-level data can also help distinguish materials based on density and detect background noise. In a typical process, we consider a limited range of X-ray energy levels, which are typically determined by a technology constraint. The image reconstruction problem, further complicated by the effects of sensor noise, is addressed in this study. An innovative, non-convex variational-based formulation is proposed, which effectively combines image reconstruction, sensor denoising, and material data analysis. The method takes into account differences between raw and noise-free sensor data, and relies on a new Bregman Bregman alternating linearization algorithm to solve the resulting non-convex optimization problem. The method is tested using numerical simulations of a variety of scenarios.

We investigate how electron spillover and nonlocal behavior affect light propagation between two adjacent metallic areas and compare this to a quantum hydrodynamics model. We demonstrate that a quantum hydrodynamics model which incorporates both phenomena yields accurate results, particularly as the gap narrows, in contrast to a local response model which generates unappealing results such as divergent fields and excessive energy losses. Notably, the desirable results obtained from the hydrodynamics model can also be achieved with a simple local approach that excludes the spillover and conventional Thomas-Fermi approximation by considering an equivalent reduced gap size.

In this research, we investigate the user's part in Contextual Named Entity Retrieval (CNER), revealing (1) that humans outperform automated methods in pinpointing context-sensitive terms, and (2) that enhanced results can be achieved when users also specify the relative significance of those terms. Although CNER bears some resemblance to related concepts such as List Question answering and Entity disambiguation, its primary goal is to gather user feedback to dynamically construct a class of entity profiles and leverage this data for extracting entities from untagged text. Our focus in CNER involves using this user feedback to teach a model to locate relevant entities without manual supervision. Our experiments, conducted on both a manufactured and a real-world dataset, prove that incorporating user-specified term importance yields a substantial boost in CNER precision and F1 scores.

Time-based data refers to information measured against the backdrop of time, giving it a distinct structural context that forms the foundation of its constituent parts. When dealing with multi-variable data sets, we often see temporal observations interwoven to create complex patterns, making them rich in meaningful content. Despite this richness, analyzing such data can be challenging due to the difficulties presented by its very nature, particularly when attempting to visualize it effectively. Consequently, much of the analytically focused software tools fail to incorporate intuitive visual representations, leaving users unguided and unhelpful support for exploratory analysis. As an alternative solution, we've developed novel visual display methods, specifically designed for interactive exploration of long-term data sets and multivariate time series. By combining dynamic, non-linear encoding techniques with non-visual cues, we've created innovative approaches for visualizing temporal and longitudinal data. These novel methods facilitate deeper, more in-depth analysis and understanding of the underlying data through interactive exploration, while retaining the ability to scale for real-time visualization.

Electronic health records, deficient in sensor data, are unable to generate predictive models.  This issue is more severe in hospitals with limited resources, struggling to implement new technologies.  This study addresses this problem by developing a novel graph neural network approach that translates single-patient EHR data into predictive models.  To achieve this, a heterogeneous graph similarity measure is employed to integrate multiple EHR data sources.  A new GNN framework called R-SAGNN, consisting of similarity measurement, local aggregation, and global aggregation layers, has been introduced.  This model leverages graph convolution networks to extract features from non-target nodes, ultimately using these features to supplement the prediction of the target node with additional information.  Experimental results validate the efficacy of R-SAGNN, demonstrating superior performance compared to existing methods on EHR datasets.  Specifically, the model achieves accurate predictive outcomes for patients from hospitals equipped with limited hardware.

Using a mean-field approach and considering both non-uniform particle sizes and solvent effects, we model a electric double layer (EDL) with a non-uniform charge distribution at its surface. Solvent effects are accounted for through Debye-Huckel theory and a modified version of the Poisson- Boltzmann equation is used to obtain the final results. The study examines how solvent polarization impacts EDL characteristics and demonstrates that solvent effects have a significant impact, particularly at low electrolyte concentrations. The research also employs a soft particle model with a charge density that gradually decreases from the particle's edge towards its interior. This model considers both the electrostatic potential and charge density within the particle to be finite at its edge. By applying the balance condition for electrostatic potential at the particle's edge, we ensure that both quantities are continuous. The research illustrates that solvent polarization leads to a non-uniform charge distribution within the particle. A comparative analysis with other models is also conducted to assess their validity.

Automating the labor-intensive and error-prone process of extracting requirements from unstructured text is a highly recommended goal for many researchers. To this end, we annotated a unique dataset, PURE, and leveraged the strengths of BERT, a cutting-edge language model, to navigate the complexities of the annotated data. Through our experiments, we refined multiple BERT-based approaches and assessed their efficacy using the PURE dataset. Additionally, we explored the challenges posed by domain-specific glossaries and terminal syntactic variations that often hindered the models' performance. To mitigate these obstacles, we experimented with incorporating standardized glossaries into the models and addressed the lexical discrepancies by combining the capabilities of rephrasing and word replacement techniques.

This research investigates the energy efficiency in a multi-user, multi-relay communication system with a maximum diversity network coding technique. The system scheduling and relay selection, as well as power allocation, are jointly optimized to maximize energy efficiency through a non-convex optimization problem that is reformed and solved using the blockwise coordinate descent and dual decomposition methods. The proposed solution offers optimal performance and is validated by a comprehensive analysis which compares its performance to a lower bound and an alternative approach that ignores scheduling, resulting in a potential loss of approximately 30% in energy efficiency. Furthermore, a combination of the proposed solution and a matching algorithm, which ensures equal throughput among users, helps to eliminate throughput disparities between users, resulting in a notable improvement of 10% in energy efficiency.

A comprehensive theoretical study of magnetic impurities on a niobium surface is conducted, focusing on insulating niobium and incorporating the effects of spin-orbit coupling and relativistic electrons in the substrate. The analysis begins by examining an Mn adatom on a niobium surface, revealing the existence of multiple bound states near the Fermi energy and identifying them as Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states localized at the impurity site. Based on this understanding, the bound states associated with a Mn dimer on a niobium surface are investigated, and the results are compared to experimental findings. The study demonstrates that a magnetic impurity pair on a niobium surface exhibits a weakly interacting double-spin impurity, characterized by two localized Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states associated with each magnetic moment. The bound states associated with this double impurity lie near the Fermi energy and display distinct dependencies on the electron filling. The study also considers the variation in niobium magnetic coupling to the impurity, including the effects of strong and weak coupling regimes. The results are compared to experimental data on an Mn dimer on a niobium surface, yielding a magnetic coupling value of approximately 0.65 eV and highlighting the need for an intermediate coupling theory. Lastly, the study considers an Mn dimer on a niobium surface in a non-local spin-orbit coupling environment, revealing a need for accurate relativistic and spin-orbit treatment in interpreting experimental results.

Techniques such as the Normal Distributions Transform (NDT) can efficiently register and accurately bound point cloud errors for scenes without moving objects.  However, traditional methods struggle in scenes where there are changes in view.  To improve point cloud registration for dynamic scenes, deep learning-based approaches have shown potential.  Despite their accuracy, deep learning-based solutions often provide little insight, which is a safety concern.  To bridge this gap, our paper introduces an approach that involves selectively removing portions of the point cloud with inconsistencies, using local network estimates to identify potential registration errors and suppress points that disagree with point cloud transforms in those areas, leading to improved registration results, with significant accuracy benefits for scenes featuring dense foliage and other challenges to traditional methods.

Satellite images are widely employed across multiple sectors, including agricultural monitoring, navigation, and urban planning, yet their potential is limited by the large amounts of data required to train deep learning models, and the need for access to recent, large-dataset-annotated images that can be trained on a standard GPU. Our solution involves the use of Canny edge detection, combined with sigma filter-based noise removal, followed by a Sobel operator-based estimate of the interior of buildings. This approach is straightforward and doesn't necessitate significant computational power or a vast storage capacity, thus enabling faster processing and reduced storage needs. Furthermore, since our method is based on established algorithms whose behavior is extensively documented, it is less susceptible to unexpected errors. When comparing the performance of our technique against other deep learning methods on a monitoring task, the outcome showed that although the edge detection was less precise than that of the best deep learning model in our analysis, the interior building area estimates were similarly accurate in most instances, resulting in comparable monitoring performance for the two methods.

The valence-band electrons' resonance interaction with the central absorbing atom's electrons during a soft X-ray absorption experiment induces a complex state shaped by competing processes. This multicomponent state evolves over time due to a balance between absorption and decay mechanisms. In this work, we develop a mathematical equation describing the absorber's electronic state as it undergoes a transition from a initial state to a final state over a period dictated by the X-ray fluence. The equation incorporates both radiative and autoionization decay rates that have a measurable dependence on the final state population. This model is applied to explain the observed broadening of a resonance in the L-edge absorption spectrum of a Cr single crystal, revealing that both decay mechanisms play a significant role. However, we observe that radiative decay dominates the initial stages of the decay process, whereas autoionization decay becomes more influential at later decay stages characterized by multi-excited final states. Ultimately, we examine how a model-based rate equation can be utilized to extract the fundamental electronic relaxation times of the absorber system.

The application of a Deep Neural Network in Automatic Modulation Classification (AMC) exhibits enhanced performance compared to traditional methods even in harsh wireless environments, but this can be compromised by targeted adversarial attacks that inject noise into wireless channels. This paper presents a new method based on a generative adversarial network (GAN) designed to mitigate the effects of such attacks by removing malicious interference before feeding data into a DNN-based classifier. The proposed approach by contrast to existing counter-measures does not rely on training, making it more efficient. Furthermore, this method has been proven to improve the resilience of existing DNN-based AMC models against adversarial attacks.

Segmentation of Multiple Sclerosis lesions is an issue that experts struggle with.
Recent studies propose using artificial intelligence-based techniques but most
methods are one-dimensional as they rely on a single, large dataset, which is
not adaptable. A more effective approach would be for the model to continuously
learn and improve its ability to identify lesion characteristics as it is exposed
to datasets from different hospitals sequentially. We have developed a new
architecture that allows the model to adapt with each new dataset it encounters
and we compare it to existing methods that train from scratch. Our experiments
involve training the model on sequential hospital datasets and we measure its
performance against a wide range of datasets from 13 hospitals. Our results
indicate that training the model to adapt continuously leads to better results than
training it on a single dataset or starting from scratch. Additionally, using the
model's underlying mechanism, we are able to evaluate the impact of individual
datasets on the model's performance and identify patterns and characteristics of
lesions that the model has learned.

A novel type of metric comparison analogous to Alexandrov comparison is presented, 
and its relationship to optimal transport between measures on a Riemannian manifold 
is demonstrated, specifically with respect to the MTW condition proposed by Xi-Nan 
Ma, Neil Trudinger and Xu-Jia Wang, involving a notion of continuity.

Many scientific models, particularly in geophysical contexts, experience inaccuracies due to simplifications like approximating complex processes or omitting non-linear components. Although some of these omissions are currently accounted for in a qualitative manner by experts with considerable experience, this understanding is largely verbal and isn't formally incorporated into the models.
